#3542. Deborah Nevins—a Legend of Landscape Architecture—Plants With Purpose

When my partner and I were starting a family, we searched high and low for a place outside New York where we could imagine our future children growing up. We looked upstate, in Connecticut, and at all those charming hamlets strung along the eastern end of Long Island known as the Hamptons. Toured hundreds of houses, clicked thousands of listings. But not one felt like home.

It looked like something out of a medieval fairy tale. A great furrowed trunk rising from a froth of flowering vines that split into enormous limbs sweeping improbably far across the garden. Its arrangement was so baroque—veiny, muscular wood twisting and reaching, dissolving overhead into a canopy of green delicacy. We could picture our children climbing its winding branches, little hands against its ridged, mossy bark.

Our twins’ arrival was imminent, so we made an offer in February, closed in April, and brought home babies Grace and Noah on Memorial Day weekend. Now we joke that we didn’t buy a house—we bought this tree.

But what is it? A butternut tree? An oak? A black walnut? Deborah Nevins, one of the most revered living landscape designers, created this garden for the previous owners in 2004. In the fall, she invited me to her white-shingled cottage in Springs, East Hampton, to find out. Her living room has triple-hung windows like those in Monticello, Thomas Jefferson’s house in Virginia, which go down to the floor so it’s easy to wheel in her potted lemon trees when the seasons change. “Winter is divine; it’s when they bloom,” she coos. “The house smells of lemon blossoms.”

David Geffen’s pool at his former Beverly Hills estate, once home to Warner Bros.’ Jack Warner.

“Butternut!” she declares, slamming the book shut with all the force of her petite five-foot-nothing frame. “For sure.”

This is our tree. A butternut that likely sprouted generations before she came along. “It’s a native tree, probably a hundred years old. But I’d have to know the caliper—the diameter about a foot up—to be more precise.” She decided it’d be the anchor for our yard design the moment she saw it—existing mature trees are “sacred” and must be preserved at all costs. At its base, she dared to plant clematis, usually a climbing vine, that now rambles across the ground, softening the old tree’s trunk with a tangle of flowers. The butternut divides the rest of the property into distinct passages, including an ornamental reflecting pool bordered by hornbeam hedges, a lap pool shaded under locust trees, and a gravel path lined with rounded boxwoods.

GREEK MYTHOLOGY It took Nevins eight years and some 20 trips to Greece to complete her collaboration with architect Renzo Piano on the Stavros Niarchos Foundation Cultural Center. What was once a parking lot is now planted with more than 1,500 trees, 128,000 shrubs and perennials, and 164,000 grass plugs.

A rendering of the 40-acre park at the Stavros Niarchos Foundation Cultural Center in Athens.

To Nevins, the tree is an excellent example of her greater gardening philosophy: “I’m interested in creating unfolding spaces which intensify [the viewers’] experience, your sense of place and movement through a garden,” she says. She frequently builds hedges and allées to control viewers’ attention, like horse blinders. “Not every aspect of the garden is seen at once. You have to stop and think.”

Over the last four decades, Nevins has been entrusted with the grounds of some extraordinary spaces. Her clients include media mogul David Geffen, fashion designer Tommy Hilfiger, former Disney chairman Michael Eisner, and hotelier Ian Schrager. Commissions can range from tiny residential spaces (like mine) to huge commercial projects abroad. It took her eight years and some 20 trips to Greece to complete a 40-acre park at the Stavros Niarchos Foundation Cultural Center in Athens. That was a collaboration with architect Renzo Piano on a landscape that climbs over the buildings themselves, planted with native grasses from the hills of Attica and fragrant Mediterranean herbs, including lavender, rosemary, and oregano. Nevins’s mantra for the project was simple: “Speak Greek.” The execution was anything but simple. More than 1,500 trees, 128,000 shrubs and perennials, and 164,000 grass plugs fill the public work. Nevins conceptualized the totality of the park. “I chose every single tree!” she says. “We had to propagate hundreds of thousands of plants throughout Greece, and we decided to hire various nurseries so that if there was a disease or fire, the entire crop would not be wiped out.” Her effort impressed Piano. “It is always special when, beyond the work on a project itself, you realize that you share the same values and ideas,” says Piano of Nevins, whom he describes as a “wonderful professional and human adventure.”

“There is discipline in her work but never rigidity,” says Scott Mitchell, the West Coast–based architect who met Nevins at a dinner honoring architect Richard Meier in 1997 and went on to work with her on properties for Geffen in both California and New York. “Her landscapes don’t compete with architecture; they give it a place to belong.”

He recalls the “emotional power” of her work for Geffen at the Warner estate in Beverly Hills, former home of Warner Bros. cofounder Jack Warner. “Endless sweeps of white azaleas, a driveway lined with ancient, gnarled native sycamores, and 11 acres of rolling meadow beneath giant coast live oaks,” Mitchell says. “World-class projects require cohesion between architecture and landscape. They have to play from the same sheet of music. Debby totally gets that. Her response to architecture is clear and harmonious—confident but never overstepping.”

Tommy Hilfiger and Dee Ocleppo at their Mustique estate.

Gil Schafer, a New York–based architect who has worked with Nevins on more than 25 houses and gardens, also commends her command of structure. At his own house near Millbrook, she built a 12-foot-high hornbeam enclosure nestled into the surrounding farm fields that has, he says, “an almost abstract sculptural quality—as if Richard Serra had suddenly decided to work in hornbeam rather than Corten steel.”

Nevins was born in Manhattan at what was then the Doctors Hospital on the Upper East Side. The family resided in the penthouse of the same building where Greta Garbo lived. Her father died of a brain tumor at 43, when Nevins was six months old, and so her mother had to return to work. At six, she was sent to Camp Taconic in Massachusetts. “I was tiny! My mother might have been arrested today.” She remembers walking in the woods, finding a strawberry, and reporting the discovery in a letter home. The seed had been planted—pun quite obvious.

Fleur Cowles, the formidable editor behind the short-lived, extravagantly inventive magazine Flair, was a maternal relative and had an outsize impact on her childhood. “She knew everyone, and she was so brilliant,” Nevins says, offering me an issue of Flair from another bookshelf like a cherished family heirloom. Another influence was her mother’s sister, Miriam Sampson, an interior decorator who lived across from Carnegie Hall. “In this big apartment, she had her office in one room, and she had little models of apartments. I was so intrigued,” Nevins recalls. She’d cut out pictures of interiors and gardens from magazines and assemble them in scrapbooks. “But I didn’t even know about this idea of being a landscape architect.”

When Nevins was 14, her mother remarried and the family moved to New Haven, Connecticut. She went on to attend Boston University for undergrad and returned to New York for graduate school at Columbia. “They didn’t think that landscape history, which is what I wanted to study, was academic enough. And they probably had no one to teach it anyway,” she says. So she earned an MA and an MPhil in art history. Travel became a form of individualized study. “I learned by looking,” she says. She sought out Le Corbusier’s buildings in France, including La Tourette, Maisons Jaoul, and Villa Savoye, and drove from Paris to Santiago de Compostela looking at Romanesque and Merovingian churches. She made her first of many pilgrimages to Sissinghurst, a garden in Kent created by the writer Vita Sackville-West and her diplomat husband, Harold Nicolson. “There’s nothing more beautiful than Sissinghurst,” she sighs.

One of Nevins’s greatest champions has been Geffen, whom Victoria Newhouse, the renowned architecture critic and widow of longtime Condé Nast chairman Si Newhouse, introduced her to. On her first meeting with Geffen, Nevins arrived to present her work with a carousel of 80 slides. “After maybe 30 slides, he says, ‘That’s enough. You’re hired.’ And I thought to myself, Who is this guy?” When she looked him up, she read that one of his attributes is spotting talent. “And that was that.”

At the Warner estate in Beverly Hills, she removed one swimming pool to open up the landscape, built a new one with a new patio house where Warner had a putting green, and relocated several mature oak trees on the property. “David is not afraid of big moves,” she says. (They preserved the fountains and terraces Warner had commissioned from Florence Yoch, who designed the grounds of Tara for Gone With the Wind, of course.) However, according to Nevins, when Warner’s daughter came to see what Geffen had done, she looked around and asked if they had changed anything. “ ‘What did we change? We changed everything!’ ” Nevins remembers Geffen saying. “The idea that we didn’t do a thing is crazy, but that it looked like it was meant to be—that’s a good thing. The ultimate compliment that looks like I did nothing.”

An aerial view of Deborah Nevins’s Hamptons garden.

Hilfiger hired Nevins for a property in Mustique in the early 1990s, and again for his Denbigh Farm in Greenwich in 1995. In the Caribbean, she created palm promenades and a courtyard of white flowers; in Connecticut, she brought the elements of an old estate into a coherent whole. “I knew she was incredibly passionate about her work, and that always interested me because I love working with people who are passionate about what they do,” Hilfiger says. “Her execution was impeccable, and she delivered exactly what she promised.”

Nevins’s office is based in New York City, and she keeps between 5 and 10 new projects going at all times. “Almost any job is interesting unless I hear in advance that the people aren’t nice,” she says. “Also, art collectors, in my experience, have been great patrons. If you’re an art collector—and you’re truly not collecting just to make money from art—you have an interest in beauty and understanding.”

PLEACHY KEEN “She is very intuitive, so she needs to walk a site and feel what it has to say,” architect Gil Schafer says of Nevins. “She feels this deep kinship with the natural world, with plants and with the trees of a site, which guides how she approaches her interventions on a property.”

On average, it takes two years to get a garden up and running, three years if she needs to build new structures. But a garden is never finished. Roberta Denning, who with her husband, Steve, commissioned Nevins for her family’s property in Greenwich in 2006, describes the pleasure of living with something that acquires depth while continuing to change. “What she created has grown more valuable with time,” Denning says of her property, which includes a walking labyrinth among chestnuts and beech trees. “Nearly 20 years on, the gardens feel both that they have always been here and that they are continually renewed.” Nevins says clients have joked that hiring her is like a marriage because it’s a long-term relationship, and it requires work. “So I guess I’m a polygamist?” she smiles.

Patience is a big part of her process. “She is very intuitive, so she needs to walk a site and feel what it has to say, and this is one way that we are so similar in our approach,” Schafer says. “You need to give her the space to read the land and sort out how she wants to approach it. I think she also feels this deep kinship with the natural world, with plants and with the trees of a site, which guides how she approaches her interventions on a property.”

People joke that Nevins speaks to the plants, but Schafer isn’t sure it’s an act. “I think she really does!”

“I do love them,” Nevins says of her botanical family. “I was at a nursery with someone the other day, and I said, ‘It’s problematic. I get crushes on plants, but sometimes they don’t really have a place, and it’s so disappointing. It’s like a failed romance.’”

A walking labyrinth in Greenwich, Connecticut.

Currently her crush is Stewartia pseudocamellia. “It has amazing bark, and the flower looks like a camellia, but it’s not a camellia, it’s a tree.” One plant she doesn’t love? Flowering forsythia, which Schafer reports she often refers to as “spring vomit.”

Nevins believes her greatest asset is the ability to blend both architectural history and botanical skill. “I have such a strong academic background in architectural history,” she says. “I know exactly what these references are that they make to historical, even modern historical buildings.”

In another part of Long Island, Nevins combined the elements into what she calls a “beech house”—pun absolutely intentional. Martin Filler, an architecture critic and longtime contributor to The New York Review of Books, met Nevins when they were graduate students in Columbia’s art history department in the early 1970s. At the time, his wife, Rosemarie Haag Bletter, an architectural historian and professor emerita of art history at the CUNY Graduate Center in New York City, was working on her PhD and teaching undergraduates. According to Filler, Nevins promised back then to design them a garden one day. “Since we didn’t have a house and never expected to, we said to ourselves, ‘Yeah, right,’ ” he says. “But who knew that someday we would, and that gardening would become such a large part of our lives, especially Rosemarie’s?”

In the mid-1990s, they bought a cottage that had been part of Stanford White’s Breese estate, The Orchard, in Southampton. “Debby said that she would now make good on her promise to design a garden for us,” Filler remembers. “By that time she had become one of the top landscape designers, but she insisted on doing it and refused to be paid.” She stayed with them for a winter weekend and spent hours walking the property. “Then she sat down at our dining table with a roll of yellow tracing paper and the surveyor’s map, and she designed the whole thing within a few hours. She joked, ‘Don’t tell anyone how fast I was.’ ”

THE GIVING TREE When Derek C. Blasberg first saw the majestic tree in the backyard of a property in the Hamptons, he knew he’d found a home for his family. The hunt to identify it led him to Nevins’s larger body of work. “We could picture our children climbing its winding branches.”

The Beech House, a 16-foot-by-16-foot-by-16-foot living gazebo made of 26 purple beech trees (Fagus sylvatica “Dawyck Purple”), is the centerpiece. The trees were sourced from Buffalo, trucked to Southampton, and replanted in the same orientation in which they had been grown. (“Each tree had to be marked with a dot of blue paint to indicate due north and then planted in that same geographical direction,” Filler remembers.) They were wired and trained over a wooden inner framework shaped like the schematic outline of a house and then clipped into shape on the exterior. The floor was paved with bluestone squares and rectangles in a random-looking pattern Nevins designed.

“Each year when we meet with our accountant to do our tax return, he’s always shocked that we spend so much on the garden,” Filler says. “We tell him: ‘You have clients who have boats, you have clients who have classic cars—well, this is our pleasure, our indulgence.’”

#3541. 5 Of The Best Sci-Fi Movie Black Friday Deals Under $20

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Not to paint with too broad of a brush here, but I feel like there is a tremendous amount of crossover between hardcore science fiction fans and physical media collectors. I say this as a proud member of both parties. To that end, Black Friday is a good time for sci-fi lovers who also happen to still buy Blu-rays and 4K Ultra HD copies of movies they love, and 2026 offers no shortage of deals to take advantage of.

There are plenty of underrated sci-fi movies people need to watch. There have been plenty of outstanding sci-fi movies released this past year, including "Project Hail Mary." The options are endless and, fortunately, this year's Black Friday offerings cover the spread. We've dug through the sales and picked out a handful of the best options available to prospective buyers out there.

From classics in the Criterion Collection to one of the greatest science fiction movies of the 21st century and everything in between, these are five of the best sci-fi movies you can get for under $20 during this year's Black Friday sales. Let's dive in, shall we?

Recent entries in the "Godzilla" franchise, most notably "Godzilla Minus One" and "Godzilla Minus Zero," have brought a lot of people to the party. This is a franchise with over 70 years of history though and much, much more to enjoy. For those looking to dig into the character's history a bit more, there's no better way to do that than 1989's "Godzilla vs. Biollante." A little wacky but also breathtaking, it's one of the best "Godzilla" movies of all time.

For Black Friday, Amazon has the Criterion Blu-ray on sale for $19.88, which is 50% off. It's tough to get Criterion releases this cheap and this one is truly stellar. Not only is the restoration incredible but it comes with a pretty amazing poster and new artwork. Unfortunately, the 4K is $24.98 and a little above our $20 threshold. That said, the Blu-ray more than cuts the mustard here, in my humble opinion.

A grieving scientist blends human DNA with a rose and mutated Godzilla cells to engineer a massive plant-based beast dubbed Biollante. The King of the Monsters then emerges from the sea to fight this new threat. The plot itself is absolutely wild but it features some of the most impressive practical creature effects ever put to film. Biollante, specifically, is a truly masterful work of visual effects. It's nothing shy of incredible and that's precisely why Criterion added it to the prestigious collection.

You can grab "Godzilla vs. Biollante" on Blu-ray from Amazon.

We arrive at what is likely the best out-and-out bargain on this list. "Mars Attacks!" wasn't a success in its day but for '90s kids of a certain age, it was a formative movie. It was Tim Burton at the apex of his career as a bankable A-list director taking a big, weird swing. It's sci-fi with a capital S and a capital F. It's strange. It's funny. It's violent. It's beyond star-studded. It rocks. And it's a ridiculously great deal right now.

As part of Amazon's Black Friday sale, the 4K Ultra HD edition of "Mars Attacks!" is on sale for just $11.99. That's a whopping 60% off. For those who don't want to go through Amazon, it's also on sale via Gruv for $12.99. And Gruv does offer free shipping in a lot of situations, for what it's worth. So for those who don't have Amazon Prime, that may actually be the better option.

Earth is invaded by Martians with seemingly unbeatable, superior weaponry and a cruel sense of humor. Delightfully and darkly humorous chaos ensues. This may be the movie that made Burton take a break from Hollywood, but it's also arguably his most underrated work to date. Ahead of its time and wholly unique a fully 30 years later, it's very much worth revisiting. Especially in glorious Ultra HD. Who doesn't want to see Jack Nicholson playing multiple characters at the height of his powers?

You can grab "Mars Attacks!" on 4K from Amazon.

In the realm of blending sci-fi and horror together, it truly doesn't get much better than 1997's "Event Horizon." Rivaled only by a few stone cold classics such as John Carpenter's "The Thing," this is a true gem of the genre and one that has only gotten better with age. It also recently got an overdue upgrade on 4K Ultra HD, which is included as part of this year's Black Friday offerings.

The 4K/Blu-ray combo pack (which also contains a digital code) is on sale on Amazon right now for $16.99. That's "only" 35% off the standard retail price, but it's a damn fine release with some excellent box art that will look great on the ol' physical media shelf. It's not the biggest discount of the bunch but it's a solid price.

"Event Horizon" is essentially a haunted house movie in space focused on a state-of-the-art research spacecraft that mysteriously vanished without a trace on its maiden voyage seven years ago. A signal prompts a rescue crew to head out on a bold rescue mission. However, what they uncover is an unimaginable interstellar horror. With a star-studded cast led by Laurence Fishburne and Sam Neill, it's the business.

Directed by Paul W.S. Anderson, of "Mortal Kombat" and "Resident Evil" fame, "Event Horizon" is one of the best (and scariest) sci-fi horror movies ever made. It's a worthy addition to any science fiction fan's collection. Even those who don't typically go in for horror.

You can grab "Event Horizon" on 4K from Amazon.

Certain critics remain very cynical when it comes to the "Transformers" movie franchise. At a certain point, that cynicism was justified as later entries such as "Age of Extinction" and "The Last Knight" overstayed their welcome. But when Michael Bay first brought the robots in disguise to life in live-action in 2007, it was movie magic for people of a certain age. And few movies benefit from a 4K upgrade more than the original "Transformers" live-action movie.

Admittedly, this one isn't on a deep discount but the 4K/Blu-ray combo pack with a digital code is just $12.73 on Amazon for Black Friday. That's only a 15% discount from the $14.99 retail price, which is pretty darn good as is. But why pay more for it if you don't have to? Bayhem in Ultra HD for less than $13 screams bargain to me.

The first movie in the series sees the heroic Autobots and the evil Decepticons come to Earth, with a clue to the ultimate power held by a teenager, Sam Witwicky (Shia LaBeouf). Come for the nostalgia, stay for some of the most impressive CGI you're ever likely to see in a mainstream blockbuster.

When I participated in /Film's 50 hottest movie takes list a few years ago, I argued that "Transformers" was one of Bay's very best movies. A lot of people who came of age in the '90s would probably agree with me, no matter how one feels about the later entries in the series. With Bay and Steven Spielberg returning for the next "Transformers" movie, now feels like the perfect time to revisit the beginning of this multi-billion-dollar, globally popular franchise.

You can grab "Transformers" on 4K from Amazon.

Last but certainly not least, we come to one of the best science fiction movies of recent memory. Director George Miller's "Mad Max: Fury Road" wasn't just the best reviewed movie of 2015, it's earned its place as one of the best sci-fi movies ever made, as well as one of the best action movies ever made. Dare I say, it's just one of the best movies period? The point is, nobody is going to argue against owning this movie and, fortunately, it's on a deep discount during Black Friday.

The 4K Ultra HD edition of Miller's modern masterpiece is going for $14.99 right now — a steep 57% off the usual retail price of $34.98. That makes it not only probably the best movie on this list, but one of the best deals as well. It's hard to go wrong. Even for those who may own this one on Blu-ray or DVD, it's well worth the upgrade. Few movies will benefit more from the extra fidelity on offer from UHD.

The movie sees the tyrannical Immortan Joe enslave survivors inside his desert fortress, the Citadel. When Furiosa (Charlize Theron) leads the despot's five wives in a daring escape, she forges an alliance with the quiet loner Max (Tom Hardy) in a fortified armored War Rig. The most epic car chase in cinema history ensues.

I can't say anything about "Fury Road" that hasn't been said by other people more eloquently. I don't need to convince anyone that this movie kicks wholesale a**. But I can humbly suggest that if you have $15 to spare, this is one of the best ways to spend it during Black Friday.

You can grab "Mad Max: Fury Road" on 4K from Amazon.

#3540. These Are the Best Ways to Encrypt Your Email

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

As this in-depth explainer from Adaptive Security describes, most emails are encrypted in transit via Transport Layer Security (TLS), which prevents anyone from reading your message as it travels from server to server. However, encryption is temporarily stripped at each server: content is received and processed in plaintext and then re-encrypted when it leaves, meaning it could be read, logged, and distributed by the server provider.

Emails are also typically encrypted at rest—for example, while sitting on Google's servers and in a Gmail recipient's inbox. But this only prevents someone with physical access to the server hardware from reading messages, as Google still holds the encryption key and can access stored data. And, as PCMag points out, Google is scanning your messages to a degree, and it (along with other email providers) can and will hand emails over to law enforcement and government agencies in some cases.

If you have an account with a major email provider like Gmail, Outlook, or Apple Mail, you can add a third-party tool that layers an encryption protocol like OpenPGP on top of your existing account. PCMag recommends PreVeil, SecureMyEmail, and Virtru (which is limited to Gmail users in Chrome) for those who want to keep their current emails. Mailvelope is a browser add-on (and therefore a desktop-only tool) available in Chrome, Firefox, and Edge, though it can also be installed on other browsers, like Brave, that are built on the same architecture. FlowCrypt integrates with Gmail and Google Workspace on desktop and mobile.

Note that enterprise users of Google Workspace and Microsoft 365 have access to true end-to-end encryption without third-party add-ons. Gmail's Confidential mode and Outlook's Encrypt feature, available to all users, are not E2EE equivalents, as Google and Microsoft, respectively, still manage the keys.

For those who are willing to start fresh with a new email address (or who have a custom domain), providers like Proton Mail or Tuta offer native end-to-end encryption. The caveat: by default, this is only between users on the same service, so from one Proton user to another. If you want to send an end-to-end encrypted email from Proton to a Gmail user, for example, you have to set up password protection (and share the password via another secure channel) or use a PGP-compatible tool like those listed above. You can also Proton's Gmail integration does allow for end-to-end encryption, but only if both Gmail parties are using the Proton integration.

Light spoilers for Madden lie ahead, so read on with that in mind.

Madden is one of the latest titles to hit the 2026 movie schedule, and it features plenty of wild moments. David O. Russell’s biographical sports comedy centers on the life and career of football guru John Madden (played by a prosthetic-wearing Nicolas Cage) and, with that, it covers key parts of his life. One big moment is Madden’s well-known resignation as the head coach of the Oakland Raiders in 1979. It’s a key point in the movie, and CinemaBlend recently learned that it marked the first day of shooting for one of the film’s main stars.

CB had the opportunity to speak with Madden cast members Kathryn Hahn and Sienna Miller about their performances as Virginia Madden and Carol Davis, respectively. During the chat, I also couldn’t help but ask about what it was like for them to shoot that quitting scene. Surprisingly enough, filming for that scene began during Miller’s very first day on set. The Horizon star admitted to having felt “abject terror” over the prospect of starting with that scene and working with Hahn, Cage and Christian Bale. Miller recalled:

I was like, ‘Hi, nice to meet you. I'm doing a — Hii, Nic.’ And then action, yeah. So that whole scene is a bit of a blank. I remember David kind of schooling me for futzing too much, being like, ‘Carol, I hate it. Stop it!’ And I was like, ‘Oh God, I felt the tears burning in the eyes.’ No, and then you understand what you're making and who you're making it with, and you surrender. But I was very intimidated that day.

Honestly, I can understand exactly where the Jack Ryan: Ghost War star is coming from. Sure, she’s been on more than her fair share of movie sets, but to have to start her job with such a massive scene and doing so with such talented actors. She wasn’t the only person on set feeling a bit of pressure, though, as Hahn – who’s done Marvel projects at this point – said she was nervous as well:

Oh my god, I was intimidated that day, and I'd already been there for like every day. It took a second to be like, ‘Okay, okay, here we are.’ Like we were talking before, they're massive, massive talents and all. So totally closed in prosthetics. So it was an intense thing to jump into.

The scene in question sees John and Virginia meeting with Raiders owner Al Davis (Bale) and Miller so that Madden can quit the team due to serious health issues. During the chat, Al and Carol try to convince John that his bleeding ulcer will pass and that he should continue coaching in the pursuit of more Super Bowl titles. While John is briefly swayed to hold onto his job, he – at Virginia’s urging – does ultimately retire, much to Al’s disappointment. It’s an over-the-top scene that’s as important as it is ridiculous.

David O. Russell certainly puts his actors in some wild positions in this film due to his wild screenplay. From the grandiose gameday celebrations to the birth of John Madden’s eponymous football video game, O. Russell drops a number of surreal scenes in this film. It probably tracks that the sometimes eclectic filmmaker would take such wild swings while telling a real-life story worthy of a sports biopic.

In any case, though, Sienna Miller rose to the occasion when filming the quitting scene, and the same can be said for Kathryn Hahn. While their behind-the-scenes story is fun, it’s also a reminder that even the most experienced actors get a bit anxious from time to time. You can check out the scene for yourself by checking out Madden, which is now playing in select theaters and streaming with a Prime Video subscription.

#3538. From a gown purchased with wartime rations to a secret engraving on the ring: Inside the historic royal wedding of Queen Elizabeth II and Prince Philip

Queen Elizabeth II and Prince Philip married in 1947, going on to make history by achieving the longest marriage of any British sovereign couple. Back then they were, of course, Princess Elizabeth and Prince Philip of Greece and Denmark, tying the knot in the rather austere years of post-war Britain. So, what really happened on their wedding day?

November 2, 1947: Queen Elizabeth—then Princess Elizabeth—with Prince Philip, Duke of Edinburgh, King George VI and Queen Elizabeth (right) and members of the immediate and extended Royal Family at Buckingham Palace after their wedding

The Queen and Prince Philip’s love story began back in 1939. Princess Elizabeth was just 13 years old; her dashing distant cousin, Prince Philip of Greece and Denmark, was five years her senior and about to join the Royal Navy. They met as she toured the Royal Naval College at Dartmouth; he was the young officer assigned to escort her around that day.

Determined to marry for love, Elizabeth was said to be rather taken with Philip, who was described at the time as ‘handsome as any film star.’ The pair were soon writing letters to each other, and later, occasional chaperoned meetings took place.

In 1946 Philip proposed in Scotland, and she immediately said yes. However, her father, King George, reportedly insisted the couple resist announcing their engagement until the Princess, who was just 20, was a little older. In the end, her parents gave in to her wishes, and Philip officially proposed to Princess Elizabeth in 1947, with a three-carat diamond ring he designed using stones taken from a family tiara that belonged to his mother, Princess Alice of Battenberg. It was created by London jeweller Philip Antrobus Ltd.

Princess Elizabeth with Philip Mountbatten on their wedding day

The Royal Family were adamant that the wedding of Princess Elizabeth and Prince Philip would reflect the country’s post-war situation while also offering a chance for the nation to celebrate.

Like many brides at the time, Princess Elizabeth had to save her rationing coupons to buy the materials for her dress but was given an extra 200 from the government to help. While well-wishers generously sent their own to the royal, they had to be sent back as rules dictated that coupons could not be shared outside of households.

Designed by Norman Hartnell, Princess Elizabeth’s wedding dress was made from ivory silk, duchesse satin and silver thread; the dress featured crystals, 10,000 seed pearls, a fitted bodice, heart-shaped neckline, long sleeves and a 15-foot train. It was made in just seven weeks by 350 skilled women since the wedding took place only four months after the couple’s engagement announcement. Norman Hartnell also designed Elizabeth’s going-away outfit.

Princess Elizabeth’s wedding day tiara was called the Queen Mary Fringe Tiara. It had belonged to her grandmother, Queen Mary, and had been given to her as a wedding present in 1893. It was remade from a tiara/necklace that Queen Victoria had bought from Collingwood and Co.

As Elizabeth was getting ready on the morning of the wedding, it snapped. Luckily, royal jeweler Garrard was apparently on hand to fix it, and the Queen later revealed, “I think he taped up the spring.”

Princess Elizabeth’s other wedding day jewelry included two pearl necklaces. The shorter of the two necklaces was the “Queen Anne” necklace, said to have belonged to Anne, the last Stuart Queen. The other was known as the “Queen Caroline,” and is said to have belonged to the wife of King George II. Both necklaces were left to the Crown by Queen Victoria and were given to Elizabeth as a wedding present by her father.

All royal bridal bouquets contain myrtle from a myrtle bush planted by Queen Victoria at Osborne House. Princess Elizabeth’s also had white orchids and was laid on the grave of the Unknown Warrior at Westminster Abbey the day after the wedding.

There were eight bridesmaids at Princess Elizabeth and Prince Philip’s wedding: Princess Margaret, Princess Alexandra, Lady Pamela Mountbatten, Diana Bowes-Lyon, Lady Elizabeth Lambart, Margaret Elphinstone, Lady Caroline Montagu-Douglas-Scott, and Lady Mary Cambridge.

Her two pages were Prince William of Gloucester and Prince Michael of Kent, both aged five at the time.

The bridesmaids were given silver Art Deco-style compacts with the couple's initials and a crown engraved on the lid, set with five cabochon sapphires.

The Duke of Edinburgh's best man was David Mountbatten, the Marquess of Milford Haven.

Knowing that Elizabeth hated cigarettes, Prince Philip reportedly gave up smoking on the morning of his wedding “suddenly and apparently without difficulty,” according to his valet, John Dean.

The wedding took place at Westminster Abbey on November, 20th, 1947 at 11:30 a.m. Princess Elizabeth was the 10th member of the Royal Family to be married at Westminster Abbey.

Princess Elizabeth and Prince Philip walking down the aisle of Westminster Abbey, followed by their bridesmaids and pages

There were 2,000 guests in attendance, including the likes of the King of Iraq, Princess Juliana and Prince Bernhard of the Netherlands and the Hereditary Grand Duke of Luxembourg and Princess Elisabeth of Luxembourg. The ceremony was broadcast on the radio to millions of listeners.

Together with her father, Princess Elizabeth left Buckingham Palace in the Irish State Coach. (In her later years, it had been Queen Victoria’s state carriage of choice, as she declined to use the Gold State Coach following the death of Prince Albert.)

The wedding ceremony was officiated by the Archbishop of Canterbury, Geoffrey Fisher, and the Archbishop of York, Cyril Garbett.

The organist and Master of the Choristers at the Abbey, Australian William Neil McKie, was the director of music for the wedding and there were 91 singers; the abbey choir was joined by the choirs of the Chapel Royal and St George's Chapel in Windsor.

The service started with a specially composed fanfare by Arnold Bax and finished with Felix Mendelssohn's “Wedding March,” with ceremony hymns including “Praise, my Soul, the King of Heaven” and “The Lord's my Shepherd.”

The bride and groom knelt on orange boxes covered in pink silk at the altar as a nod to post-war austerity.

On the day of the wedding, Philip was given the title of Duke of Edinburgh by his father-in-law, King George VI. After the Queen ascended the throne in 1953, she made the decision in 1957 to make Philip a prince of the UK, in addition to his dukedom.

The wedding rings were made from a nugget of Welsh gold which came from the Clogau St David's mine, near Dolgellau.

According to Royal biographer Ingrid Seward, who wrote Prince Philip: Revealed, Philip had a secret message inscribed inside his wife's wedding band, a message that only the engraver, Queen Elizabeth, and her husband knew the contents of.

After the service, a wedding breakfast was held in the Ball-Supper Room at Buckingham Palace for 150 guests only, with Filet de Sole Mountbatten, Perdreau en Casserole and Bombe Glacée Princess Elizabeth on the menu.

During the breakfast, the string band of the Grenadier Guards played music while guests were greeted with individual posies of myrtle and white Balmoral on their place settings as the wedding favors.

The couple waving from the balcony of Buckingham Palace

Famously, the newlyweds went onto the balcony at Buckingham Palace to wave to the huge crowds on the Mall.

Although the royal couple received 11 wedding cakes, the official traditional fruit cake was baked by McVitie and Price and was four tiers and nine feet high. The wedding cake was decorated with both coats of arms, including the monograms of the bride and groom, sugar-iced figures of their favorite activities, and regimental and naval badges.

Mr Schur, chief confectioner at McVitie and Price, putting the final touches to the wedding cake

The newlyweds cut the cake using the Duke's Mountbatten sword, which was a wedding present from the King.

Over 10,000 people sent telegrams congratulating Elizabeth and Philip, and around 2,500 wedding presents were sent from around the world. These included a cloth from Mahatma Gandhi that he’d woven himself, which Queen Mary mistook for an “indelicate” loincloth.

After their wedding breakfast, Princess Elizabeth and Prince Philip headed to Waterloo station, joined by Elizabeth’s corgi, Susan, catching a train to Hampshire to spend their wedding night in Broadlands, the home of Philip's uncle, Earl Mountbatten.

The rest of their royal honeymoon was spent at Birkhall on the Balmoral Estate in Scotland.

Princess Elizabeth and Prince Philip being showered with rose petals as they leave Buckingham Palace, London, for their honeymoon.

#3537. 10 Privacy Hacks Every Mac User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Enabling the macOS Firewall (which is off by default) adds a layer of protection against external devices on your wifi network, as well as unauthorized apps from initiating a connection to your device. Turning on Stealth Mode prevents your Mac from even responding to these requests, essentially making it invisible to anything that's scanning a network you're connected to. This makes it more difficult for hackers and malware to know your device exists, much less attack it. This can interfere with certain essential activity when you're on your home network, but it's a valuable security setting when on public wifi. You can leave Firewall on all the time and enable Stealth Mode only as needed. Go to Settings > Network > Firewall, flip the toggle, then hit Options to manage Stealth Mode.

Images and screenshots contain metadata, such as timestamps, device and hardware details, and, in the case of photos, physical location. Much of this information is stripped automatically when you share files to social media or via encrypted messaging apps, but if you're sending them via text or email, posting to forums, or sharing over AirDrop, metadata remains intact. You can easily remove metadata from your images right on your desktop. Select the file and hit control + click to bring up an options menu, then go to Quick Actions > Convert Image. Uncheck the box next to Preserve Metadata, then hit Convert. (This is also useful for quickly converting HEIC to JPEG without opening a separate app.)

If you're using iCloud to store photos, files, and device backups, your data is encrypted on Apple's servers and in transit. Apple still holds the decryption key, which is useful if you somehow get locked out of your account and need help recovering it, but for sensitive data—including device backups—end-to-end encryption is the most secure way to ensure no one but you can gain access. Advanced Data Protection is an opt-in setting for iCloud that encrypts your information end to end. You'll need to set up an alternative recovery method, such as your device passcode with two-factor authentication, a recovery contact, or a recovery key. Be careful, though: If you lose access to this recovery method, you will lose your data. You can enable Advanced Data Protection on your Mac under System Settings > [Your Name] > iCloud > Advanced Data Protection > Turn On. Note that some iCloud data, including passwords and payment methods, are already end-to-end encrypted by default.

#3536. Guy Pearce's Remake Of A '60s Sci-Fi Classic Deserved Better At The Box Office

Simon Wells' 2002 sci-fi flick "The Time Machine" was extrapolated from H.G. Wells' celebrated 1895 novel, one of the best sci-fi novels ever written, and also from George Pal's famed 1960 adaptation of the same story, itself one of the best time travel movies of all time. Made for a budget of $80 million, "The Time Machine" didn't overwhelm at the box office, earning almost $124 million worldwide. Critics were very unkind to "The Time Machine," and the film only has a 28% approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes, based on 151 reviews.

The movie isn't great, reducing the intellectualism of Wells' original novel into a rote sci-fi action thriller, but there was a steampunk quirkiness to "The Time Machine" that could have been more openly embraced. It was even nominated for an Oscar for Best Makeup.

Guy Pearce plays Alexander Hartdegen, the inventor of the titular device, and he learns very quickly that mucking around with time travel doesn't always provide the result he's after. Alexander's motivation for building a time machine in the first place is to go back in time to prevent the murder of his fiancée (Sienna Guillory). This isn't part of the original novel, nor of George Pal's movie. Alexander spends five years building the time machine, and manages to save his fiancée, only to lose her again shortly thereafter. Something about the universe requires she die.

This kicks off a long-ranging time-travel adventure wherein Alexander begins tripping through the centuries, hoping to find an answer about how fate operates. He eventually ends up in the very, very distant future — specifically, the year AD 802,701 — when humanity has evolved into two distinct subspecies, the Morlocks and the Eloi.

The two most notable additions to the movie of "The Time Machine" that most dramatically depart from the previous versions are characters played by Orlando Jones and Jeremy Irons. Jones' character is, I would argue, a good addition, adding someone for the protagonist to converse with. Irons' character is ... well, his inclusion is just baffling.

Jones plays Vox 114, an artificially intelligent digital library aide from the year 2030 who appears on glass screens. Because he is a computer, Vox is eager to teach people about science and the world. When Alexander, having just jaunted forward in time, asks Vox about time travel, Vox gets a little impatient, thinking Alexander just wants to talk about science fiction. Later in the film, Alexander finds Vox in a cave, somehow still operational hundreds of centuries later. Vox seems to have developed something of a consciousness over the years. He also still has a complete memory, remembering Alexander from this sojourn to 2030.

Irons, meanwhile, plays a character credited as the Über-Morlock, the psychic Cenobite-like leader of the Morlocks. As anyone who has read H.G. Wells' book can tell you, the Morlocks were an underground race of ape-like beings who feed on the Eloi who live on the Earth's surface. The Eloi, meanwhile, are placid, gentle, and defenseless. The idea is that the Morlocks evolved from old Earth's laboring classes, and the Eloi evolved from its aristocracy. Wells was clearly making a comment on class divisions, and how they will eventually play out if left to evolve along their logical extremes.

There is no Über-Morlock leading the underground monsters in the original book, and the inclusion of such a character in the 2002 movie is confusing and strange.

That said, there is at least something delicious about Jeremy Irons' performance. He sports a long white wig, pasty white skin, and wears a bizarre, black pleather outfit that looks like it could be worn to a bondage bar. "The Time Machine" climaxes with the Über-Morlock and Alexander grappling while the machine hurtles forward in time millions of years. It's such a kooky conceit that you might find yourself enjoying "The Time Machine."

Some fun trivia: Simon Wells, the director of "The Time Machine" just happens to be the great-grandson of H.G. Wells. Simon Wells also co-directed the 1991 animated film "An American Tail: Fievel Goes West" (which was Jimmy Stewart's final film), as well as "We're Back! A Dinosaur's Story," the giant '90s animated hit "The Prince of Egypt," and several others. (He also helmed the massive Disney flop "Mars Needs Moms," but we'll forgive him this time.) All of this is to say that Wells was no neophyte in 2002, and he is not a traditional nepo baby who received an opportunity primarily because of his lineage.

Critics largely hated "The Time Machine." Roger Ebert gave the film one-and-a-half stars out of four, saying that it was "a witless recycling of the H.G. Wells story from 1895, with the absurdity intact but the wonderment missing." He noted that 800,000 years into the future, it was awfully convenient that Morlock and Eloi both seem to speak English. Guy Pearce's performance also didn't match the material. Ebert wrote that "Pearce, as the hero, makes the mistake of trying to give a good and realistic performance. Irons at least knows what kind of movie he's in, and hams it up accordingly."

Okay, so "The Time Machine" is not great. But Irons is fun. It certainly didn't deserve to bomb.

I knew it had become increasingly rare for Hollywood productions to actually be filmed in Los Angeles, but Rob Lowe’s stats for The Floor really put things into perspective. The host of the Fox game show, which is on the 2026 TV schedule this fall season, just got real about why it’s filmed all the way in Ireland rather than at the network’s own lot. And, wow!

Ever since The Floor premiered back in 2023, the game show featuring 100 contestants, a giant LED floor grid and a $250,000 grand prize has been made in Ireland. When Lowe was asked why he shoots it overseas, he said this:

When people want to know how bad the economics are in California, and Los Angeles in particular in terms of the industry that created this town. It is more cost-efficient to find 100 Americans and bring them to Ireland and shoot the game show in Ireland than it is to shoot in the soundstages [on the Fox lot] right outside the window of the offices where we’re trying to figure out what we’re going to do next season.

Yeah, this really illustrates the rough situation in LA right now. When I looked deeper into it, I found out that there are a few factors that probably played into The Floor deciding to go to Ireland rather than stay in Los Angeles. One is the rigid labor regulations in Los Angeles that just don’t apply in Ireland. Another is how much more expensive it would be for the production to board the one hundred contestants during the shoots. And then, there’s the competitive tax incentives Ireland has in place to encourage productions to be there. Lowe continued with these words:

There’s a new California initiative that did pass to help bring production back into LA. And then, there's also a national one that people are talking about. But, that would still only make it competitive with some of the other [markets]. I mean, it’s 40% less expensive, 40. It’s a lot of money.

It sounds like The Floor just wouldn’t be able to exist if it were shot in Los Angeles. There are a number of TV shows that currently shoot in the City of Angels, like Dancing With The Stars, The Pitt, The Rookie, 911, Shrinking and Abbott Elementary, and some incentives in California are starting to help repair the market. However, as Lowe also shared while on Mostly Sheenius, there’s a long way to go before it becomes cost-efficient again. As he put it:

It is definitely trending up, but it is trending up from the basement of where it used to be.

Tons of Los Angeles TV shows recently moved to new locations, such as Shark Tank and American Idol moving to Atlanta and The Masked Singer to New Jersey. It’s also been reported lately (per Deadline) that America’s Got Talent is scouting a new home outside of its longtime home in Pasadena, California.

The Floor airs new episodes on Wednesdays (with the finale airing on December 2). If you’re looking to catch up on the new season, you can do so now with either a Disney+ subscription and/or a Hulu subscription. Lowe’s explanation of why The Floor shoots in Ireland kind of blows my mind, but as a Los Angeles resident, I totally see how expensive it is over here, too. Hopefully some of these incentives will change things because so much of the workforce over here relies on the entertainment industry.

#3534. Who Will Be The Next Bond Girl?

Since the beginning of the week, the James Bond frenzy has shown no signs of stopping. On November 16, new Bond owners Amazon MGM Studios finally revealed the name of the actor who will succeed Daniel Craig as 007: Robert Pattinson. After years of speculation and months of intense rumors, the next James Bond now has a new face. Now, the next question on everyone’s mind: Who will be the next Bond girl?

The exception in thie great debate is Léa Seydoux. The actor, who seems to be everywhere this year, played Madeleine Swann in Craig's final Bond films, Spectre (2015) and No Time to Die (2021). Her magnetic performance made Madeleine an unforgettable Bond girl, especially since her character plays a decisive role in the arc of Craig’s character: at the end of No Time to Die, the famous spy sacrifices himself to save her and their daughter, Mathilde. For the first time since its creation in 1953 by British author Ian Fleming, the secret agent in Her Majesty’s service was gone.

Léa Seydoux and Daniel Craig pose as they arrive on the set of No Time To Die on September 09, 2019 in Matera, Italy.

In a recent interview on Vogue's The Run-Through podcast, Seydoux was candid about how little interest she had in her successor. “I don’t really care,” she said with a laugh. “I don’t really care, guys. How can you?”

When pressed on who Pattinson's female lead might be, Seydoux expressed mixed feelings about the British spy's latest iteration. With the purchase of the Bond IP by Amazon, “It became American," Seydoux said. “But I’m sure the movie will be great because it’s directed by Denis Villeneuve, who’s a very talented director. I’m sure he will do something great.”

The online megamart took control of the storied franchise in 2023, after which Amazon founder Jeff Bezos controversially sought feedback on the title character's casting via X. The announcement of Villeneuve as the next film's director brought things back from the brink.

Bezos, who confirmed that he was “very involved” in the film's casting process, also seems to give Seydoux pause. In an interview with Variety, she admitted “was a bit sad when I heard that it was sold (…) but now that it’s Denis, I was like, Oh, at least it’s him, so it will be cinema.”

Denis Villeneuve, who directed Seydoux in Dune: Part Two, will release the final installment of this epic science-fiction trilogy will be on December 16. After that, he'll be free to focus on his next major project: reviving the world’s most famous secret agent. It remains to be seen who he will choose to star opposite Robert Pattinson as his female companion—but we know that despite her fondness for the director, Seydoux will not return: Just last month, the French actress told People “I really loved being on this franchise, but now it’s ... done.”

#3533. If Your Google Pixel's Camera Is Suddenly Broken, Here's the Fix

Updates are generally good for your devices. The latest Chrome update, for example, patches an actively exploited security vulnerability, while Apple's latest updates stop people from seeing iMessages they shouldn't have access to. In most cases, it's beneficial to update your tech to the latest software version whenever possible.

Sadly, updates aren't all perfect, as Google Pixel users are discovering this week. As reported by Android Authority, Google's November update apparently shipped with a bug that breaks some Pixel 10 and Pixel 11 cameras. Seeing as Pixels are rather famous for their shooters, this is a decidedly unfortunate glitch.

Here's the situation: Following the November update, some users are opening their Pixel Camera apps to find an error that reads, "Something went wrong. Close and open the Camera app again," with a "Learn More" link to, well, learn more. Others aren't receiving the error, but are instead running into a blank Camera viewfinder, as if the lens is totally covered. What's more, some users are reportedly saying that the issue is present on third-party camera apps, not just the Pixel Camera app. That would imply this is an issue with the camera system-wide, not just the Pixel Camera app itself.

To be clear, it doesn't seem like this is a universal issue. It's not like all Pixel users are now running with broken cameras. But based on the forum complaints Android Authority discovered, it seems reasonable to assume that this glitch isn't limited to just a handful of unlucky Pixel owners.

Luckily, there is an apparent workaround here, though it's not totally obvious. Some users are having no luck restarting their Pixels, while others report that a factory reset wasn't enough to restore camera functionality.

What does appear to work, however, is shutting your Pixel down and waiting five minutes or so. It's not clear why, but giving your Pixel a chance to "breathe" seems to shake the glitch and bring back your camera. As Android Authority reports, that fix comes from "Diamond and Gold product experts" on Google's Support forum.

If your Pixel's camera is giving you grief following the November update, this workaround is definitely worth a try—especially since more drastic measures don't actually seem to do anything. As the issue does seem to be rather widespread, I wouldn't be surprised to see Google issue a patch in the coming days. But until then, turning your phone off for five minutes may be a decent compromise.

#3532. 61 Years Later, Charlie Brown's Greatest Enemy Is Still an Undefeated 'Peanuts' Icon

Like many comics aimed at children, Charles Schulz's Peanuts doesn't have too many actual villains. It has a number of antagonists, such as Lucy Van Pelt, various other kids, or the impersonal cloud of failure that constantly hangs over Charlie Brown's head, but it's rare to see a genuinely malevolent force in Peanuts — with one exception.

One of Charlie Brown's long-standing hobbies in Peanuts was kite-flying, despite not being very good at it. Whenever he tried it, he invariably got his kite caught in trees and/or himself wrapped up in the kite string. Like every other hobby in Charlie Brown's life, he was devoted to it despite his bad luck.

That hobby eventually introduced Charlie Brown to his nemesis. The Kite-Eating Tree was an otherwise unidentified tree in Charlie Brown's neighborhood that seemed to deliberately grab and eat his kites, to the point where Charlie Brown developed a one-sided rivalry with it.

According to Schulz in the autobiographical collection My Life With Charlie Brown (2010), the inspiration for the Kite-Eating Tree was simply a bit of observational humor. Schulz had noticed that a kite that got stuck in a tree would slowly disappear over the course of several weeks, as wildlife and the elements took their toll. He decided that must've been because the tree was eating the kite, and so the Kite-Eating Tree ended up in Peanuts.

The Kite-Eating Tree was first specifically identified in March 1965, which marked the beginning of a recurring story that would last for the next 30 years.

In many of its appearances, the Kite-Eating Tree doesn't actually do much of anything. In fact, it's noted to have fallen down at one point, but Charlie Brown's subsequent run-ins with the tree suggests that either there's more than one or it's some kind of elected position. Having said that, it’s shown on more than one occasion to be actively devouring its “prey.”

The two major Kite-Eating Tree storylines are from the late 1960s and 1970s. One involves Charlie Brown escalating the stakes in the conflict and subsequently having to run from the Environmental Protection Agency, while the other involves Lucy feeding Schroeder's piano to the tree. Both stories were adopted into episodes of the short-lived '80s cartoon The Charlie Brown and Snoopy Show.

In January 1969, Lucy's one-sided obsession with Schroeder reached a boiling point. Fed up with Schroeder's refusal to pay attention to her instead of constantly practicing, she threw his toy piano into the closest tree. Unfortunately, it was the Kite-Eating Tree, which was entirely willing to broaden its diet with a piano. Despite an attempt by Snoopy to rescue the piano, it was soon gone, and Schroeder had to mail-order a replacement.

The second major Kite-Eating Tree storyline is more surreal, and lasted an unusually long time for a Peanuts arc. On Feb. 25, 1977, Charlie Brown demonstrated an unusual amount of jaw strength when he chose to retaliate against the Kite-Eating Tree. If it was going to bite his kites, he reasoned, he'd just bite it right back, and took quite a piece out of the Tree’s side.

A few days later, Charlie Brown received a letter from the EPA about the tree. While we're never told what the letter said, Charlie Brown decides to run away from home to escape the charges. Over the next few weeks, he reaches another town, sleeps in a cardboard box, ends up as the new coach of a pee-wee baseball team, and finally gets talked into going home, as the EPA has no case. Besides, the Kite-Eating Tree has since fallen over.

That didn't keep the Kite-Eating Tree from making future appearances, but it was primarily a one-joke wonder for most of the rest of Peanuts' run.

Its final appearance came in 1995, when Charlie Brown's attempt to teach Rerun how to fly a kite ended in disaster. Charlie Brown would continue to unsuccessfully fly kites from time to time until March 1999, but the Tree was out of the picture for good.

With one last kite for the road, the Kite-Eating Tree was never seen again, but one must assume that it's still out there somewhere. Waiting. Hungering for fresh kites. Annoyed that kids don't really seem to fly kites as much as they used to.

#3531. Why Beetee Latier From The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping Looks So Familiar

This article contains spoilers for "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping."

Prequel film "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" reveals the details of how Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada, Woody Harrelson in the original films) won the 50th Hunger Games ... and lost everything else in his life, turning him into a miserable man using alcohol to cope. Yet "The Hunger Games: Catching Fire" revealed Haymitch wasn't merely the burnout he first appeared to be, but a key member of the rebellion against the Capitol.

"Sunrise on the Reaping" shows the beginning of that, particularly Haymitch's early alliance with Plutarch Heavensbee (Jesse Plemons, filling in for the late Philip Seymour Hoffman). Younger versions of several past Hunger Games victors first introduced in "Catching Fire" also show up in "Sunrise on the Reaping," including the tech wizard Beetee Latier (Kelvin Harrison Jr. doing an uncanny vocal impression of original Beetee actor Jeffrey Wright).

Beetee has already been caught rebelling against the Capitol. As punishment, his own son Ampert (Percy Daggs IV) was reaped into the Hunger Games. Beetee and Haymitch collaborate as part of a conspiracy to have Haymitch disrupt the arena's mechanical systems and, hopefully, sabotage the Games once he's inside. When Haymitch does so, but the Games persist and, when the conspiracy is discovered, he takes the fall. The Capitol has already done the worst thing it could to Beetee by taking his son, and as a victor, he's too valuable and visible a symbol to kill.

"Hunger Games" fans already know this isn't the last we've seen of Beetee, and this probably isn't the first you've seen of his actor who plays him. Born in New Orleans in 1994, Harrison is the son of two musicians, but he chose acting as his primary creative path.

Harrison's film career began with incidental parts in "12 Years A Slave" and "Ender's Game" in 2013, which were followed by his first starring role in 2017's post-apocalyptic horror film "It Comes At Night." Harrison played the character of Travis, son of Paul (Joel Edgerton) and Sarah (Carmen Ejogo).

In 2018, Harrison appeared in "Monster," Netflix's adaptation of Walter Dean Myers's 1999 novel about a Black honor student accused of murder. The following year, Harrison starred in a surprisingly similar film: the psychodrama "Luce," playing a former child soldier from Eritrea adopted by a wealthy white couple (Naomi Watts and Tim Roth). Luce is a straight-A student, popular athlete, and seemingly on his way to great things ... until he writes an essay that appears to defend radical political violence as a valid means of change.

Having proved himself with those leading roles, Harrison has continued making himself into one of Hollywood's most prolific young actors even before joining "The Hunger Games." Several of his prominent roles have been in historical dramas: In 2021, he played Black Panther leader Fred Hampton in 2021's "The Trial of the Chicago 7," and in 2022's "Elvis" he played Blues musician B.B. King. Harrison also played Martin Luther King Jr. in Season 4 of National Geographic series "Genius," opposite Aaron Pierre (now known as John Stewart from "Lanterns") as Malcolm X.

But that's not all Harrison can do. He played Christian de Neuvillette in Joe Wright's 2021 musical film "Cyrano," adapting the 1897 French play by Edmond Rostand. In 2024 "Lion King" prequel "Mufasa," he voiced Scar. Being in company with Jeremy Irons and Chiwetel Ejiofor is pretty impressive for an actor Harrison's age.

"The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" is now in theaters.

#3529. Five Hacks Every Apple Watch Series 12 User Should Know

The latest Apple Watches have a lot of new features that older watches don't, so I figured it was time for a new list of hacks. While our general Apple Watch and fitness tracking hacks are still golden, Series 12 devices offer new features like native step counting, a Readiness app, an upgraded heart rate sensor, an AI-based version of Siri, and "audio intelligence" that can replay and summarize real-life conversations, within limits. Here's how to get the most out of them.

The Series 12 can finally count steps natively, a task that for some reason is only arriving now, and is restricted to just the newest Apple Watch models. Enjoy it! To add a step counter to your watch face, long-press on the clock screen to edit it, tap on a complication (that’s what Apple calls those little icons and numbers that appear on some watch faces), choose Activity, and then tap Steps.

You don’t need this creepy feature listening in to everything, but it can be nice to have it as a backup on occasion. A button in your Apple Watch’s Control Center can turn the feature on and off. Keep it off except when you have a structured conversation that you’ll want to refer to later. This feature is currently in beta (which you can try now if you want to), but is expected to be available to everyone later this year.

It's worth turning off the default setting not just because of the creepiness factor, but also because the recaps work best when there is a single subject of conversation, with a clear start and end, and just one context. If you leave recaps running all the time, your doctor’s appointment will get mixed in with your grocery shopping, YouTube watching, and everyday chatter.

To finish off a recap and make it useful, take a look at the recap shortly after the conversation, tap the three-dots menu, and hit Edit. You’ll be able to adjust the notes and add your own important details. Siri won’t identify speakers and seems to shy away from including certain details, like people’s names. You can add in what it missed and also create your own bullet points so that everything gets noted down while it’s still fresh in your mind.

This one isn’t specific to the Series 12, but if you haven’t gotten on board with the pinch and wrist flick gestures yet, now is a great time.

First, the wrist flick: If a notification is on your screen, or you’re otherwise looking at something you’d rather be done with, just flick your wrist away from you and then back toward you, as if there were a crumb on the watch face and you wanted to knock it off. This will bring you back to the watch face and close whatever you were looking at.

The double pinch is another useful one, although Apple calls it double tap. This is confusing because you aren’t double tapping the watch, you’re tapping your thumb and forefinger together while wearing the watch. You don’t need to touch the watch face at all. So, when you get a notification or a call, look at it on your watch, and pinch your thumb and forefinger (of the watch hand) together twice. The watch detects the pinch from subtle movements in your wrist, and it will open the notification. You can then use the wrist flick to close the notification. Performing a double pinch when no notification is on screen will bring up your smart stack. You can then double-pinch to move to the next card in the smart stack, or single-pinch to open that card and see its details.

If you want to learn even more gestures, go into the Watch app, and select Accessibility and then Hand gestures. You can remap a whole-fist “clench” to do the same thing as pressing the digital crown, for example, or to open the control center or Siri.

A little rude, perhaps, but helpful: With the new AI-based Siri, sometimes answers to questions can be long-winded. If Siri launches into a novel-length response and you’re not interested in hearing all that, just put your palm over the screen. You’ll instantly be transported back to your watch face, and the Siri response will stop.

If you still want to see those longer responses without having Siri read the whole thing to you, you can set this up on your phone, and the settings will carry over to your watch. On your iPhone, go to Settings and tap Siri, then Responses. Select Silent responses instead of Spoken responses. You can then read through her answers, or skim them, as you prefer.

#3528. Before Spider-Man, Kirsten Dunst Was In An Episode Of Star Trek: The Next Generation

If you're the kind of person who has fun spotting celebrities in roles they took before they were launched to the heights of their fame, you could do a lot worse than throwing on a few episodes of "Star Trek: The Next Generation" and keeping your eye out for guest stars. Before he starred in "The Rocketeer" and took on the infamous Transylvanian count in "Bram Stoker's Dracula," Billy Campbell played the roguish Okona in "TNG's" second season, and before she had her breakout role in "Double Jeopardy" opposite Tommy Lee Jones, Ashley Judd made her acting debut in Season 5, playing an ensign in the episode where the crew of the Enterprise were all taken over by an evil video game.

These early appearances are always fun to catch, especially when the actor you're spotting is both immediately recognizable and just about to break out heights so high that you'd almost need a starship to catch up to them. The best example? Kirsten Dunst, who made an appearance in the final season of "The Next Generation," long before she'd star as Mary Jane Watson in Sam Raimi's "Spider-Man" films.

On the Season 7 episode "Dark Page", an 11-year-old Dunst played Hedril, a member of the Cairn, a species of alien telepaths who, as Captain Picard puts it, "have no concept of spoken language." To help facilitate communication, the Federation sends in their own telepath, occasional ambassador and perpetual thorn in Picard's side Lwaxana Troi (Majel Barrett), the mother of the Enterprise's empathic counselor Deanna Troi (Marina Sirtis).

Unfortunately, the Cairn's first attempt at connecting with an alien species goes awry, and Hedril winds up triggering Lwaxana's repressed memories of Deanna's older sister Kestra, who died when Deanna was a baby.

As a result, Dunst plays both Hedril and, in scenes where Deanna has to explore her mom's mindscape to find out while she's in a coma, a version of Kestra — who, it should be noted, had never been seen or mentioned before on the series, and was even unknown to Deanna.

The episode aired in 1993, and while it wasn't Dunst's first role as a child actress, it was the most prominent by far at the time. Of course, that would all change the following year with the release of "Interview With the Vampire," in which Dunst had her true breakout role playing the vampire Claudia, alongside Tom Cruise and Brad Pitt. Despite Pitt's difficulties in filming that led him to start feeling like an actual vampire, the movie was a financial and critical success, and Dunst in particular earned praise from Roger Ebert for the role and an MTV Movie Award for Best Supporting Actress and a Golden Globe nomination.

Dunst would go on to bigger fame as the star of the iconic cheerleading comedy "Bring It On" and, of course, the romantic lead of Sam Raimi's "Spider-Man" trilogy. As for Hedril, she was one of many one-off characters who never returned to the Enterprise, but Kestra had a bit more of an interesting legacy. A novel set in an alternate universe called "Q and A" cast her, and not Deanna, as the counselor of the Enterprise, and in the first season of "Star Trek: Picard," it was revealed that Deanna would go on to name her own daughter Kestra in a tribute to her dearly departed sister.
