#3492. 6 Most Universally Loved Shows That Were Canceled Too Early

A TV show can be canceled for a variety of reasons, with some benefiting from an early ending, others being unfairly canceled, and others becoming universally loved TV shows after their early cancelations. Having multiple seasons doesn't guarantee that a TV show will succeed with critics and general audiences. Many of the best TV shows of all time are miniseries or had very short runs, either because they were planned like that or they were canceled too soon.

Although cancelations of great TV shows have become quite common in the current streaming era, unfair and early cancelations have been happening for years. Just like there’s no formula that can guarantee steady, long-lasting success for a TV show, there isn’t one that inevitably leads to a show’s decline and an early cancelation. In most cases, the cancelation of a TV show is unrelated to its quality, with viewership numbers being the deciding factor.

Another reason is a show’s budget, which can make it unsustainable despite good critical reception and ratings, while some were affected by bad scheduling and other terrible decisions made by their home networks. However, the quality of these shows proves that a cancelation isn’t entirely the end for them, as some of them were able to get some closure in other media or through reboots, but they have all become universally loved shows, and that’s a lot more valuable.

Wonderfalls is a fantasy comedy drama TV show created by Todd Holland and Bryan Fuller. Wonderfalls introduces viewers to Jaye Tyler (Caroline Dhavernas), a 24-year-old graduate of Brown University with a philosophy degree working as a sales clerk at a Niagara Falls gift shop. Jaye is an intentional underachiever and even avoids her loving family, who are a lot more successful than her. Jaye’s life takes a turn when inanimate animal-shaped objects begin to talk to her, which, obviously, others can’t see or hear.

These animals give her cryptic messages to perform specific actions, and if she doesn’t comply, they continuously bother her. Although this often leads to chaotic results, Jaye’s perception of the world and her life begins to shift. Wonderfalls premiered on Fox in 2004, but it was canceled after only four episodes aired, with the remaining episodes released on the Canadian network Vision TV months later. Wonderfalls was canceled due to low ratings, but it ended up becoming a cult gem.

Happy Endings is a sitcom created by David Caspe. Happy Endings has a very similar premise to shows like Friends and How I Met Your Mother, but it still managed to stand out. That said, Happy Endings follows a dysfunctional group of friends living in Chicago, with the group formed by the married couple of business overachiever Brad (Damon Wayans Jr.) and perfectionist Jane (Eliza Coupe); ditzy boutique owner and Jane’s younger sister, Alex (Elisha Cuthbert); aspiring restaurateur Dave (Zachary Knighton); slacker Max (Adam Pally); and party girl Penny (Casey Wilson).

Happy Endings begins with Dave and Alex's wedding, with Alex leaving Dave at the altar. Although they decide to stay friends, this inevitably changes the dynamic of the group, and they all do their best to preserve their friendship. Despite a mixed reception during its first episodes, Happy Endings eventually won critics and general audiences over, but that still wasn’t enough to save it. Happy Endings was canceled after three seasons due to low ratings, which was the result of season 3’s bad scheduling.

Freaks and Geeks is a teen comedy drama created by Paul Feig. Freaks and Geeks takes viewers back to the 1980s to follow siblings Lindsay (Linda Cardellini) and Sam Weir (John Francis Daley), who attend William McKinley High School in the fictional Detroit suburb of Chippewa. Lindsay joins the group known as “freaks”, formed by Daniel (James Franco), Ken (Seth Rogen), Nick (Jason Segel), and Kim (Busy Philipps), while Sam befriends Neal (Samm Levine) and Bill (Martin Starr), becoming one of the “geeks.”

On Lindsay’s side of the story, she’s doing what she can to shake off her status of proficient student and “mathlete” and become a rebel who hangs out with the troubled slackers, which, of course, causes some problems with her parents. On Sam’s side, the story focuses on his and his friends’ efforts to navigate the social sphere of high school and not die trying.

Unfortunately, Freaks and Geeks had bad scheduling that prevented it from finding its audience during its initial run, and along with creative differences between the show’s creative team and the network, Freaks and Geeks was canceled after just one season, but it became a cult classic.

Twin Peaks is a surrealist mystery horror drama TV show created by David Lynch and Mark Frost. Twin Peaks takes viewers to the title's fictional town in the Pacific Northwest, where they meet FBI special agent Dale Cooper (Kyle MacLachlan). Cooper is called in to investigate the murder of high school student Laura Palmer, and he teams up with local sheriff Harry S. Truman (Michael Ontkean). However, the investigation leads to some disturbing and surreal discoveries.

Twin Peaks premiered on ABC in 1990, but it was canceled the following year after two seasons for different reasons. ABC’s bad scheduling of Twin Peaks led to a drop in ratings, and there was also pressure behind the scenes from the network. Lynch and Frost reportedly originally planned for the mystery of Palmer’s murder to remain unsolved for longer, but the network pressured them to reveal it sooner. This also contributed to lower ratings, leading to the show’s cancelation.

However, Twin Peaks was followed by the prequel movie Twin Peaks: Fire Walk with Me and a revival in 2017.

Pushing Daisies is a comedy-drama TV series created by Bryan Fuller. Pushing Daisies introduces the world to Ned (Lee Pace), a pie-maker with an exceptional ability: he can bring dead things back to life with his touch. However, if something is revived for more than one minute, a similar “life value” in the vicinity dies to keep balance, and if he touches the revived being or thing again, they die for good.

Now, Ned is a pie-maker who runs his own restaurant, while also using his powers to help private investigator Emerson Cod (Chi McBride) solve murder cases by briefly reviving the victims to get information. Ned’s life takes a turn when his childhood sweetheart, Chuck (Anna Friel), is murdered, so he brings her back to life, but he can’t bring himself to touch her again. Pushing Daisies is a unique combination of mystery, comedy, drama, and a colorful, whimsical, and vibrant aesthetic, being labeled a “forensic fairy tale.”

Despite being a hit with critics, Pushing Daisies was impacted by the 2007-2008 Writers Guild of America strike, which later led to a drop in ratings that made ABC decide to cancel the show after just two seasons. As a result, season 2 had a rushed cliffhanger ending, and Pushing Daisies became one of the best and most unfairly canceled shows of the 2000s.

Firefly is a space Western drama TV series created by Joss Whedon. Firefly takes the audience into the year 2517, after humans have arrived at a new star system. The two surviving superpowers have united to form the central federal government known as the Alliance, deciding that all the planets must join under its rule. Of course, this sparked disagreement, leading to the formation of a group of Independents and a Civil War – unfortunately, the Alliance won.

Firefly, then, follows Captain Mal Reynolds (Nathan Fillion), his second-in-command Zoe Washburne (Gina Torres), and their crew, all of them on the side of the Independents, as they travel through space while running away from the Alliance and working (mostly illegal) odd jobs to survive. Firefly is now one of the best sci-fi TV shows of all time, but it was canceled after 11 of its 14 episodes aired.

The main reason for Firefly’s cancelation was low ratings, but this was a result of Fox airing the episodes out of order and in a terrible time slot that didn’t allow it to find its audience. The show’s high production costs were also a problem with such low ratings, and so Firefly was canceled. However, the show got a movie, Serenity, which served as the much-needed conclusion to the show.

#3491. AirPods Pro 3 keep getting better, here’s what’s new in iOS 27

AirPods got a variety of new features this fall in iOS 27, several of which are exclusive to AirPods Pro 3 (now only $179). Here’s everything new.

Custom EQ is a feature that some AirPods users thought Apple would never ship, but iOS 27 adds it.

With Custom EQ, Apple now lets you set your own sound profile for AirPods. Per Apple:

AirPods are designed and engineered by Apple to faithfully represent music, TV shows and movies, and calls. If you prefer a different sound profile, you can customize how AirPods represent any audio played.

You can change the EQ by going to your AirPods’ settings ⇾ Audio & Routing ⇾ Equalizer ⇾ Custom. From here, you can adjust the sound profile for low, mid, and high frequencies.

Custom EQ is available on AirPods Pro 3, AirPods Pro 2, AirPods Max 2, AirPods 5, and AirPods 4.

Apple GymKit has been available for years, but only for Apple Watch. It lets you pair and sync workout data with compatible cardio equipment, like treadmills, ellipticals, indoor bikes, and more.

In iOS 27, GymKit expands to support iPhone using AirPods Pro 3’s heart rate sensor. My colleague Zac gave it a try:

The setup is simple. I tapped my iPhone to the treadmill, picked Indoor Walk (Indoor Run is also offered), and started the workout from the treadmill. With GymKit, workout data is stored privately on iPhone and removed from the equipment.

Once the workout started, the treadmill received heart-rate data from AirPods Pro 3. Meanwhile, the Fitness app on iPhone received the treadmill’s distance, pace, incline, and calorie data. Treadmills know details that an iPhone and AirPods can’t know on their own, especially incline and precise belt distance.

For more details on iOS 27’s GymKit feature for AirPods Pro 3, check out Zac’s full hands-on below.

Read more: iOS 27 basically turns your iPhone and AirPods into an Apple Watch at the gym

For most AirPods users, the single biggest upgrade in iOS 27 is Siri AI.

Siri AI is available on compatible iPhone hardware in iOS 27, and Apple made sure to expand full support for the AI assistant to AirPods too.

AirPods are essentially becoming an AI wearable thanks to the new Siri. It will let users do a lot more than the current Siri. Here are some key features via Apple’s website:

Earlier this year when AirTag 2 launched, Apple brought Precision Finding support to Apple Watch for the first time. Until now though, it’s been limited to AirTag 2.

But with iOS 27 and watchOS 27, Apple expands Precision Finding on the Watch to AirPods Pro 3.

AirPods Pro 3’s case includes the latest second-generation Ultra Wideband (UWB) chip, letting you find it with greater precision and step-by-step guidance right from your wrist.

With every batch of new AirPods features that debuts, the AirPods settings screen in the Settings app gets more cluttered.

But in iOS 27, Apple has a welcome fix: it’s redesigned and reorganized all AirPods settings.

Now, you’ll find AirPods settings organized into more categories and submenus, accompanied by colorful icons. It makes finding the right setting way easier and more intuitive than before.

Read more: iOS 27 revamps AirPods settings in a big way, here’s the new design

#3490. ‘Josephine’ Review: Another Heartsick Horror Film About Real Monsters from ‘Soft & Quiet’ Filmmaker

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on January 23, 2026 during the 2026 Sundance Film Festival. Sumerian Pictures will release the film in limited theaters on Friday, November 20, with a wide release to follow on Friday, December 4.]

At this point, filmmaker Beth de Araújo is two for two. Not just in terms of the quality of her films — impeccably crafted fever dreams of very different stripes and horrifyingly similar themes — but in how these films make the viewer feel.

More concisely: with her “Soft & Quiet” and “Josephine,” de Araújo remains undefeated when it comes to making stunning films that I will both heartily recommend and never, ever watch again. Related Stories If There’s Generative AI in ‘The Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,’ It’s Not the First Time David Fincher’s Used It Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage

The word that comes to mind when watching a de Araújo feature is heartsick. That applies to the feeling bestowed on both the audience and her characters (the good guys and the bad guys). While her first film, the unrelenting “Soft & Quiet,” was cleverly designed to appear as if it was shot in a single real-time take, her sophomore feature is more about the steady accumulation of dread. The heroines of “Soft & Quiet” recognize what they are dealing with almost immediately (the force of the evil that is bent on destroying them is what’s surprises most), but the star at the center of “Josephine” is not just wounded by the sickness that suddenly infiltrates her young life, but her complete lack of understanding about what is happening to her and why.

In both films, it’s not just bad deeds that upends everyday lives, it’s real evil, actual monsters, perversions that don’t only show up in a movie screen. That’s true terror.

Based loosely on an experience de Araújo, who both wrote and directed the film, experienced as a child, “Josephine” initially lulls us into a false sense of safety. It’s early morning in San Francisco, and fledgling soccer star Josephine (Mason Reeves, riveting in her first role) is getting ready for a run with her devoted dad Damien (Channing Tatum, bringing incredible girl-dad energy to the role). It’s something the pair do every Sunday morning: get up early to watch Premier League football, run through a woodsy neighboring park, and kick the ball around.

For her second film, de Araújo leans less on clever camera tricks, though she and cinematographer Greta Zozula occasionally put us in Josephine’s own perspective, shooting as if we are looking through the eight-year-old’s eyes. As with “Soft & Quiet,” the gimmick works, grounding us in Josephine’s world and immersing us, if briefly, in what the world looks like from her vantage. Jo-Jo, as her dad calls her, is plucky and fun and filled with energy, so when she briefly zips ahead of her dad while on their run through Golden Gate Park, it just seems like everyday high-jinks.

But when the path forks (about as heavy-handed a metaphor as de Araújo will ever employ), Josephine goes to the left, while Damien goes to the right. What she finds there will forever alter the course of her life, and set “Josephine” off on a heart-wrenching journey with no easy answers. Curious and watchful, Josephine ducks behind a tree when she sees a woman (Syra McCarthy) running into a public bathroom at the bottom of a scrubby hill, and she sinks even further down when a young man (a bone-chilling Philip Ettinger) follows the unknown woman into the tiny building.

De Araújo’s approach to portraying on-screen violence only furthers that heartsick feeling: straightforward, unsparing, and absolutely devoid of any possibility of being compared to “torture porn.” What we see, what Josephine sees, is something no person should ever witness or experience. And that’s the root of the film’s power: how do we talk about things that we should not have words for?

When Damien arrives on the scene, it kicks off what will become one of Tatum’s best performances yet, a deep-feeling and heartbreaking exploration of layers of emotional unease. Damien does everything “right,” ensuring both Josephine and the woman are safe, chasing after the assailant, calling the cops, a neat little checklist of “how to handle an emergency.” And yet, the damage has already been done. There will be more to come.

Even when Josephine begins to seek out answers to what she’s seen (snatching her mom’s phone to search “raip,” reeling at what she discovers), it’s impossible to make sense of everything. There are things to fear she never even know existed, and the deep-seated powerlessness that overtakes her causes her to act out in chilling and increasingly volatile ways. Her parents’ reactions don’t help: her exceedingly calm mother Claire (Gemma Chan, thrilling as a character just barely holding it together) wants her to see a therapist now, her more action-oriented dad is eager to put her into self-defense classes. The mixed messages both give off (to say nothing of their own barely concealed terror) do little to help Josephine, who soon becomes someone almost entirely different than the care-free kid she just was.

She also picks up a new friend: Ettinger begins to appear to her, a literal haunting figure, never saying a word, yet barging into nearly every moment of Josephine’s already upended life. It’s the sort of choice another filmmaker fight fill tricksy or silly, but that de Araújo delivers with the maximum of impact. And that we, like Josephine and only Josephine, can see him only furthers our immersion into her world. It almost goes beyond empathy.

Josephine’s steadily unfolding breakdown is only compounded by the arrival of yet another situation no eight-year-old should ever have to encounter: handling the messy investigation of the crime itself. How she might help (or not) drives one more wedge between Josephine and her parents, who all have a different take on what the “right” thing to do is.

If these questions sound heady and heavy, they are, but de Araújo’s masterful ability to interrogate tension on every level keeps the film clipping along, each turn both a surprise and an inevitability. The monsters are here, they are real, and they’re coming.

“Josephine” premiered at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival.

#3489. Star Wars’ 2-Part Sci-Fi War Thriller Has One of the Best Seasons in TV History

A quiet, grounded rebellion unfolds through intimate losses like no other in Disney's sci-fi thriller

In 2022, Disney was having a pretty strange year with its franchises. There were some major wins, such as the hugely financially successful release of Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness and Turning Red becoming a streaming hit. Its films also earned $4.9 billion at the box office that year.

However, some franchises fared much worse with their fans than others. After the poor reception of The Book of Boba Fett in February and the controversy surrounding Obi-Wan Kenobi in May, Star Wars fans weren't particularly hopeful that Andor, Tony Gilroy’s gritty spy series, would restore the franchise to its former greatness.

Those fans were wrong. Gilroy didn’t just renew fans' hope that Star Wars could be more than a franchise for children; he delivered a culturally relevant story about the sacrifices people make — love, comfort, and friendship — in the fight against tyranny, all within a single season. The series also expanded the background of a beloved character, Cassian Andor, so that even if a second season had never arrived, that story would have worked perfectly as a sequel to Star Wars' most beloved films.

Though Andor’s second season is more critically acclaimed — and has a handful of awards under its belt — its 12-episode first season is immaculate at showcasing how the Empire’s oppressive grip destroys the hope of those living under its regime. It also kickstarts Cassian Andor’s ascent into the hardcore rebel fans know from Rogue One.

The series opens with Cassian (Diego Luna) searching for his sister on Morlana One, where he runs into trouble and kills two Pre-Mor security officers. On the run, he returns home to the planet Ferrix and tries to sell an Imperial Starpath unit to fund his escape, but he gets caught up in the machinations of the rebel organization known as the Axis Network, led by Luthen Rael (Stellan Skarsgård).

A survivalist first and foremost, Cassian is staunchly opposed to getting caught up in the rebellion against the Empire — right up until he can no longer look away from the Imperial machine and the horrors it inflicts.

Star Wars has always been a story about a group of revolutionaries fighting a tyrannical empire, but most of the audience’s time has been spent following big-shot heroes and chosen ones like Han Solo, Leia Organa, and Luke Skywalker. There were always Jedi, and the good guys rarely, if ever, lost.

That isn’t the case for Andor, which, like its predecessor Rogue One, follows the little guys — the people who aren’t showered with public praise and given medals as rewards. Even in the brief time we spend with minor characters like the insurgents on Aldhani and the prisoners of Narkina-5, each is given complexity and a compelling reason to fight the Empire. No one is driven by the Force or has a secret, epic backstory. They're on the ground fighting for what they believe in, or in most cases, because they have no other choice.

It helps that Andor is possibly the most beautiful Star Wars has ever looked on television. From Aldhani’s cultural event in the Scottish Highlands — one of Star Wars’ most heart-stopping moments — to Ferrix, built brick by brick, Gilroy’s production values are unmatched. It doesn’t just look like a Star Wars show’s backdrop. Each planet feels lived-in, with communities that feel unique in both appearance and behavior.

Andor season 1 is Star Wars at its very best: an epic, winding tale of Cassian’s journey from thief and scoundrel to a man who would inevitably sacrifice himself to give the Rebellion those all-important Death Star plans. The people he meets along the way, from Mon Mothma to Luthen Rael, are equally brilliant at showing how far people will go to bloody the nose of the Imperial machine.

Andor’s second season is every bit as compelling as the first, with each trio of episodes in the 12-episode season spanning a year. Still, Gilroy’s original five-season plan being cut to two is evident in the leaps in character development between episodes, leaving some choices unearned and, frankly, at odds with what audiences see in Rogue One. It is still leagues above many Star Wars shows — though Rebels will always remain my favorite — but compared to how tightly contained season 1 is in telling Cassian Andor's story, season 2 just doesn’t compare to the masterpiece that is the debut season.

#3488. How to Transfer Your Playlists to Tidal Music for Free

I recently switched music streamers from Apple Music to Tidal. I like Tidal's strict anti-AI features, the fact that it pays higher royalties to artists than other major streamers, and its focus on high quality audio. I wrote a post featuring eight hacks for Tidal users, but I wanted to highlight one in particular: How to transfer playlists without paying anything.

Tidal points new users toward third-party transfer tools like TuneMyMusic and Soundizz, which are both easy to use, but they're subscription services, and they only transfer a few hundred tracks for free. I have thousands of tracks, saved in a ton of playlists. The easy solution was to grumble and sign up for a month, then cancel when the tracks were transferred, but it just didn't sit well with me. A playlist is just a collection of song names, so why should I have to pay anything to transfer it? To solve the problem, I came up with a simple script that transfers playlists from Apple Music, Spotify, and any other service that lets you download your tracks as a text file to Tidal. I will not be charging a fee.

Download your playlist as a .txt file. You can do this directly from Apple Music under File>Library>Export Playlist. You can't from Spotify, but the free site Exportify will download any of your playlists as a spreadsheet file you can save.

Install Python on your system. Double click "install certificates" in the folder that opens after installation.

Download this script. Save it in the same file as your playlist.

Run the script: (For Mac, open Terminal. For Windows, go to the Command prompt. Type python3 on a Mac or py on Windows.) Drag the script into the terminal window and press enter. It should ask you to drag your downloaded playlist into the window next.

Sign in to Tidal. Hit "Approve" to give permission for Tidal to run the script.

Have a banana. The script is going to search for all the songs on your playlist and match them to Tidal's library, so it can take a little while. I tested it with a playlist from Apple Music with 2,397 songs. It took about 20 minutes and found 2,362 of my tracks, a 99% success rate.

Fix the leftovers: The program creates two separate text files for "orphans." One is songs it couldn't find and one is songs it might be worth double-checking manually.

If everything goes well, your large playlist should be available on Tidal.

Note: The script uses a community-created library to talk to Tidal, so it could stop working if Tidal changes things up.

#3485. Eight Important Router Settings You Should Check (or Change)

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Your router is a key piece of your home network, as it connects all of your other devices to the internet. This also makes it a highly valuable target for attackers and can leave your data vulnerable—especially if you simply plug your router in with its default settings unchanged. Whether your router is brand new or it's been a while since you audited your existing setup, these are the key settings to check and change right now.

Your router's security protocol determines how encryption and authentication work to protect data that's transmitted over your network. WPA3 Personal is the newest standard and the most secure, so if it's available on your router, enable it. It's compatible with devices that support Wi-Fi 6. Some older devices may not work with WPA3, in which case the WPA2/WPA3 Transitional mixed mode is a good alternative. At minimum, set your router to WPA2 Personal (AES).

Some routers ship with factory default login credentials, which are the username and password you need to access your device's admin dashboard. (This is not the same as your network name or wifi password, which you set up later.) Default router passwords are searchable online, which leaves your router's admin settings open to anyone. Once you get into your dashboard for the first time, change the default credentials and enable two-factor authentication for your admin account if available.

While some newer routers do have unique, device-specific defaults, it's a good idea to check this setting and ensure it's secure. If you're prompted to create custom admin credentials during the setup process, do it.

Your network name, or SSID, is how your network appears when you search for available wifi. By default, this may be the name of the router brand or a short string of characters, but you should choose something unique to your network. Make sure there's no identifying personal information, such as your name or house number. While you may be tempted to hide your network and obscure your SSID, this may actually make your information less secure, so keep this setting disabled. You can, however, add "_nomap" to the end of your network name, which prevents your router's physical coordinates from being mapped by location databases.

The password to access your network should also be unique and secure and should not include obvious personal information. One option to keep it memorable and easy to type is to create a passphrase using five to seven unrelated words that, combined, have at least 16 characters.

Being able to log into your router's admin dashboard from anywhere may be useful if you have complex networking needs or troubleshooting issues that often have to be addressed when you're away from home, but it also leaves an entry point open for attackers. Turn off remote management to prevent anyone from accessing your dashboard unless they are on your network. (This is also a great reason to have strong, unique admin credentials.)

Two additional settings that leave your network vulnerable are Wi-Fi Protected Setup (WPS) and Universal Plug and Play (UPnP). The former lets users connect to your network with a PIN, which can be vulnerable to brute-force attacks. The latter allows smart devices to easily connect to your network—but this also allows malware to spread more readily. You may need to have UPnP on in order to connect devices initially but should disable it afterward.

Any easy win for your network security is segmenting traffic to different networks, so if one is compromised, the data on the others remain unaffected. Many wifi routers have a "guest mode," which creates a separate SSID and password that you can share with visitors instead of giving them your primary network credentials. You can also set up a separate network for all of your smart home and IoT devices so exploitable vulnerabilities in these devices don't put your computers, phones, and other connected devices at risk too.

Routers run a type of software—called firmware—just like any other device. Firmware controls the router's core functions and is not immune to vulnerabilities, which can be exploited by bad actors. And, just like other types of software, manufacturers occasionally push updates to patch these flaws. Check your router's dashboard to see if automatic updates are toggled on. Some devices require an opt-in for auto updates during setup, so you should enable them if they are off. Some routers may even require manual updates—in this case, set a monthly or quarterly (at minimum) calendar reminder to check for patches.

#3484. Epic accuses Apple of withholding 122,000 documents, seeks daily fines

In a new filing, Epic Games accuses Apple of withholding more than 122,000 documents related to its proposed App Store commissions and asks the court to impose daily fines until the company complies. Here are the details.

As a result of the lawsuit Epic Games brought against Apple in 2020, Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers ruled in 2021 that Apple would have to, among other things, allow developers to direct users to alternative payment methods outside the App Store.

Apple responded by allowing external payment links, but imposed a commission of up to 27% on purchases made through them. This, in turn, led the court to find Apple in civil contempt for violating its injunction. Since then, Apple has been trying to overturn that ruling, a dispute that has now reached the Supreme Court.

At the same time, district court proceedings will determine what, if any, commission Apple may charge on purchases made through external payment links. Apple submitted its proposal on August 13, calling for commissions ranging from 5% to 15%, and Epic is expected to respond after Apple completes its document production.

In a new filing, however, Epic is accusing Apple of withholding more than 122,000 documents related to how it arrived at its proposed commission rates.

One of the many aspects of the ever-sprawling battle between Epic Games and Apple centers on document production.

In its new filing, Epic says Apple has repeatedly failed to produce documents detailing how it arrived at its proposed commission rates, accusing the company of withholding materials it deems irrelevant to the proceedings.

Epic argues that Apple previously used questionable claims of attorney-client privilege to withhold documents during the contempt proceedings, but has now changed tactics.

Apple does introduce one tactical change from its prior campaign of delay. Whereas during the contempt proceeding Apple used bogus claims of privilege to evade its discovery obligations, this time Apple withholds thousands of documents on bogus claims of irrelevance. For example, Apple is withholding well over 99% of the documents returned by running the agreed-to search terms on the files of the four custodians Apple says decided on the proposed fee (Tim Cook, Eddy Cue, Carson Oliver, and Kevan Parekh (Apple’s new CFO)) and three other key individuals (Nate Barton, Alex Roman, and Phil Schiller). Apple claims these withheld documents are not relevant to this proceeding-even though they hit on case-specific terms such as “proffer,” “contempt,” “injunction,” and “link-out.” To put this into context, while Apple produced 632 custodial documents returned by these search terms (including families), Apple is withholding over 122,000 based on a claim of non-responsiveness. Moreover, Apple claims that it completed its production from the files of these custodians, yet its production does not include a single substantive email discussing the rates Apple ultimately proposed; any notes or communications reflecting what occurred at any meeting where these rates were discussed or decided; any internal analysis of the financial or business impact of the proposed commissions; any App Store profit and loss statements; or any support for Apple’s assertion that its incremental link-out costs are “essentially zero.”

Epic goes on to state that “Apple cannot be trusted to fix this problem on its own,” proposing instead that the court order Apple to produce all non-privileged documents matching the search terms agreed upon by both parties, regardless of whether Apple considers them relevant.

Under this proposal, Apple would still be allowed to review documents for attorney-client privilege, but it would be up to Epic to determine which of the remaining documents are relevant to the case. Epic argues that existing confidentiality protections would prevent it from using any of the information for purposes unrelated to the litigation.

Given Apple’s position, Epic respectfully submits that the Court should order Apple to produce to Epic all non-privileged documents that hit on the Parties’ agreed-upon search terms, so that Epic itself can sift the wheat from the chaff. Doing so will avoid further delays and place no burden on Apple. Moreover, doing so would not raise any of the concerns that required Special Master involvement in the prior proceeding, namely concerns around the production of privileged Apple information to Epic. Under Epic’s proposed remedy, Apple would be allowed to continue its review for privilege. For these reasons, Epic asks this Court to order Apple to produce all non-privileged documents that hit on any of the Parties’ agreed-upon search terms by December 2, 2026 (one week after Apple’s deadline to substantially complete production), irrespective of any relevance or responsiveness assessment.

Finally, though Epic does not propose a specific dollar amount, it “asks that the Court impose on Apple a daily monetary sanction for each day Apple fails to comply after December 2, 2026.”

According to the court docket, a hearing on Epic’s motion was initially scheduled for November 24 before Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers. However, a new order filed today, which has yet to be made public, refers the discovery dispute to a magistrate judge and includes a notice terminating deadlines and hearings.

#3483. GTA 6: Should You Choose Cut Or Pure In "Dealer's Choice"

Chapter 3 of Grand Theft Auto 6 will finally take Jason and Lucia to Vice City proper, and they'll be in for a whole new laundry list of shenanigans throughout their time in the big city. One of the very first missions you can embark on in Chapter 3 is "Dealer's Choice," Jason's first foray with the legendary Boobie.

As you listen to Boobie's explanation for the job, he'll make it clear that there's a way for Jason to make a little extra money if he can cut the product, and eventually players will need to make a choice about whether to use the cut product for some extra cash or to stick with the pure product.

Choosing the cut product in "Dealer's Choice" is a much more violent and chaotic option. Once you arrive at the meetup with the buyers and hand over the cut cocaine, one of them will take it into the car to check it out, noticing right away that something is off. They'll call Jason out and you'll have to make a choice of whether to hand over the product for half the price or tell them to take it or leave it.

If you give it to them half price, you obviously only get half the money, and they won't take the product because it's impure. If you choose to go the violent route, there will be a quick-time event that you'll need to complete to avoid getting capped in the head, and then it will be a full-on shootout with the buyers where you and Dre'Quan will need to escape.

When Jason and Dre'Quan go to Boobie's supplier, Tyrone, he'll further iterate that there's an opportunity to make some extra money if you go with the cocaine that's cut with baby powder. Dre'Quan will leave the decision up to Jason, and you'll be given a choice between the cut product with a bunch of dollar signs or the pure product by itself.

Choosing the pure product will result in the deal going off without a hitch and Jason acquiring the funds as expected, and you'll be able to complete the mission relatively easily, despite not making any "extra" money from cutting the product.

There really aren't any benefits to choosing the cut product, despite it appearing that you'll make more money if you do so. There are only downsides in fact, with the buyers either giving you only half of what's owed or trying to kill you outright. The alternative is much better, and the only potential altercation is with a vagrant on your way out as opposed to having to shoot your way out through dozens of enemies in the street and then making a getaway.

Ultimately, choosing the Pure product is a much safer and easier decision in Grand Theft Auto 6's "Dealer's Choice" mission in Chapter 3.

#3482. 30 Years Later, Sean Connery's Secret James Bond Thriller Is Officially Free on Streaming

Back in the 1990s, Michael Bay was really cooking. Before the slog that was 2001’s Pearl Harbor and his divisive Transformers movies that simultaneously hurt and enhanced his career by sidelining him for decades, Bay debuted as a director with a trio of really exciting movies that prioritized a fun experience for the viewer. First there was 1995’s Bad Boys, the Will Smith and Martin Lawrence buddy-cop film that became a popular franchise. He closed out the decade with the genre-defining end-of-the-world disaster film Armageddon. And in between those two, he gave us a tightly crafted thriller that is currently free to stream (with ads) on Pluto TV.

The Rock stars Sean Connery in one of his last great roles as John Patrick Mason, a cunning British Army officer who was imprisoned 30 years earlier without a trial​​​​​​​, for stealing classified U.S. information. He’s also the only man to ever escape Alcatraz, and the U.S. government​​​​​​​ is now offering him his freedom if he’ll help a team of Marines break into the long-shuttered prison he once broke out of.

Alcatraz, nicknamed “The Rock,” has been taken over by rogue Marine general Francis X. Hummel (Ed Harris) and a brigade​​​​​​​ of loyal soldiers. Hummel is bitter about the government covering up some Marine deaths during Operation: Desert Storm and now he’s demanding restitution for the families (and himself). He’s also holding Alcatraz tourists hostage​​​​​​​ and has deadly chemical weapons pointed at San Francisco, which he’ll fire into the city if they don’t comply.

That’s why the government also pairs Mason with bookish FBI agent Dr. Stanley Goodspeed​​​​​​​, a chemical weapons expert played by Nicolas Cage.

As a duo, Connery and Cage have wonderful chemistry in the film. While Connery was well into his 60s at the time (as was his character), Mason​​​​​​​ was an adept ex-spy who was specially trained by the British intelligence service MI6​​​​​​​ and is still very capable for his age. This contrasts nicely with Cage’s character, who has no field experience and is nervous on the mission, but proves himself to be brave, capable, and adaptable. While not overly comedic, their relationship follows the typical buddy movie bromance where both gain respect for each other over the course of the film and they become trusted partners by the end of it.

The movie is also relentlessly entertaining. It begins with a heist by Hummel’s forces to get the missiles, followed by their takeover of Alcatraz. Being the most knowledgeable person alive in regards to Alcatraz, the government calls upon Mason, who soon escapes in a wild car chase through San Francisco, just to get a little face time with his estranged daughter (Claire Forlani). Despite tearing apart the city with a stolen Hummer, Mason is quickly forgiven and the mission to sneak into Alcatraz proceeds normally. Once they get to the island, the movie has one tension-filled action set piece after another​​​​​​​. It’s what Bay does best.

The movie has no subtext and little subtlety​​​​​​​, but that’s honestly fine. It knows what it is and embraces its status as a fairly mindless action movie. There is some of the clunky dialogue that sometimes plagues Bay’s movies, but it’s not distractingly bad, I think because The Rock has three excellent leads who know how to work with subpar​​​​​​​ material and still create a compelling character.

I rewatched The Rock last night; it was my first time seeing it in more than a decade.​​​​​​​ Not only did it still hold up as a fun watch, but I kept in mind the internet fan theory that Mason is actually Connery’s James Bond using an alias, having been captured by the U.S. for stealing some intelligence on behalf of MI6​​​​​​​. And while I’m not a Bond expert, it all does seem to line up pretty well with Mason’s personality and backstory. While the theory certainly isn’t canon to The Rock or the Bond films, it’s an interesting, added lens through which to watch the film.

Finally, another great thing about this film is that it was made during an era when all of these explosions were done with practical effects. While digital effects have certainly come a long way, you can feel the difference in a movie like The Rock. It’s the kind of thing that makes you long for ‘90s action films and kind of makes you wish that Bay never got involved in the Transformers franchise at all.

#3481. The iPhone Duo Is Getting Face Unlock

Apple dropped iOS 27.2.1 last week, patching a handful of security vulnerabilities and bugs—including two iMessage flaws that let people read messages they shouldn't. But while most of us are running this version (or should install it as soon as possible), others are running something different—iOS 27.3.

Apple is currently beta testing the third major update in the iOS 27 era, and anyone—developer and public tester alike—is free to install it at their leisure. With it, comes the return of the Health app, vertical Safari tabs, and Siri AI app actions, among other new features. But for users of Apple's first foldable, the iPhone Duo, iOS 27.3 brings two rather notable changes—both of which are for the better.

With the second iOS 27.3 developer beta, Apple is introducing face unlock for the iPhone Duo. The foldable famously ships with Touch ID, the first new iPhone since the third-gen iPhone SE to do so. While that isn't a problem per se, many of us are used to unlocking our iPhones with our faces. This update just lets new Duo owners keep up with that muscle memory.

Now, take note: This isn't Face ID. No software update can introduce new hardware, so the iPhone Duo still doesn't have the camera tech required to power Apple's Face ID system. As such, the Duo's face unlock is likely not as secure as Face ID on other iPhones. Perhaps that's why your iPhone Duo will require Touch ID for Apple Pay and passwords, or after 45 minutes of inactivity. This feature seems to be one of pure convenience: If you want to be able to unlock your Duo with your face (at least, some of the time), you can.

What's more, this isn't a default setting. If you're running the beta, or if you're reading this after iOS 27.3 drops, you can find the option in Settings > Touch ID & Passcode.

Apple made a big deal about the continuity involved with opening and closing the iPhone Duo. As you do, your content moves with you seamlessly—a very Apple thing to do. That said, you might expect folding the Duo to lock it, but it doesn't. You need to hit the side button to actually put the phone to sleep.

iOS 27.3 changes that. If you so choose, you can enable a setting to lock your Duo whenever you close it. That won't work for everyone, of course—some users may still want to move between modes without worrying about locking their Duos. But for those who would rather lock their devices whenever they fold them up, the new option is under Settings > Display & Brightness.

#3480. Report: iPhone set to gain market share in 2027 amid industry-wide slump

Apple could see iPhone shipments rise 7% next year, giving it a 26% share of global smartphone shipments, according to a new report. Here are the details.

As detailed by AppleInsider, a new Morgan Stanley research report says Apple is poised to ship approximately 270 million iPhones in 2027, a 7% bump from 2026.

The forecast comes amid a change of pace for Apple, which launched only the iPhone 18 Pro models and iPhone Duo this fall, with the rest of its iPhone lineup reportedly set to arrive early next year.

Morgan Stanley notes that this could push some purchases from late 2026 into 2027, contributing to the projected shipment growth without necessarily reflecting an increase in underlying demand.

The report also comes as Apple and the rest of the smartphone industry continue to grapple with rising memory and storage prices, though previous reports have suggested that Apple is better positioned than many of its competitors to absorb those costs.

Apple raised iPhone prices in September, after keeping them stable for much of the year while competitors had already introduced price hikes. In some cases, they raised prices more than once within a matter of months.

Back to the report, it notes that global smartphone shipments are expected to drop 5% next year, compared with a previous forecast of 3.6% growth. That said, it’s still an improvement over the estimated 13.8% decline in 2026.

When it comes to Apple and the iPhone specifically, Morgan Stanley notes that consumer interest in upgrading has remained largely unchanged year over year, with 37% of iPhone owners saying they are extremely likely to upgrade within the next 12 months. That’s compared with 41% of smartphone owners overall, a figure that dropped by 2 percentage points year over year.

As for the market’s reaction to the iPhone Duo, Morgan Stanley found that 22% of non-iPhone users surveyed expressed interest in switching to Apple’s foldable device, with that figure reaching 34% in China.

Importantly, Morgan Stanley’s survey was conducted after the iPhone Duo was announced, but before it launched, so these figures reflect consumer interest rather than actual purchasing behavior.

Apple Intelligence was another factor examined in the survey, with Morgan Stanley concluding that AI features are becoming less important in driving iPhone upgrades, while factors such as battery life and upgrade eligibility are gaining importance.

Finally, Morgan Stanley found that Apple’s customer retention rate increased three percentage points to a record 93%, while its net switching rate improved to 12%.

Huawei was the only other major smartphone brand to show a positive and improving net switching rate, while Samsung and Google remained relatively neutral, and Xiaomi, Motorola, Honor, Oppo, and Vivo recorded negative rates.

#3479. ‘Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall’ Review: PTA’s Spellbinding Concert Doc Is a Gorgeously Tender Performance

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on October 2, 2026 during the 2026 New York Film Festival. Janus Film will release the film in limited theaters on Friday, November 20.]

Paul Thomas Anderson‘s eye for vivifying music onscreen dates back to the late 1990s when, after “Boogie Nights,” he made Technicolor mini-masterpiece music videos with his ex-girlfriend Fiona Apple — or made a San Fernando Valley-sized shrine to Aimee Mann with his third feature, “Magnolia.” Since then, he’s kicked around with HAIM while turning one third of its Los Angelino triumvirate, Alana Haim, into a screen actress. He’s shot for Radiohead and made a regular collaboration with band member Jonny Greenwood to create some of the 21st century’s most memorable scores. Many young cinephiles now associate the mischievously lilty notes of “Phantom Thread” with the poison promise of new love and obsessive creation. Related Stories If There’s Generative AI in ‘The Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,’ It’s Not the First Time David Fincher’s Used It Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage

Last December, PTA teamed up with Geese frontman Cameron Winter to film, while operating his own Panavision camera, his solo stage performance at Carnegie Hall, running through sparse piano arrangements of tracks off his solo album, “Heavy Metal.” The result, a 72-minute film now being distributed roadshow-style by Janus Films before inevitably living on the Criterion Collection, is a stunning arrangement of its own: a deeply achey, sincere but never cloyingly earnest concert movie that’s tender to the point of frailty. (Benny Safdie counts as a co-producer, and the film’s scratchy New York quality and setting can’t help but have his imprint.)

The matted-hair, lithe Winter can seem a bit uncomfortable in his own skin in the public eye, as he did onstage ahead of “Cameron Winter at Carnegie” at its New York Film Festival world premiere at Alice Tully Hall. But on the piano, laser-beamed into his songcraft, he’s quietly electrified, at seemingly at peace as his tenorous vocal glissando and nimble fingerwork on the piano produce shiveringly tender folk ballads that echo Harry Nilsson and Van Morrison. (The usual comparisons to Tom Waits and Rufus Wainright are right, too, but Winter is his own strange thing.) If you weren’t previously sold on the wily Winter antic rock chaos of Geese — rapidly becoming one of the most popular contemporary art rock bands of these times — you’re about to. Paul Thomas Anderson has created a rhapsodic shrine to the man that is nonetheless ballad-sized in its emotional scale.

Winter, in December, played and sang to a sold-out crowd of more than 2,700 at the stately cultural temple that is Carnegie Hall, and this film can at times feel like a religious experience, an incantation, a lonely vigil. The singer/songwriter was 23 at the time of the performance, one year older than Bob Dylan when he headlined Carnegie Hall, and similarly at the precipice of major fame. Fixed on a mobile rig that will at times careen and whoosh across the stage when not otherwise holding on Winter, Anderson’s camera catches the expressionism and chiaroscuro of stage lights illuminating and fading off the singer’s face.

The result is hynoptic, a concert film up there with “Stop Making Sense” but for introverts. Songs like the popular single “$0” acquire an even more wrenchingly somber quality as a lovelorn protagonist rues being exploited by a relationship (“You’re making me feel like a dollar in your hand / You’re making me feel like I’m a zero dollar man”). Stripped of production, his indie hit “Love Takes Miles” plays even better. While many of the songs sort of hover in the same key and bleed into one another, that makes for an all the more transfixing experience. The lack of an interstitial anything save for a sweet prologue and moving coda make for experience also that’s immersive, deep, and the kind whose truth you can feel somewhere in your body even if you can’t quite articulate it.

“Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall premiered at the New York Film Festival. Janus Films will release it in theaters starting November 20.

If you want to take things up a notch, consider this 5.1 channel sound system. Not only does it include far more channels than a single soundbar, but you're also adding a dedicated subwoofer to the mix. A subwoofer will make those thuds, explosions, and low vibrations much more pronounced than on a soundbar alone. For $149.99 (originally $249.99), you can get the ULTIMEA 5.1 surround sound system, which comes with a soundbar—replicating left, right, and center channels—two rear speakers, and a subwoofer.

I love projectors and Roku. To me, a Roku projector just makes sense, especially at $119.99 (originally $389.99). This projector is portable and has the Roku OS already installed, so it's easy to project it against a wall, ceiling, or screen, whether it's indoors or outdoors. It's easy to set up; you just need an outlet nearby and to dim or turn off the lights. If you have Bluetooth speakers, you can hook them up to create a more immersive sound.

The TCL Q51GB is a QLED Google TV that is a great value for anyone looking for size, color, and features. The 98-inch class is heavily discounted at its $898 price (originally $1,499.99). TCL makes one of the best QLEDs for the money, and their technology keeps getting better. This TV supports Dolby Vision and Dolby Atmos, and if you're a gamer, you get a refresh rate of 240Hz that is automatically triggered with its Auto Game Mode feature.

Gaming monitors can get pricey fast. At $159.99 (originally $299.99 at launch), this 27-inch Samsung Odyssey G55C curved gaming monitor offers a 1440p resolution, a 1000R curve, a 165Hz refresh rate with FreeSync and G-SYNC compatibility to keep screen tearing to a minimum, and features like Samsung’s Virtual Aim Point and Contrast Enhancer. It's a solid choice for gaming, especially at this price point.

Alienware makes great gaming laptops, and the Aurora is a great option for anyone who wants to get all the essentials without spending too much. At its current $1,099 price (originally $1,999), the Alienware Aurora 16 becomes a mid-tier gaming laptop at a "budget" price. We reviewed the higher-tier Aurora 16X and were impressed with it. The Aurora 16 has a slightly slower processor, a dimmer display with half the refresh rate, a smaller battery, and a weaker graphics card, but given its price, it's great for a gamer looking for a solid gaming laptop in the $1,000 range.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Yes. Walmart, Best Buy, Target, and Home Depot will all have in-store deals, some of which you might not find online, so if you're able to take a trip to your local retailer, keep your eyes open for different deals.

Amazon has a much larger inventory of tech products on sale, but the ones they both sell are mostly priced the same. While Amazon may have more deals, Walmart usually has a couple of surprise flagship tech products on sale that Amazon will later price match. So taking all of that into consideration, the best one will be whichever has whatever you're looking to buy at the lower price.

#3477. John Wayne And John Ford's Best Movie Is The Searchers

​​August is a freelance film writer. She studied journalism and cinema at American University. She is a member of the journalism honor society, Kappa Tau Alpha. August has written for various networks and publications, including PBS, Gargoyle Magazine, TheThings, and Identity Theory Magazine. Before returning to entertainment writing, August worked in the Automotive section of U.S. News & World Report. In her free time, August enjoys watching movies in theaters, watching movies at home, listening to podcasts about movies, reading books about movies, watching video essays on movies, talking about movies, thinking about movies, and doing crosswords.

Director John Ford and actor John Wayne are one of the most prolific film-making duos in cinema history. The two collaborated on 14 movies over their 50-year friendship and professional partnership. They are particularly well known for their powerful influence on the Western genre, producing nine such films together. In 1956, Ford and Wayne released their greatest Western of all time—The Searchers.

This iconic duo met when a young Wayne—known as Marion Morrison at the time—worked a summer job on the Fox lot. Ford, who was already an experienced director at the time, took a shine to the kid and helped propel his early career (via PBS). Following various walk-ons and side roles in Ford films, Wayne had his first lead role in the 1939 Stagecoach. Considered among the best Westerns ever made, this classic movie launched Wayne’s name into Hollywood stardom and cemented the actor-director duo.

Wayne then led a plethora of iconic Ford Westerns, and five non-Western films, such as The Quiet Man (1952). The two made consistently competent movies and helped forge the Hollywood Golden Age. Wayne and Ford made their greatest masterpiece of all time in 1956.

From Warner Bros. Pictures, The Searchers stars Wayne as Ethan Edwards, a Confederate veteran searching for his niece who was taken by a Comanche tribe. The anti-heroic figure fights not to save his niece, but to kill her so she will not assimilate into the Native American culture. The gritty Western is a seminal and influential classic.

The Searchers is widely considered the best Western movie of all time, with Stagecoach not trailing far behind. It is a clear standout among Ford and Wayne’s 13 other movies, despite fierce competition.

Starting with Stagecoach, Ford generally cast Wayne as the standard Western hero with an individual but strong moral compass. Wayne’s Hollywood stardom was synonymous with his good guy persona. In The Searchers, Ford casts Wayne as his grittiest and most complex character yet, perhaps of all time.

Playing against type, Wayne gives a visceral performance as the racist and vengeful Edwards. Throughout the film, Edwards is driven by an obsession for revenge and an outdated, warped understanding of the world. The lone rider becomes so out of touch with civilized standards that, by the end, he cannot return home and is left wandering the rugged wilderness.

Wayne appears to delight in this meaty role and delivers a career-topping performance. Both Ford and Wayne are at their best in The Searchers.

The Searchers transcends the Western genre to become one of the most influential movies of all time. It is number 12 on AFI'S 100 YEARS...100 MOVIES list, above Star Wars, which is inspired by The Searchers. The film is both groundbreaking and timeless for its masterful story, characterization, and thematic cinematography.

The narrative follows the classic “hero’s” journey formula of The Odyssey, in which a battered man attempts a long quest home and uncovers new inner-truths along the way. In the case of Edwards, he returns home only to realize that he has lost touch with humanity and no longer belongs in a civilized home space—relegating him to life as a wondering lone rider.

This classic formula, reimagined and repopularized by The Searchers, has influenced cinema for the past five decades. Film critic Stuart Byron once proclaimed, “in the same broad sense it can be said that all recent American cinema derives from John Ford's 'The Searchers’” (via The Washington Post).

The Searchers is credited as one of the first revisionist Westerns, paving the way for modern gems like No Country for Old Men. It also introduced ideas such as the central anti-hero that would gain traction in Spaghetti Westerns of the 1960s. Outside the Western genre, The Searchers has directly influenced a variety of modern movies, including Martin Scorsese’s 1976 crime-drama, Taxi Driver.

The influential cinematography in Ford's film cannot be downplayed either. The 1956 Western impressively used visual language to express and highlight narrative themes. This is particularly true in the film's iconic final shot, which communicates Edwards' inability to return home by framing his body through a doorway as he wanders into the distance.

While Ford and Wayne’s storied professional partnership has produced a plethora of stellar films, The Searchers remains their greatest accomplishment.

#3476. WhatsApp’s first-party chat history backup service moves ahead

Select WhatsApp beta testers on iOS are now seeing an option to use the app’s own backup service as an alternative to iCloud. Here are the details.

A few months ago, WABetaInfo reported that WhatsApp was working on its own backup service as an alternative to the current method of backing up chats, which relies on Apple’s iCloud.

At the time, the feature wasn’t available even to beta testers, but WABetaInfo’s report provided details on how it would work, including 2GB of free storage, optional paid plans for larger backups, and mandatory end-to-end encryption for backups stored on WhatsApp’s servers.

Now, the site reports that some WhatsApp users running the latest TestFlight build are seeing the option to switch from iCloud to WhatsApp’s own backup service, suggesting that a wider rollout may not be too far off.

Users can switch to WhatsApp cloud storage from the Chat backup screen. Here, users will have to choose the backup provider they want to use. If they choose WhatsApp, they will have to secure their backups using end-to-end encryption. Since encryption is mandatory, users cannot skip this step. However, they can choose a different method to encrypt their backups. For example, users can secure their backups using a 64-digit encryption key. Users who do not know what to choose can opt for the passkey, which is the default method WhatsApp recommends. After users complete the setup, they can back up their chat history on WhatsApp’s servers. WhatsApp keeps the backup on its servers for four months after a subscription expires. If users do not renew their subscription, WhatsApp deletes the backup permanently.

Importantly, the site notes that backups stored on WhatsApp’s servers cannot currently be used to restore chats across platforms, meaning users switching from iPhone to Android, or vice versa, will still need to rely on WhatsApp’s built-in chat transfer feature.

Although the feature appears to be rolling out to beta testers first, the report notes that “the latest version available on the App Store is also compatible with this functionality,” meaning WhatsApp could theoretically enable it for users running the public version without requiring another app update.

To read WABetaInfo‘s full report, follow this link.

#3475. GTA 6 Makes It Nearly Impossible to Play Without Killing Anyone

In my defense, I don’t know how to drive IRL or in GTA

Grand Theft Auto 6 is out now, and for my initial playthrough of Rockstar’s latest giant open-world game, I wanted to try something a bit out of left field: How long could I play without killing anyone? I’d do my best Batman impression: brutally beating my foes, crippling them with excessive medical debt, but keeping them alive.

Yeah, that didn’t last long. Turns out trying to not commit crime in the game that’s all about committing crime is a difficult task.

The first mission was easy enough. Jason has to rescue drug runner Donnie from a gang of rednecks who keep tigers in cages. (Surely that will end well for them.) After I rescued him, I got into a fist fight with a beefy boy and knocked him out. So far so good. Jason had a pistol on him and could pick up weapons around the swamp base, but, trying to avoid a shootout at all costs, I stealthily booked it away from the rednecks and toward the water, avoiding any detection (and potential for violence).

That was the opening mostly-on-the-rails mission, but things quickly went south when I was left to my own devices. During the next in-game day, players are given a few mission options. I met up with Cal, Jason’s buddy who’s not cut out for a life of crime, and we drove to a police impound lot. I needed to steal a car with a trunk full of weed, and this is where shit hit the fan.

Look, I never learned how to drive in real life, and am not the biggest fan of it in video games. Driving for more than a few feet without hitting anything or anyone is an impossible challenge in games, and driving in GTA 6 feels especially difficult; I can never figure out the right speed to go, and sharp turns are the bane of my existence.

So maybe I was always doomed to run over a cop on my way out of the impound lot.

Police officers swarmed Jason after he unhooked the red Phoenix and hotwired it. Too much was happening at once: an on-screen message about how I could open the gate, cops flinging open the driver’s side door and trying to rip Jason from the vehicle, and police radio chatter pouring out of my controller speaker. I’m not ashamed to say I restarted this mission several times just trying to figure out how to get out of the lot by carefully not running over any cops.

And then, who pulls up in front of the gate I’m about to crash through but a do-gooder cop hopping out of his vehicle? I assumed the giant pool of blood leaking out of him after our collision meant he wasn’t long for the world.

I did get caught on that attempt (again, driving is hard), and had to restart. On my next attempt, I got away blood free. Did that mean I succeeded in not killing anyone, or did the roadkill cop mean I failed? Didn’t matter, since soon after I killed someone and there was no going back.

If you need to check Snapmatic, pull over

After purchasing a longarm from an Ammu-Nation, Jason gets jumped. This was my first fistfight, meaning I had to navigate on-screen messages telling me how to fight while trying not to die. I was just pressing buttons, y’all. Instinctively I pressed whatever button flashed up on screen, which meant, after knocking out one dude, I picked up his knife and started attacking with it. Knives — much more lethal than Jason’s fists!

I killed one goon before dropping the knife and knocking out the third and final guy. I checked my playthrough stats and, yep, that guy was definitely dead. And I was barely two hours into the game. There’s a lot to do in GTA 6, and plenty of control schemes to learn just to be able to do all that stuff. Players have already accidentally kicked bodega cats (heinous) because of a fumbled button press.

Still, not to be deterred by my early-game kills, I tried to soldier on with committing as little murder as possible. I soon learned this was impossible. During the “Hey, Arnold” mission, Jason gets into a car chase with one of landlord Brian’s old buddies. Arnold’s got goons on motorcycles protecting him and, ya know, I said I wasn’t very good at driving.

I tried my damndest not to kill them, but that wasn’t going to happen. I accidentally ran into some, and they didn’t survive their facetime with Brian’s big-ass truck. But, hey, at least I got to spare Arnold at the end.

I’ve played a few hours since, and have tried to keep up my “no killing” policy. It’s especially tough in shootouts as Rockstar’s third-person shooting has never been the most fluid, and aiming for nonvital parts of people — when getting shot at myself — is a tall task. Still I’ve kept it up. I’ve enjoyed how you can incapacitate enemies by shooting them in the legs; the hit indicator will turn yellow to show that they’ve been wounded, but not killed. Now, is that guy I shot — but didn’t kill! — who then lay unmoving and face-first in knee-high water really going to get back up again? Who knows, but I did my best to not kill him.

GTA 6 is hyperrealistic, to the point that sometimes people can’t tell the difference between GTA 6 footage and real life. That realism extends to each of its hand-crafted NPCs. They look and behave so much like real people that I’m hesitant to just pull out a gun and start blasting, a sentiment that prospective players shared ahead of the game’s release.

Violence toward very-real-looking humans is something I’ve thought a lot about this year, and the restrictions on it in 007 First Light is part of what made that game really appeal to me. Pragmata and Onimusha: Way of the Sword are two of my favorite games this year, and I have to think that’s partly due to the fact that the violence in them is directed toward robots and demons, respectively. I don’t really have to think twice about slicing a people-devouring demon in half. Firing on small-time crooks in Vice City? That’s something that will give me pause.

I don’t know how much longer I’ll try to keep up my self-imposed difficulty modifier and continue on with as little violence as possible. After all, the appeal of this series is, ya know, committing crime. Hey, sometimes you gotta shoot some dudes in GTA 6 before they shoot you. But it was certainly fun while it lasted.

#3474. What ‘Digger’ Has in Common with Gary Oldman’s Winston Churchill and Charlize Theron’s Megyn Kelly

Tom Cruise‘s performance in Alejandro González Iñárritu‘s “Digger” is one of the boldest and most entertaining of the actor’s career, as he suppresses not only his usual movie star charisma but his entire way of walking and talking to play paunchy, aging oil tycoon Digger Rockwell. Cruise is barely recognizable in the role, which is about as far from heroic characters like Pete “Maverick” Mitchell and Ethan Hunt as Cruise’s Ron Kovic in “Born on the Fourth of July” was from race car driver Cole Trickle almost 40 years ago.

To aid in his complete transformation, Cruise called on one of the best prosthetic designers in the business, Kazu Hiro. Hiro has turned Gary Oldman into Winston Churchill (“The Darkest Hour”), Charlize Theron into Megyn Kelly (“Bombshell”), and Dwayne Johnson into “Smashing Machine” Mark Kerr, but transforming Cruise into Texas oilman Digger Rockwell was a whole new task — one made even more challenging by Iñárritu and Cruise’s persistent striving for perfectionism, and constant eagerness to try new approaches. Related Stories If There’s Generative AI in ‘The Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,’ It’s Not the First Time David Fincher’s Used It Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage

“Alejandro is an amazing director, and he has lots of ideas,” Hiro told IndieWire. “Every day he comes in with a new idea, and we have to come up with an answer for how to achieve it. And Tom is really professional, and expects everybody else to be at that same level, ready for any situation. After the first day of testing, I learned that I had to stay flexible to respond to whatever they wanted.”

To that end, Hiro created modular prosthetics whose parts could easily be swapped out and moved around, so that Cruise and Iñárritu could constantly try new looks. “Sometimes with heavy makeup, you can’t change it,” Hiro said. “I created prosthetics that could be mixed, so we could make new designs on the spot — try this forehead with these cheeks and this nose, then change it.” Creating Cruise’s look was a constantly evolving process throughout the long prep period. “We didn’t have a clear answer until the end of rehearsal.”

Hiro’s mandate at the beginning was a bit open-ended, which gave him room for artistic exploration but also made it difficult to zero in on a precise look. “Alejandro said the character was 76 years old and an oil tycoon,” Hiro said. “He also said he didn’t want the character to look like Tom, but he still wanted to see Tom in the character.” To try to find a concrete image for Digger Rockwell, Hiro immersed himself in research.

“I researched real oil tycoons and how they aged and what kinds of lifestyles they had,” Hiro said. “Those lifestyles affect how they age.” As Hiro did more and more research, however, he realized that there was no one look that defined the entire profession he was trying to represent. “Everybody looked so different, so in the end I relied more on the storyline and how this particular character behaved.” The idea, in keeping with the slightly heightened style of the film as a whole, was to exaggerate Cruise’s features but keep the character realistic.

Hiro began with a 3D scan and life cast of Cruise, which he used to sculpt his designs. His paramount concern was allowing the actor to be as expressive as possible under the makeup. “The important part is to make the prosthetic very soft so he can move,” Hiro said, noting that three weeks before shooting, Iñárritu called with a significant change. “He decided that Digger should be 65, not 76, so I quickly made a new design. Tom is around that age, but he looks much younger than a normal 65. Under his eye was exposed and the rest of the face was covered, but I made it thin to give him freedom.”

In addition to Digger’s face, Hiro was also tasked with creating an upper body for an early scene in which Cruise would be seen stripped down to his pajama pants. The body prosthetic was intended only for that one scene, with a lighter bodysuit created for the rest of the movie. “We made a light version of the padding for under the costume, because we don’t need to see the skin after that first scene,” Hiro said. “For the first scene we made a silicone prosthetic that was a lot heavier — the body padding was around 10 pounds, but the silicone was 40 or 50.”

During one of Cruise’s costume fittings, he told Hiro he wanted to feel the weight of the silicone throughout production. “He tried the body prosthetic on and said, ‘I like this, I want to wear it every day,'” Hiro said. “I told him it would be really heavy and hot, but he said he was training and would be fine.” Since gluing the body prosthetic on every day would be extremely time-consuming, Hiro created a strong spandex foundation and glued the prosthetic to it so Cruise could slip it on each day.

“He wore that for the whole film,” Hiro said. “One time he said, ‘This is so heavy, it’s really hard on my back.’ I thought, ‘Okay, you asked for it,’ but he went through with it and finished the film, so that was amazing.”

#3473. iFixit tears down Apple HomeView, finds lots of glue and endless frustration

iFixit’s teardown of the new Apple HomeView is now up, revealing a device that seems nearly impossible to take apart and repair. Watch it below.

Following last week’s launch of the Apple HomeView, iFixit today published its teardown of the device.

Contrary to recent teardowns, which found significant repairability improvements with greater component modularity and easier access to internal components, the HomeView put up a fight nearly all the way through.

With heavily glued or adhesive-bonded components, including the display, speakers, antennas, and logic board, the teardown proved particularly challenging, even after the adhesive securing the display’s speakers was soaked in isopropyl alcohol.

At one point, one of them broke apart during removal, while the logic board required considerable force to separate from the chassis due to the thermal adhesive holding it in place.

iFixit’s teardown covered the two HomeView variants: the tabletop model and the wall-mounted version. Interestingly, there are some internal differences between them, as the wall-mounted model has a slightly wider logic board to accommodate capacitors that are housed in the base of the tabletop version.

As a result, the wall-mounted HomeView also has smaller internal speakers, which helps explain the differences in their audio systems that Apple had already acknowledged at launch.

Back to the tabletop model, iFixit’s teardown also showed that separating the display from the base requires either specialized tools or extensive, potentially destructive disassembly of the display assembly, thanks to the way Apple routed the connecting cables through the pivot mechanism.

Once iFixit was in the base, however, there was some good news: the USB-C port is modular and relatively easy to access, as are the passive radiators and the board powering the lower assembly.

Still, an extremely short cable connecting the woofer to the board underneath made disassembly difficult, with iFixit questioning how anyone would be able to reconnect it during reassembly.

Percentage of Apple owners who are interested in repairing their device. 0.000001%

Percentage of Apple owners who will actually try and repair their device. 0.00000001%

Given all these repairability challenges, Shahram Mokhtari joked that while iFixit doesn’t have an official repairability scorecard for this category of device, he would give the Apple HomeView a “BEEP this thing” out of 10.

To check out iFixit’s blog post, which features an interactive 3D CT scan of the HomeView, follow this link.
