#3446. Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage

Looks like Hollywood could be heading into the new year with relief on a national level. The push to pass a federal film and television tax credit by the end of 2026 picked up momentum on Friday at a White House press conference, where President Trump said his administration was actively negotiating the measure and predicted it would pass.

“It’s running its way through Congress, and it has unbelievable support,” Trump said. He singled out Senator Adam Schiff, the California Democrat who introduced the bill with Republican Senator Tim Scott of South Carolina back in September, and said, “I tell you what, Adam Schiff said, ‘Wow, we love that bill.’ Adam Schiff said that.” Related Stories ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch How World-Class Filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev Came Back to Life for ‘Minotaur’

Trump mentioned Georgia and New Jersey by name as states with good tax credits for film and TV production, but argued that those incentives alone would not bring enough production work back from overseas. With a federal credit, he said, “Hollywood would open again.”

Trump said his administration was also negotiating whether to extend the measure to benefit movie theaters, but said the matter was unsettled. He first publicly called for a federal production incentive in August after meeting with actor Jon Voight: one of three industry “special ambassadors” he appointed early last year.

The bill’s sponsors announced more than 60 new House cosponsors and four new Senate cosponsors on Thursday morning — with lawmakers from both parties signing on in both chambers. The following day, Trump himself brought up the Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act in response to a question about whether he could work with Democrats. Calling the bill “very bipartisan,” he said, “I can tell you right now it’s going to happen.”

Trump gave no timetable, though earlier this week, Representative Linda Sánchez, one of the bill’s House sponsors from California, called for Congress to pass it before 2027 so productions could qualify for benefits on the first of the year.

“Members of both parties have watched jobs in their districts move overseas,” she said in a release from Schiff’s office sent to the press. “Momentum is on our side, and we need to strike while the iron is hot by passing this bill before the end of the year.”

A floor vote has yet to be announced, but multiple sources told IndieWire the measure would move faster if attached to a stopgap government funding bill. If passed and approved, the federal initiative would give qualifying film and TV productions a 20 percent credit on labor expenses for American workers. The credit could reach 30 percent for productions that qualify for bonuses.

For crews accustomed to watching projects follow tax breaks to Canada or the U.K., the proposal would give producers a clear financial incentive to keep that work here for them in the U.S. The bill’s new Senate cosponsors include Republicans Katie Britt of Alabama and Thom Tillis of North Carolina — as well as Democrats Chris Coons of Delaware and Dick Durbin of Illinois.

The AFL-CIO and the American Hotel & Lodging Association also endorsed the bill, joining a coalition that already included IATSE, SAG-AFTRA, the Directors Guild of America, and the Motion Picture Association.

“Given the support from Republicans and Democrats in both chambers and the president, we can get this legislation across the finish line,” Schiff said.

#3445. Nintendo's Black Friday Deals Are Actually Pretty Good

Black Friday is nearly upon us. From now through Cyber Monday, retailers and companies alike are offering deals and discounts on their wares. While I always keep an eye out for Nintendo deals offered by stores like Amazon, Best Buy, and Walmart, it seems the company is offering its own discounts this year—and, surprisingly, they're actually pretty solid.

Last Thursday, Nintendo announced its Black Friday discounts. We've already seen Switch 2 sales ahead of the Black Friday season, but now, Nintendo has confirmed an official discount for the console.

Starting Nov. 22 through Dec. 5, you can pick up Nintendo's Switch 2 Mario Kart bundle for $499.99, down $50 from $549.99. That includes the console, a download of Mario Kart World, and a 90-day Nintendo Switch Online Individual Membership.

If you already have a Switch 2 console and/or Mario Kart World, you're not left out of the Black Friday deals here. From Nov. 22 through Nov. 29, Nintendo is also running discounts on several high-profile Switch and Switch 2 games:

Donkey Kong Bananza was one of Nintendo's launch titles for the Switch 2. And while it's been out for over a year, Donkey Kong's first 3D game is still among the best-reviewed titles on the console. Nintendo is taking $30 off the game's MSRP for this promotion.

Kirby Air Riders on Switch 2 is only the second installment in the series. The original launched all the way back on the GameCube, and while the title typically runs for $69.99, Nintendo is letting it go for $39.99.

Metroid Prime 4 arrived last year after an 18-year wait from Metroid Prime 3: Corruption. The game typically retails between $59.99 and $69.99 for a physical copy, but Nintendo is selling it for $39.99 during its early Black Friday promotion.

Super Mario Galaxy (both the original and the sequel) are beloved by fans. These titles originally launched on the Wii, and Nintendo rereleased both for the Switch. (The company offers a free upgrade to the Switch 2 edition.) Nintendo asks $69.99 for this combo, and while you can find it for under $60, you'll officially be able to pick it up for $39.99 before Black Friday.

Nintendo's latest Mario Party, Jamboree, has a Switch 2 edition with a rather staggering MSRP of $79.99. While it's the version of the game with the most features, it's also the most expensive. You'll be able to buy it for $39.99 for Black Friday, saving up to $40.

Nintendo rarely offers official discounts on some of its biggest titles, especially in this current era. In addition, Nintendo announced a sale on its digital store that runs from Nov. 19 through Dec. 2, though it didn't say which titles would be on sale. Just keep an eye on all these dates: The Switch 2 console promotion runs longer than the physical and digital games discounts, while the digital sale runs longer than the physical sale. Nintendo says that these discounts will be available "at select retailers," as well as its brick-and-mortar locations in New York and San Francisco. You can also buy the Switch 2 bundle through Nintendo's website.

It depends! Its Nintendo Switch 2 bundle deal runs from Nov. 22 through Dec. 5; the select games listed above will be on sale from Nov. 22 through Nov. 29; and digital titles will have discounts from Nov. 19 through Dec. 2.

While we don't know which digital titles will be discounted yet, we do know that physical copies of Donkey Kong Bananza, Kirby Air Riders, Metroid Prime 4: Beyond, Super Mario Galaxy + Super Mario Galaxy 2, and Super Mario Party: Jamboree will be on sale for $39.99 each.

Yes! The Switch 2 alone costs $499.99, so you essentially get the game for free. Mario Kart World is also one of the console's best multiplayer titles right now, so it makes sense to pick it up in this bundle.

#3444. The 8 Best Miniseries of the Streaming Era, Ranked

We are living in the streaming era of television. Though Netflix launched streaming video-on-demand as far back as 2007, they didn't produce their first original series, Lilyhammer, until 2012; and it wouldn't be until 2013, with the release of shows like House of Cards and Organge Is the New Black, that streaming would truly gain cultural hegemony over the entire televisual medium. Gone was the era of network television, and in came the era of streaming.

Miniseries in particular find their roots in the British serials of the 1950s, but it was when American television adapted the format in the 1970s that it really became a cultural phenomenon. From classics like Roots to 21st-century masterpieces like Band of Brothers, the era of network TV delivered many a great miniseries. The streaming era of television has definitely not fallen behind, though, giving us in the likes of Adolescence and xxx some of the greatest miniseries of all time. Only streaming originals can qualify for this list.

After actor Stephen Graham read a news article about a young boy stabbing a girl to death, he proposed telling a story inspired by this wave of violent attacks by young boys against girls in Great Britain through the miniseries format. He and Jack Thorne then co-created Adolescence, a scathing critique of incel culture, male rage, toxic masculinity, and the "manosphere." It's an awfully timely yet sensitive topic, but the series treats it with precisely the care it deserved.

The result is one of the best miniseries of the last five years, composed of four episodes all shot in a single take, which lends the series an air of urgency and raw authenticity that elevates both its emotional and intellectual impacts tremendously. Bolstered by its exceptional cast (including Graham himself and a revelatory Emmy-winning turn by young Owen Cooper) and its excellent writing, it's one of the most important crime drama series of the 2020s.

Beth Macy's non-fiction masterpiece Dopesick: Dealers, Doctors, and the Drug Company that Addicted America deals with the origin and evolution of the opioid epidemic that began in the United States around 1996 with the release of OxyContin. In 2021, Hulu adapted that story in Dopesick, which just so happens to be one of the most perfect miniseries of the last 25 years. It's every bit as ambitious, expansive, and insightful as the book it's based on.

It's such a devastating investigative drama that it's most definitely not an easy watch, but boy, is it an important one. It's a 360-degree systemic portrait of absolutely every link in the chain of the opioid crisis, from the Purdue Pharma boardroom to the victims of the crisis. Elevated by its incredible cast (including the likes of Michael Keaton and Peter Sarsgaard) and its non-linear structure, it's about as urgent as streaming-era miniseries get.

Far more than just one of the best movies of the last 100 years, Francis Ford Coppola's The Godfather is one of those artistic masterpieces so great and so important that they straight-up transcend their medium. What really makes it such a special movie, however, is that the story behind it is every bit as interesting and compelling as the film itself; and that story is the subject of Paramount+'s The Offer.

Making-of dramas can either be so full of propulsive energy that they're irresistibly entertaining, or so cold in their approach that they feel like Wikipedia pages come to life. The Offer definitely belongs to the former group. The larger-than-life performances, far from just being impressions, are truly phenomenal; the writing turns Hollywood politics into a genuinely momentous thriller; and the show's approach to the story should be enough to make any cinephile melt in enjoyment.

Western television hadn't really been a particularly prominent part of the mainstream for several years now, but Taylor Sheridan apparently never got the memo, because with his Yellowstone universe, not only did he become one of the kings of streaming-era television, he also made Western shows mainstream again. Case in point: the Paramount+ prequel 1883, one of those modern Western shows that are absolute masterpieces.

Visceral, poetic, and emotionally devastating, it's not only one of the best television prequels of the streaming era, but also one of the most unflinchingly realistic Westerns that the small screen has seen in years. Leaving behind the soap-opera tone of the franchise's flagship show and stripping the Western genre of its nostalgia and problematic myth-making, it's a series fully dedicated to showing just how unforgiving the Oregon Trail really was. The characters are engrossing, the performances are top-notch (Sam Elliott's in particular), and the visuals are some of the best of the whole franchise.

There are plenty of great Netflix shows with under 30 episodes—many of them miniseries—, and one of the best is undoubtedly The Queen's Gambit. Based on the eponymous 1983 novel by Walter Tevis, it rapidly became one of the biggest Netflix sensations of the COVID-19 pandemic lockdowns, launching Anya Taylor-Joy's mainstream popularity into the stratosphere.

Pivot[s] around many of the usual clichés that tend to make sports drama miniseries trite.

One of the most kinetic, visceral, and utterly addictive character studies that the small screen has seen in years, Queen's Gambit proved that it was perfectly possible to tell an absolutely fascinating and exhilarating story built around chess. Pivoting around many of the usual clichés that tend to make sports drama miniseries trite, Queen's Gambit is elevated by its stunning visuals, its tight pacing, and its constant intelligent subversions of the "tortured woman genius" trope.

Four Netflix characters, four completely different ways of showing up for somebody. This is the one who fits how you actually do friendship, and what having them in your life would be like.

You do not do friendship at half volume, and neither does he. What you want is somebody who says yes to the plan before you have finished describing the plan.

You are the friend who makes things happen, and so is she. Together you would be mildly exhausting to everyone around you and completely delighted with yourselves.

You have no patience for pleasant lies, and she has no ability to tell them. What looks like coldness from the outside is the most reliable friendship on this list.

You look after whoever is having the worst day. So does he. It is the least strategic way to move through the world and the best possible quality in a friend.

History has seen many creatives put on the crown of Television's King of Horror, and there's a strong argument to be made that the man currently wearing that crown is Mike Flanagan. Though he's also a filmmaker, Flanagan is perhaps best known for his work on the small screen, with the Netflix miniseries The Haunting of Hill House often being credited as the project responsible for turning him into a household name in the field of mainstream horror.

One of the scariest TV shows of all time, Haunting of Hill House is a landmark in the history of streaming-era horror television. The 2010s saw the rise of "elevated horror" on the big screen, referring to a form of horror filmmaking that proved the genre could be full of artistic merit, and this was one of the first true "elevated horror" projects that the small screen ever saw. Rooted in themes of grief and family dynamics, Haunting of Hill House is a masterclass in atmosphere and non-linear storytelling.

It's an absolute tragedy that it was canceled after only one season, but Scavengers Reign was originally pitched as a self-contained miniseries anyway, so the series fortunately managed to come to a satisfying conclusion. Though fans have been clamoring for a follow-up for years (and creators Joe Bennett and Charles Huettner have confirmed that there are definitely ideas in the tank), regardless of whether it ever does actually come, this will be one of the best miniseries of the 2020s anyway.

There are plenty of sci-fi miniseries that belong on everyone's bucket list, and this is arguably one of them. Proof that animated science fiction deserves far more respect than many people are willing to give it, Scavengers Reign is a cartoon unlike any other, with some of the most layered world-building and most deliciously complex character work that any sci-fi miniseries has seen in years. HBO Max really dropped the ball with this one.

Back in 1989, five Black and Latino teenagers were wrongfully convicted of the rape and beating of Trisha Meili in New York City, a case that came to be known as the Central Park jogger case. They were exonerated in 2002 after DNA evidence matched another man's confession, but the damage was done, and the foundations for a gripping Netflix miniseries created and directed by Ava DuVernay were laid down. One of the most hopeless Netflix shows to date, When They See Us is the best that streaming-era miniseries have had to offer thus far.

Part psychologically intimate character study; part razor-sharp critique of systemic injustice and tabloid sensationalism; part unflinching depiction of coercion and systemic failure within the American justice system, When They See Us is a must-see for anyone who enjoys watching flawless television. Indeed, it's one of the most flawless shows of the last decade, complete with some exceptional tour-de-force performances, deeply layered writing, and top-notch production values.

#3441. 20 Best Revenge K-Dramas, Ranked

The revenge genre is perhaps the single greatest, most unique expression of South Korea's storytelling flexibility across television and film. It's produced timeless hits like Park Chan-wook's Vengeance Trilogy, and inspired ill-fated Western attempts to capture its greatness. But a big aspect of what makes South Korean revenge storytelling work, particularly in K-dramas, is the sliding scale to which it applies its moral ambiguity, with often spectacularly compelling results.

This produces the typical action-packed revenge tales such as Netflix's thriller, Agent Kim Reactivated. But revenge can also present itself in complicated psychological battles, whether it be in the workplace or between lovers and married folk, with motives scaling from self-preservation to idealistic notions of justice in the face of society's failings.

The best revenge K-dramas are thus not of one single subgenre, but across a spectrum, with exemplars featuring some of the medium's all-time greats, with little to no evidence that creative minds in the industry are running out of ideas anytime soon.

Starring none other than Alchemy of Souls male lead Lee Jae-wook, The Impossible Heir had plenty going for itself as a combined workplace and revenge thriller. The series follows Lee as Han Tae-oh, a cold and calculating son of a murdering father who helps plot the rise of Kang In-ha (Lee Jun-young), the illegitimate scion of the chaebol Kangoh Group, to take control of the corporate empire, alongside Na Hye-won (Hong Su-zu), the daughter of a debt collector.

One of the best aspects about The Impossible Heir that's not necessarily as common in other K-drama genres is the compelling power drama that unfolds over the course of its run. It's a psychological battle with succession being the ultimate goal, featuring the usual transgressive undertones that make Korean revenge cinema and television the envy of the world, with The Impossible Heir easily being worth checking out for these qualities alone.

Most revenge K-dramas are some of the darker series to come out of South Korean television. Crazy Love takes a slightly more light-hearted approach to revenge because the series is a romantic comedy with some telenovela tendencies.

When the powerful GOTOP CEO Noh Go-jin receives death threats, he fakes amnesia so that others will be more likely to help him. His secretary, Lee Shin-ah, decides to take advantage of that amnesia, pretending to be his fiancée as a way to enact revenge against him for the way he’s treated her at work. That isn’t the wackiest plot point in this series, though, as it gets both more dramatic and sillier as the show goes on.

There are exes enacting schemes of their own, terminal illnesses, and an attempted murder plot. The revenge plot might not be exactly the same as those looking for a darker series would expect, but it’s definitely a unique entry into the subgenre.

Pyramid Game is inspired by a webtoon of the same name, and it’s set in an area ripe for revenge: an all-girls school. The show doesn’t take a long-term look at revenge as so many other K-dramas do, but a more immediate one.

In this school, popularity polls are used to rank classmates. Those with the most positive rankings are treated well by the other students and teachers, while those who fall to the bottom are relentlessly targeted and bullied. When a transfer student named Seong Su-ji finds herself the target of harassment and even violence, she decides to change the game. She makes it her mission to climb the social pyramid of the school in order to save herself, but it leads to revenge and rebellion.

The series was named among NME’s best K-dramas of 2024 and earned Jang Da-ah a Blue Dragon Series Award nomination for Best New Actress.

Featuring Start-Up's Nam Joo-hyuk, Vigilante is a stellar example of the strong revenge thriller and overall mature lineup found on Hulu and Disney's content distribution network. Nam stars as Kim Ji-yong, a student at his police academy who dons his "Vigilante" alter ego at night, spurred on by his traumatic past as he saw his mother die at the hands of Choi Sung-soo. Despite the killer being found guilty, his soft sentencing prompts Ji-yong to hunt him down, as well as others who escape true justice.

Much like other recent Hulu and Disney+ K-dramas like Connect, Vigilante is based on a manhwa hosted by Naver Webtoon, with this series co-created by CRG and Kim Kyusam. The series follows Ji-yong's antics as Vigilante, picking up the media's attention, including reporter Choi Mi-ryeo (Kim So-jin) and the support of wealthy DK Group vice-chairman Jo Gang-ok (Lee Joon-hyuk). The series explores the classic moral quandary about vigilante justice against those who slip through the cracks, while mixing in some stellar action throughout.

The World of the Married took some fire from critics when it first premiered in 2020, with some believing that it featured too much sex and violence. Despite that, it became one of the most-watched shows in South Korea in 2020 as well as one of the highest-rated K-dramas on television at the time.

The series follows Ji Seon-u, who appears to have the perfect life to outsiders looking in. She’s a successful doctor with the seemingly perfect husband. She, however, discovers that her husband has been having an affair and that her friends know about it. With the knowledge that everyone in her life has been lying to her, she decides to attempt to take revenge on everyone who has hurt her.

The World of the Married is a riveting drama that leaves the audience on the edge of their seats and wondering just how far one woman will go to get even.

Time travel shows make for a fascinating subgenre on Korean television. There has been an influx of them since 2020, but only a few of them tie into the concept of a revenge K-drama. Reborn Rich melds the two concepts together in an interesting way, and South Korean fans loved it, making it the most-watched K-drama of 2022 in the country.

This series kicks off with a murder. Yoon Hyun-woo, an employee at a chaebol (a huge family-owned business in South Korea) sees something he suspects is wrong and ends up killed for trying to do the right thing. Hyun-woo gets a second chance to make things right, though, because his soul is brought back to life as the youngest member of a chaebol family years before his murder.

Reborn as Jin Do-jun, the protagonist decides to start using what he knows of the future to improve his life and to take revenge against those responsible for his death.

Perfect Marriage Revenge was originally a webnovel before being adapted into a webtoon, and finally, a live-action K-drama. Like Reborn Rich, the series combines time travel elements with those of revenge.

It features a young woman, Han Yi-hoo, who was adopted by a wealthy family and tries her best to please them. Nothing she does is ever good enough, though, as she discovers her husband has feelings for her little sister and her mother has been selling her reproductions of paintings as counterfeit art and framed her for the crime. When she ends up dead, she wakes up one year before all of these events unfold, giving her the chance to get revenge on her family.

A number of great K-dramas employ a romantic theme that calls for the two lead characters to go from hating each other to falling in love.

She strikes up a deal with the man she knows her little sister has had a crush on, marrying him and agreeing to help gain the approval of his grandmother in exchange for his help. The family drama combined with the revenge elements make this one fascinating K-drama.

Rugal is a sci-fi action thriller following a former South Korean elite police officer, Kang Gi-beom, who, after being framed for his wife's murder, joins an organization armed with biotechnological enhancements to fight against a national crime syndicate in his quest for vengeance. The show is extremely bloody, featuring very realistic execution-style murders, so it's not for the faint of heart.

Rugal also features impressive production quality and visuals, but being a webtoon adaptation, it encounters some pitfalls common to adaptations, with forced musical montages and network TV quality. The series is a bloody revenge tale, with Gi-beom not only seeking revenge for his wife's brutal murder but also for framing him for her murder. It also has tinges of sci-fi, as he is blinded in the attack on his wife and receives two artificial eyeballs to regain and enhance his sight, a sort of superpower.

Revenge of Others follows Ok Chan-mi (Shin Ye-eun), a high schooler seeking revenge after her twin's mysterious death. Teaming up with the morally upright but troubled Ji Soo-heon (Lomon), they navigate a creepy, gothic school filled with suspects, including school bullies and a repeat senior with a shady medical history. The show's excessive use of dramatic plot twists can be overwhelming.

Yet, the engaging lead performances and the show's stylish execution that blends in early 2000s teen horror still make it worth the watch. The series is all about revenge, as Ok Chan-mi is looking for the person she believes is responsible for her brother's apparent suicide, and she won't stop until they find those responsible and makes them pay for the death. Since the police deemed it a suicide, she is in this alone, which adds to the stakes of everything she does. The series premiered on Disney+ in the United States.

The Innocent Man, listed on Netflix as Nice Guy, follows the story of Kang Maru (Song Joong-ki), who seeks revenge against the woman who betrayed him. Once a promising medical student, Kang Ma-ru's life spirals when his love, Han Jae-hee, lets him take the blame for a crime he didn't commit. Years later, Ma-ru, now a bartender and gigolo, plots against Jae-hee using Seo Eun-gi, a chaebol heiress and the woman he once loved's step-daughter, only to fall for her.

Despite criticisms due to a particular amnesia plotline, the show is full of some emotional moments that tug at the heartstrings. This is a very different revenge tale, as it isn't revenge against criminals, but it is revenge against someone who hurt him, and he is targeting a daughter instead of the woman who betrayed him. However, as a romantic story, it hits the right notes and is a fan favorite. It went on to win six honors at the KBS Drama Awards with 13 nominations.

#3440. If There’s Generative AI in ‘The Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,’ It’s Not the First Time David Fincher’s Used It

The uproar over the alleged use of generative AI imagery in “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” has taken a familiar path. Early responses to the Netflix film penned by Quentin Tarantino and directed by David Fincher have pointed out egregious examples of generative video artifacts sticking out in key flashback moments in the film — including one shot from the trailer where it certainly looks like a video AI program rendered a wagon the wrong way around.

The criticism is of the use of generative AI in principle as a fundamental betrayal of the creative process — but it’s also of Fincher, as a director who, historically, has been meticulous with the level of detail and intention in every single shot of his films. In the early responses to Fincher’s latest, there’s been a lot of surprise and disappointment about this particular filmmaker being caught up in an AI controversy. Related Stories Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch

At first blush, his approach seems at odds with using generative AI video, which relies on regurgitated (and, it bears repeating every time, stolen) data. But Fincher has defended his use of AI to the LA Times as a way to continue to innovate on an art form that is, after all, just over a hundred years old.

That defense really shouldn’t be surprising, given Fincher’s history with AI specifically. Although he’s been critical of generative tools in the past, Fincher admitted to using them (never publicly disclosing which) in the 4K remaster of “Se7en,” which the director described as a process of needing to remake the negative in order to battle the ravages of time (and the thousands of tiny scratches that would show up in 4K). “If you could see a 30-year-old negative and what it looks like even when immaculately stored — it was an enormous amount of fixing, just digs and scratches and cinch,” he told EW at the time.

That kind of image restoration technology was around long, long before the Anthropic IPO failed to save the stock market, but its level of precision has increased enormously in the past year. There were also sequences in the stored “Se7en,” though, where generative tech filled in gaps from the original. For one example, Fincher talked about a moment where a camera pan overshot the mark and changedh a shot. The performance had been good enough to use a technically flawed take — and, combined wit an unused take, allowed software to generate the missing information and restore the intended image.

“It ends up being the most thrillingly stupid fix in the world because if you see it, we didn’t do our jobs. And you probably won’t see it. You probably won’t be aware that it’s happened. But you look at it, and you just think to yourself, ‘It’s so nice that we can fix that kind of stuff today,'” Fincher told Collider about that moment in “Se7en.”

By Fincher’s own lights, then, the problem with AI in “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” is that people are painfully aware of it. AI critics might make a distinction between video restoration tools that work on existing projects and those tools being used because they can more quickly and cheaply generate originals that would’ve otherwise needed to be crafted by human hands. Having something AI-generated isn’t necessarily better than nothing when it comes to art, and choosing to AI-generate a Western chase sequence inside of, say, 10 seconds isn’t a solution to all.

Still, Fincher knows what he’s doing. This past week, he emphasized to the LA Times that he’s not a Luddite when it comes to film: “We’re talking about a thing that’s a hundred years old, and everyone’s going, ‘Stop. Pencils down. No more iterating. It’s not necessary to have at your fingertips the ability to change the color of that person’s eyes.’ Well, it exists. Should we not use it?”

The answer is an emphatic “No!” to some And they can certainly be mad, or disappointed, or disheartened about Fincher’s decision to use AI tools. The one thing they shouldn’t be is surprised.

At this stage in its theatrical run, the most expensive Indian movie ever made will likely struggle to break even theatrically. The film entered production as the first installment of a planned duology, based on an epic text sacred to Hindus all over the world. Both movies cost more than $400 million combined, according to their primary producer.

The first film was released ahead of the Hindu festival Diwali, which significantly boosted its box-office performance. In fact, the film reached the $100 million mark at the worldwide box office before Godzilla Minus Zero, pulling ahead of the acclaimed sequel. That said, Godzilla Minus Zero has a reported budget of $15 million, continuing the frugal approach that director Takashi Yamazaki took with 2023's breakout hit Godzilla Minus One.

Buoyed by excellent reviews, Godzilla Minus Zero has grossed more than $100 million worldwide so far, and is expected to surpass the $57 million domestic haul of its predecessor in the coming weeks. Four worlds and four completely different ideas of what a good life looks like. This is where you belong, what it would ask of you, and what you would get back in return.

You belong somewhere old enough that the mountains have names and somebody can still tell you who gave them. Middle-earth is for people who think the right thing is worth doing even when it will not be finished in their lifetime.

You want the sea, a crew, and absolutely nobody telling you where you are allowed to go. The Grand Line is the world for people whose main ambition in life is finding out what is over there.

Events in the mythological text serve as the foundation of not only the Hindu festival of Diwali, but also Dussehra.

The movie has so far grossed more than $150 million worldwide, pulling ahead of 2023's word-of-mouth sensation RRR, as well as this year's Supergirl and Mortal Kombat II. Distributed domestically by Sony, the film debuted in more than 1,400 theaters. It lost more than 300 theaters in week two, and its theater count is expected to fall to 681 this Friday in week three—a decline of more than 700 from its opening count.​​​​​​​ You can still watch Ramayana on the big screen and stay tuned to Collider for more updates.

#3436. All 7 Steven Spielberg Adventure Movies, Ranked

The master Steven Spielberg is probably most commonly associated with sci-fi movies, and while some of his best sci-fi movies did set the blueprint for lots of sci-fi filmmakers in his wake, he has always been surprisingly versatile when it comes to his genre choices. What matters the most to him are stories that make his audience feel.

Spielberg helped invent the very idea of blockbuster filmmaking. Even when he's telling stories in high-concept genres like hard sci-fi or historical biopics, he is as focused on the same tenets of his approach to story. Whether you're watching a Spielberg thriller, his visual identity is instantly recognizable. And it's arguably in the adventure genre where Spielberg's eye for spectacle, character, and heart converge best.

Over the past five decades, Spielberg has directed some truly great adventure movies. In fact, even some of his harder genre movies, like Jurassic Park and E.T., which are primarily sci-fis, hit a lot of the same beats as traditional adventure movies. But because they are primarily sci-fis, they don't qualify in this ranking. We're sticking with pure adventure movies, and since cutting his teeth in the early 1970s, Spielberg has made seven, but which is the best?

If you were to take some of the more venomous criticism of the fourth Indiana Jones movie to heart, you would think that The Kingdom of the Crystal Skull was an irredeemable disaster that dragged the good name of Indiana Jones into the mud. Released 19 years after Temple of Doom, it is a step down in quality, but rewatching it now, some of the harsher critiques feel a little unnecessary.

The most baffling complaint centers on the reveal that aliens are real and visited Earth, as if that is any less believable than the biblical and supernatural elements of the original trilogy. Spielberg being a master of sci-fi, embracing an alien invasion story also makes a lot of sense. Some fans also saw The Kingdom of the Crystal Skull as simultaneously too much like the first movie, damning it with direct comparisons.

The replacement of the Nazis with Cold War enemies, headed by Cate Blanchett's Irina Spalko, does slightly take something away from Indy's original spirit, but it was never enough to really sink the movie. This is fundamentally not a terrible movie... It's just a little wayward in its good intentions. The addition of Shia LaBeouf's Mutt was also far from the catastrophe that was claimed, and there are some really good set pieces and a lot of the same magic that made the original trilogy great.

An unfortunate box office bomb, Spielberg's expensive take on one of Roald Dahl's most famous fantasy adventures is widely remembered as one of his more disappointing releases. But, there's nothing really wrong with Spielberg's adaptation. It's beautiful, thanks to his reunion with frequent collaborator Janusz Kamiński, the music is great because John Williams was brought in again, and the acting performances, led by the brilliant Mark Rylance as the BFG, are all very good.

It is arguably more of a Spielberg take on the story than a truly faithful Roald Dahl adaptation because Spielberg couldn't resist the temptation to shave off some of the darker edges. The result of that is, while it's incredibly charming and very witty, it doesn't quite have the moral complexity of the original story, which might explain why it didn't quite land at the box office. It also didn't help that it was released at the same time as Finding Dory.

Look a little more closely at The BFG, and it's not massively different to E.T., given that it's also about an unconventional friendship. While calling it a classic is perhaps a little bit overcooked, it remains technically very impressive and a fun bit of Spielbergian whimsy and wonder.

It almost feels unfair to rank The Adventures of Tintin quite so comparatively low because it is a great film and a very strong adventure, but it just doesn't quite have the same cultural impact or footprint as some of the movies that beat it here.

Spielberg had actually picked up the film rights to The Adventures of Tintin way back in 1983 and then reoptioned them in 2002. There was then a troubled early production, so it was delayed until 2011, with Jamie Bell replacing original star Thomas Brodie-Sangster. But Spielberg was always a self-confessed fan of Hergé's work, and The Adventures of Tintin draws from multiple stories with the kind of faithful commitment to the spirit of the originals that only a fan could really capture.

And despite this being motion-captured animation with an iconic character in its own right, it does rather feel like it could be a young Indiana Jones adventure. Spielberg uses the same thrilling storytelling approach, there are great set pieces, the character work is excellent, and it has that same confident swashbuckling feel as the Indiana Jones movies. There's also a great nostalgic element to it that really sells Spielberg's patented Amblin sense of wonder, and it's grown remarkably in charm over the years. Thankfully, we're finally about to get a new Tintin sequel from Peter Jackson after many years of trying.

Bafflingly rejected by critics when it was released, Hook was thankfully embraced more by audiences who looked on Spielberg's embrace of sentimentality more favorably than the professionals. It's an inventive take on the already very familiar story of Peter Pan, leaning into some patented Spielberg emotional existentialism at the same time, and the world-building of Neverland is just delightful.

Robin Williams offers a surprisingly restrained performance as the middle-aged Peter Banning, who has grown up and unthinkably forgotten his past in the magical world of Neverland, sparring across courtrooms rather than with real-life pirates. The rest of the young cast is great alongside Williams, and everybody's having a lot of fun. But the best performances are definitely Bob Hoskins as Smee and, of course, Dustin Hoffman as the delightfully theatrical and surprisingly nihilistic Captain Hook.

It might not be the most challenging or narratively complex movie that Spielberg has ever made, but the sense of wonder here is palpable, and it's exactly what a family adventure blockbuster should be.

At the time of its release, Temple of Doom tricked critics into believing that it might be too dark for its core audience, but over the years, the reception of the second Indiana Jones movies has only grown. It is absolutely darker than Raiders of the Lost Ark, but not to its detriment. Instead, there is an admirable refusal to speak down to the family audience who would have been drawn in by the first movie. It makes no apologies for the fact that it's a brilliantly imaginative adventure that has more grown-up elements alongside some goofy ones.

If there are criticisms, it's not quite as precise as Raiders of the Lost Ark, even if lots of people do vehemently back it as the best of the original trilogy. It is a wilder and more violent movie than the first, but it often gets forgotten how much sillier it is, in a good way. The addition of Short Round was also a very smart move to keep the levity and make sure that it wasn't too intense for younger audiences.

Meanwhile, the action sequences are fast-paced and actually rather relentless, and it feels more in line with the early movies Spielberg was paying tribute to, even if some critics saw its darker elements as a little challenging.

The critical reception to Temple of Doom's darkness may have been somewhat overblown, but Spielberg still listened to it, opting to go in a more lighthearted direction with 1989's The Last Crusade with a little more comedy thrown in. It is a fundamentally more charming movie, and a lot of that comes down to the brilliant decision to cast Sean Connery as Indiana Jones's father. The chemistry between Connery and Harrison Ford was excellent and helped explain some of Indy's more prickly character traits very well.

The Last Crusade feels like a living tribute to the lost B-movie era, has some excellent action sequences, and at times feels like the most swashbuckling of the trilogy. There is also an admirable attempt to get under the skin of Indiana Jones, which could have derailed the adventurous spirit of the story, but it all zips along very quickly. None of the journey to the heart of Indy's darkness really compromises that - if anything, it just enriches the character and allows for the interplay between Connery and Harrison Ford to take the stage it deserves.

While the Indiana Jones trilogy is one of the most definitive movie events of the 1980s, Raiders of the Lost Ark belongs to an entirely different era, offering a modern take on serial films that had been popular decades earlier. It was, of course, George Lucas's idea, but his decision to focus on Star Wars paved the way for Spielberg to take over and create a brain trust that also included Lawrence Kasdan, the scriptwriter. Remarkably, early polling revealed little audience interest, but it went on to be the highest-grossing film of the year, with audiences spellbound by its set pieces and Harrison Ford's immediately iconic performance as the whip-snapping archaeologist.

Raiders of the Lost Ark was instrumental in establishing the blueprint for later comic book movies because it was so inherently inspired by the childhood stories told in serial movies and comic books. It was also a huge part of establishing the identity of blockbuster movies and still feels like pure escapism even watching it now. It outstrips the other Indiana Jones movies, not just because of its novelty, but also because it has better villains. The story of the Nazi race to find the Ark of the Covenant is just slightly more compelling than the other MacGuffin-led stories.

Even beyond Ford's career-defining performance as Indiana Jones, the supporting characters are crucially strong enough to hold their own. Karen Allen's Marion Ravenwood offers spirited moxie alongside him, John Rhys Davies' Sallah basically set the model for all adventure movie sidekicks, and the villainous duo of Paul Freeman's René Belloq and Ronald Lacey's sadistic Gestapo agent Arnold Toht were brilliantly cartoonish in their villainy. It's still a joy to rewatch now, and every time you do, you're overcome with the wish for this franchise to continue on forever.

#3434. 'Ghost Accounts' Are Putting Your Security at Risk, but You Can Protect Yourself

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

In all the years you've been online, you've likely created more accounts than you can remember, whether to shop on a website you made one purchase from, sign up for a newsletter you've since stopped reading, or download apps for school or work that you no longer need.

These so-called "ghost accounts"—all the old, forgotten logins that are still active but not in use—could expose your data in the event of a breach, increasing the risk of your information being used in malicious ways. That's why it's important to go through the effort to find and delete dormant accounts. Here's how to get started.

As McAfee describes, ghost accounts may retain lots of sensitive data, such as your contact details (phone numbers, emails, and addresses), purchase histories, payment details, and passwords. While this doesn't mean your information is sure to be compromised, the more places it lives, the more opportunities there are for bad actors to get ahold of it.

You're less likely to be keeping tabs on activity in older accounts, which may also have weak or reused passwords that haven't been updated in years. If that company or service experiences a data breach, not only is your stored data there exposed, but that information (including your password) can be used to access other accounts using tactics like credential stuffing and phishing. This also increases the risk of identity theft, as threat actors can use your name, birth date, and other information to open fraudulent accounts.

Unfortunately, finding and removing forgotten accounts can be tedious. If you have a password manager, the easiest way to start is to audit older items as well as look at security reports that identify weak or reused passwords, as well as data breaches that have impacted your accounts. If you've saved credentials in your browser keychain, go through the same process to find dormant accounts.

The next place to look is in your email: Search for account confirmation and verification emails as well as password resets using keywords like "verify your email," "free trial," "welcome," "confirm your account," or "sign up." Add a date filter to narrow down older accounts. Do this across all of your email addresses.

Once you've found accounts you no longer use, the next step is to deactivate or delete them, which you may be able to do through the settings or by reaching out to customer support. At the very least, remove all identifying information and change the password, and if possible, update the address to a burner using your browser's or password manager's hide-my-email feature. If you no longer have access to an old account, that doesn't mean it's been deactivated and your information removed, so you may need to reach out to customer support to find out how to access and delete it.

#3432. Forget 'Bosch,' Netflix's 5-Part Detective Drama Is a Perfect Binge

Prime Video's Bosch was one of the most exciting police procedurals on television. For seven seasons, from 2014 to 2021, we got to follow along with Los Angeles Police Department Detective Harry Bosch (Titus Welliver) as he investigated some seriously fascinating cases. The series has inspired two spin-off shows, including the three-season Bosch: Legacy and Ballard starring Maggie Q. MGM+ will be capitalizing on Bosch's devoted fanbase with another spin-off, a prequel called Bosch: Start of Watch, which is set to arrive in January. If you're looking for more in the vein of Bosch, there's another compelling detective drama, and it's one you might not even know about.

There have been a lot of cop shows in the history of television. But few of them have been as well-made as Southland. The underrated series, which ran for five seasons from 2009 to 2013, is a captivating look at law enforcement in Los Angeles. The drama, created by Ann Biderman (Ray Donovan), is a brutally realistic portrayal of the many complicated aspects of working in the LAPD. We gain entry into this high-stakes world by following the story of several LAPD officers, including rookie Officer Ben Sherman (Ben McKenzie). Ben is brand-new to the force, and is completely in the dark about the danger he's just walked into. His training officer, John Cooper (Michael Cudlitz), tries to show him the ropes, but as a closeted gay man, John is desperate to keep his personal life hidden from his co-workers. We also meet two inspirational women in the LAPD: Detective Lydia Adams (Regina King, pre-Oscar win) and Officer Chickie Brown (Arija Bareikis), who are both facing an uphill battle to make their way in a male-dominated field. Each character provides valuable insight into the complex life of these public servants.

Unlike some other cop shows, Southland creates an altogether authentic picture of the LAPD. There are the typical car chases and fight sequences, but these moments of high-intensity action serve the storytelling in a realistic way. The drama explores everything from gang violence and corrupt cops to the somber mental health and addiction struggles the officers face. The gritty style of Southland ensures that none of the storylines ever feel cheesy or predictable. The series also digs into the lives of these characters, so that they become fully dimensional people. The writing allows the viewer to feel the depth of their sorrow and traumas, as well as to celebrate some of their wins. It's easy to feel drawn into the world of Southland from the very first scene, which means the series is perfect for a binge-watch as you'll want to zoom ahead to catch every twisty episode.

Before he was Dr. Abbot, Shawn Hatosy was Detective Sammy Bryant.

The writing in Southland ensures there are zero bad episodes, but one of the most remarkable elements of the series is its extraordinary cast. McKenzie is spot-on as the naive Ben, and his scenes with Cudlitz crackle with tense electricity. King is a perfect addition to the cast, and her performance as Lydia provides a certain grounded feeling to the series. Shawn Hatosy, who recently won an Emmy for his work in The Pitt, brings a necessary frantic energy to his role as Sammy Bryant, an officer who can't seem to get out of his own way. C. Thomas Howell is also a bright spot in the cast as Bill "Dewey" Dudek. Howell provides much of the comic relief for the otherwise tonally dark series. In Season 4, Lucy Liu joined the cast as Officer Jessica Tang, delivering a riveting performance. The entire cast serves as a strong foundation that allows the storytelling to flourish, even when the subject matter is incredibly heavy.

For a while, it seemed like Southland would have a short run. Despite a second season renewal, NBC decided to cancel the show after Season 1. Luckily, TNT swooped in, and aired several more seasons. In 2013, TNT announced that Southland would be cancelled after five seasons, with no reprise in sight. Despite the fact that the show could have carried on for much longer, there are still 43 brilliant episodes for you to binge as a Bosch replacement.

Southland is available to stream on Netflix in the U.S.

#3429. iPhone Duo is getting three new features in iOS 27.3

iOS 27.3 launches next month and includes several exciting changes for iPhone Duo, here’s what’s new for Apple’s foldable model.

Apple is granting iPhone Duo users one of their biggest feature requests: face unlock is coming with iOS 27.3.

Face unlock isn’t a full-fledged Face ID, and it doesn’t work for features like Apple Pay, but it is a convenient new option for unlocking your iPhone Duo just by looking at it. Per Apple:

Use the front camera, along with a recent Touch ID or passcode authentication, to quickly unlock iPhone Duo when it’s closed. Face recognition data never leaves your device.

If your iPhone Duo has gone unused for 45 minutes or more, face unlock won’t work and you’ll need to authenticate with Touch ID or your passcode. But for most users, that probably just means using Touch ID first thing in the morning, then relying on face unlock the rest of the day.

On a related note, you can also enable Attention Aware features in iOS 27.3. These are available whether you use the face unlock feature or not, but are limited to the outer display. Once enabled, they can automatically lower the volume of alarms and timers, keep the display from dimming, and more.

Read more: iOS 27.3 adds new face unlock feature for iPhone Duo

Reachability is available on other iPhone models to move onscreen content down vertically, closer to your thumb. But on iPhone Duo with iOS 27.3, Apple has a unique twist on the feature.

Instead of helping you reach content vertically, Reachability on iPhone Duo works horizontally.

If you’re using the outer screen and find that buttons or other UI elements are out of reach, you can swipe from the side to have onscreen content shift closer to your thumb.

You can always disable Reachability if you find yourself accidentally triggering it too often. But if one-handed iPhone Duo use gives you trouble, Reachability is a great new option to have.

Read more: iOS 27.3 introduces new iPhone Duo feature for one-handed use

What should happen when you close your iPhone Duo’s folding screen? Apple has found that users have different preferences. Some want the iPhone to stay unlocked for continued use, while others prefer that it automatically locks when closed.

In iOS 27.3, Apple adds a new setting so users can enable whichever behavior they prefer.

By default, iPhone Duo will work as it always has, staying unlocked after being closed. But inside Settings ⇾ Display & Brightness, iOS 27.3 provides the option of automatically locking upon being closed instead. You could achieve something similar before with Shortcuts, but now there’s a built-in setting too.

It’s not exactly a “new feature,” but iPhone Duo users will also find that the system keyboard has changed in iOS 27.3. Apple tweaked the outer display keyboard to push keys closer together and make one-handed use easier.

Here’s a comparison of the old and new keyboards via Beta Profiles on X:

iOS 27.3 beta tweaks iPhone Duo's outer display keyboard, with narrower keys and a slightly thinner, smaller font. pic.twitter.com/BDKCBZc52Z

#3427. Every Version of 'A Christmas Carol,' Ranked (and Where to Stream Them)

Charles Dickens’ A Christmas Carol is the greatest story about Christmas ever written—even better than the one with Mary and Joseph and the manger. The 1843 tale of a miser browbeaten by self-righteous ghosts is (probably) the most filmed story of all time. Dozens of cinematic adaptations of A Christmas Carol have been released in theaters and on TV since Scrooge; or Marley's Ghost came out in 1901. Hundreds or thousands if you count re-imaginings and very special episodes of sitcoms. But which version is the very best?

I've carefully considered every major theatrical and TV adaptation of A Christmas Carol and rated each in terms of holiday spirit, Dickensian whimsy, and Scrooge-osity to arrive at the definite, no-argument-possible best-to-worst list of Christmas Carols.

To rank Christmas Carols, you have to decide what A Christmas Carol is to you. My criteria for inclusion: It has to be full-length (at least around an hour long); it has to have been released widely, either in theaters, on network television, or through a larger streaming service, and it has to be fairly close to a direct adaptation—modernizations, re-imaginings, sequels, and that episode of The Six Million Dollar Man don’t count (sorry, Scrooged fans). Using those criteria, I’ve winnowed the Carols down to the 17 you see below, ranked from best to worst, along with where you can stream each one.

It's tough to pick a single adaptation of A Christmas Carol as the absolute best of all time, but the 1984 TV movie version starring George C. Scott is unassailable. Other versions do some things better, but this one does everything right—no mistakes. It stays close to the original text; it's perfectly produced; and it has a consistency of tone and vision that makes it the most balanced of all versions of the story. A Christmas Carol might not have the best Scrooge of all time, but George C. Scott's performance is a solid nine out of ten, and this version features the most adorable and pitiable Tiny Tim of all and the best Ghost of Christmas Present, played by Edward Woodward, who played the policeman in The Wicker Man.

Shot in the midst of the Great Depression, the first sound version of A Christmas Carol digs deeper into the despair and horror of the story than any other adaptation. It’s a bleak, German expressionist Christmas flick, and Seymour Hicks’ sickly, haunted portrayal of Ebenezer Scrooge fits the tone perfectly. Instead of delighting in his own crapulence, Hicks plays Scrooge like Satan in The Divine Comedy—he's not the ruler of Hell; he's its most tormented prisoner. Scrooge's miserliness is played as pathology. He wears dirty, torn clothing and shivers miserably while eating gruel because he can’t bring himself to burn a single scrap of coal. Even when he converts, it seems like a manic episode instead of Christmas spirit, suggesting this could be a story about an old man going mad.

Where to stream: Sadly, the version on free streaming services like Tubi and Plex is colorized, but you can watch it on YouTube in glorious black and white.

This big-budget musical take on the Yuletide classic turns Dickens up to 11. Scrooge is huge, a raucous, crowd-pleasing musical with hundreds of extras, elaborate sets, and a scenery-chewing central performance from Albert Finney to hold it all together. But Finney and company also manage to keep the emotional core of the story intact. The music is great, with memorable tunes like “I Hate People,” a song that Finney snarls instead of sings. Scrooge has the best ghosts of any version of A Christmas Carol, too—you can't beat the cheesy awesomeness of big-money 1970s special effects.

Before Hallmark devoted its corporate life to forgettable holiday-themed romantic comedies, it co-produced one of the best versions of A Christmas Carol ever made. This entire movie belongs to Patrick Stewart, whose nuanced, layered portrayal of Scrooge is the best that has ever been done. His "conversion" scene is so visceral and honest, it brought a tear to my eyes, even though I've seen the exact scene performed in at least 40 other movies, stage plays, and episodes of 1980s sitcoms. Sadly, the paucity of basic cable budgets in the 1990s results in some chintzy-looking sets and laughable special effects that mar an otherwise top-notch production.

Horror director Ti West's Carol adaptation muddies the moral clarity of Dickens' tale and suggests there's something deeply troubling beneath all the Victorian holiday catharsis. With a few exceptions, Ebenezer hits the familiar beats of A Christmas Carol: It delivers the crowd-pleasing rich-jerk-turns-good story moviegoers expect, but West layers in subtle hints along the way that suggest the floorboards are rotten, and if you dance with Christmas joy too hard, you'll fall into the dark basement below. Ebenezer seems to whisper to audiences, "How much does the conversion of one miserly wretch matter in the face of systemic injustice? And isn't he going to snap out of it when the fright wears off anyway?" Bonus: As you'd probably expect from a Ti West movie, the ghosts are genuinely scary.

I'm sticking A Muppet Christmas Carol randomly here on the list because you can't reasonably compare it to other versions of the story. The Muppet version is a thing unto itself. Like the Ol' Dirty Bastard, its style has no father. A Muppet Christmas Carol is absolutely delightful from start to finish, for children, grown-ups, cats, dogs, space aliens, and anything else you got. It shouldn't even work to set Michael Caine's serious portrayal of Ebenezer Scrooge against a supporting cast of puppets, but somehow it all seems natural.

Alastair Sim takes Ebenezer Scrooge on a real journey in this movie. In the first act, he plays Scrooge like Capitalism personified, an uncaring, amoral monument to pure acquisition. He seems like a Scrooge who'd scare away ghosts, but when Marley shows up dragging his trademark chains, Sim is instantly reduced to pop-eyed fear, like the single chink in his armor is the supernatural. Scrooge then regresses to a childlike, bashful figure as ghosts lead him to different visions, finally emerging from his symbolic death to his rebirth as a Christmas-obsessed guy who lives to serve others. This movie might be among the best of the genre, but an unnecessary subplot about Scrooge's business sandbags the movie through part of the second act.

Mr. Magoo's Christmas Carol was the first animated version of A Christmas Carol and the first animated holiday special ever shown on American TV. The main character, Mr. Magoo, was the star of a one-joke, limited-animation cartoon popular in the early 1960s about an old man who couldn’t see very well, so it’s surprising how carefully crafted and effective this version of A Christmas Carol is. It's weirdly meta too: Jim Backus voices Mr. Magoo, who is a (blind) actor performing as Scrooge in A Christmas Carol on Broadway, so the play is bookended with "this guy can't see!" bits. The songs are strange, memorable and funny (listen to "Razzleberry Dressing" above once and you'll never forget it), but the emotional core of the story remains surprisingly powerful. Jim Backus is amazing.

I'm breaking my own rule about not including shortened versions of the story because this animated Carol is that great. Its evocative, graceful, hand-drawn look belongs to animation legend Richard Williams and was inspired by the illustrations from the original version of A Christmas Carol. It's a cartoon, but it's not a kiddie cartoon, so the darkness of the ghosts isn't glossed over. Plus, Scrooge is voiced by Alastair Sim, reprising his role from 1951's Scrooge.

There's nothing wrong with this brightly lit, by-the-numbers take on A Christmas Carol, but it seems designed to appeal to as broad an audience as possible, so the rough edges of the story have been sanded off. The ghosts aren’t that scary. Scrooge isn’t that miserly, etc. It’s fine for a Christmas movie to be lighthearted fun, but the lowered stakes ultimately blunt the emotional resonance of the climax, leading to a mediocre Christmas Carol.

I'm including this version of A Christmas Carol because it's Lifehacker editor Meghan Walbert's favorite. Sorry, Meghan, but this flimsy 1970s TV movie adaptation hasn't aged well. Henry Winkler does a good job as Scrooge, and it's cool to see Burgess Meredith and other old-timey stars, but overall, this is a schmaltzy, plodding film that unwisely replaces a lot of Dickens' best writing with the work of 1970s TV hacks.

Where to stream it: Pluto, Tubi, Amazon Prime

I really wanted to like Disney’s A Christmas Carol. Robert Zemeckis is a great director and Jim Carrey is a force of nature, but I couldn't get through it. There might be a lot to recommend this version of the story, but using 2009’s technology to create realistic-looking characters was such a puzzling choice. The whole movie looks like a video game cutscene from a PS3 game, and I kept wanting to hit “A” to skip ahead to the gameplay.

It doesn't seem like the producers of this obscure 2012 straight-to-streaming feature had much money to work with, which is too bad. If they had, they might have been able to better realize some of the intriguing ideas behind this movie. It's a straight-up horror take on the tale, but it just isn't scary. Sadly, you can't carry a feature film on good intentions. Overall, a swing and a miss.

The animation in this 1997 musical cartoon version of A Christmas Carol is dated, pedestrian, and ugly. The songs are forgettable, and Scrooge has a pet bulldog for some reason. (The one good joke is that he named his dog "Debit.") It’s just not good, which is a shame, because the cast is overflowing with talent, including Tim Curry as Scrooge, Ed Asner, and Whoopi Goldberg.

This BBC drama goes for a philosophical, moody version of Scrooge, but it doesn’t come together. It’s dark, grim, and so ponderously self-serious that it collapses under its own weight. In an effort to present aspects of A Christmas Carol that haven't been seen before (like "How Marley got his chains"), A Christmas Carol rewrites the original text from the ground up, but it comes across like Dickens' first draft with a bad case of Surf Dracula.

The current state of Dickens adaptation is not good. Netflix's uninspired, sappy, CGI version of A Christmas Carol tries to tart the story up with slapstick, songs, and jokes, but it’s all cynical, lowest-common-denominator horseshit. The dialogue has been dumbed down and joked up. Scrooge has a silly dog for comic relief. They added scatological humor. Think about this: The minds behind Scrooge: A Christmas Carol read Dickens and concluded, “This story would be better with a wacky dog and fart jokes.”

A Christmas Carol is such a solid story, even a grade-school production of it can be fun to watch. But a cynical production of it is extra terrible, given the message of the story. This terrible ego project is a bottom-of-the-barrel Christmas Carol because it feels like a money grab. Kelsey Grammer sucks as Scrooge, mugging his way through a lightweight performance. Jason Alexander sucks as Marley. Jennifer Love Hewitt is, well, actually pretty good as Scrooge’s Christmas-past romantic interest. She is a rare bright spot in this dreary movie, however. Everything else is mid to terrible. It’s shot and lit like a TV show; the sets are bland and the songs forgettable. Overall, it has the cynical feeling of assembly-line, “let’s get this shit over with” TV production.

#3424. The Best Tech Deals From the Sam's Club Early Black Friday Sale

Retailers are churning out early Black Friday deals already, including the likes of Amazon, Best Buy, Walmart, and others. If you're waiting around for Friday, Nov. 27 to do all of your shopping, you might miss out on some deals and unnecessarily make the day more stressful than it needs to be. If you're a Sam's Club member, you have access to many early Black Friday deals worth checking out. I spent some time combing through their website and rounded up my favorite tech deals below.

The Bose SoundLink Flex SE is a portable Bluetooth speaker with an IP67 waterproof rating. The speaker even floats in the water, so you can bring it with you into the pool. While it doesn't offer full EQ customization in its companion app, the sound has rich bass depth and clear highs out of the box. It also features a speakerphone, allowing you to take calls and speak with it. It's light and portable, and the Bluetooth 5.3 supports multipoint connectivity and SBC, AAC, and aptX codecs. You can get the Bose 2nd Generation SoundLink Flex SE for $89 (originally $139).

Skullcandy makes fun speakers and headphones, although they're not designed for audiophiles (their sound signature is very bass-heavy). Their Skullcandy Stomp XL Max is their attempt at making a portable party speaker. It comes with two wireless mics, making it a great option for karaoke. It holds 12 hours of battery life (up to 20 hours with certain settings), has an IPX5 water resistance rating, and has LED lights that sync to the music. You can get it for $99 (originally $199).

Getting a soundbar can exponentially improve anyone's entertainment system, but a 5.1 system with rear speakers and a subwoofer takes it to the next level. The Samsung HW-Q65F 5.1 Channel Soundbar is $299 (originally $399), and it's a wireless setup that will keep the harmony of "too many cables" in the house. It supports Dolby Atmos and DTS Virtual:X to give you a 3D audio feel, and it has a dialogue feature that will let you hear the whispers.

Gaming monitors can get expensive quickly, but you can get decent options on a budget. A great example is the 31.5-inch MSi gaming monitor selling for $129 (originally $179). It has a 250Hz refresh rate and a 1ms response time to make gaming smoother. There's also AMD FreeSync Premium to get rid of tearing and stuttering.

These kinds of sales are always a good time to upgrade laptops. If you're looking for a powerful computer that is well-rounded, consider the 16-inch HP OmniBook 7 Flip going for $699 (originally $899). This laptop comes with an Intel Ultra 5 processor, 512GB of SSD, and 16GB of RAM (which, honestly, is the minimum anyone should be buying in 2026).

If you need a bigger screen, the 17.3-inch HP OmniBook 3 is a good choice for a bit less money. It comes with an Intel Core Ultra 7 processor, 512GB of SSD, and 12GB of RAM. Part of the bigger screen means a bigger keyboard, so if you deal with numbers a lot, you'd likely appreciate the numeric pad.

If you want your laptop strictly for gaming, the ASUS TUF F16 Gaming laptop is $1,149 (originally $1,399). With an Intel Core 7 processor and the RTX 5060 graphics card, you'll be well set up to tackle heavy games. It comes with a 165Hz refresh rate, Advanced Arc Flow fans and vents to keep your machine cool, and 16GB DDR5 RAM to keep your loads short.

Budget TVs get big discounts during Black Friday, and the 58-inch Vizio QLED TV is one of them. You can get one for $178 (originally $298), and it supports Dolby Vision HDR for better color and contrast. The operating system is the Vizio OS, but of course, you can always change it with a TV dongle if you prefer a different one.

If you prefer to splurge for a better QLED but still get a good deal, the 65-inch Samsung QN90H QLED TV at $1,197.99 (originally $1,497.99) is a great option. It upscales lower-resolution pictures to 4K with AI. It works for gaming with its 144Hz refresh rate, and because the operating system is Tizen OS, it comes with Samsung TV Plus, which brings over 2,700 free channels. The TV also comes with Dolby Atmos, so you can hear audio with a 3D effect as the audio follows objects around the display.

A 100-inch TV makes a statement: You take your entertainment system seriously. The 100-inch Vizio QLED TV is a budget-friendly option with a $300 discount, currently going for $1,198 (originally $1,498). This TV supports Dolby Vision HDR for more vivid images and has hundreds of free channels with the Vizio OS.

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

#3421. HBO’s ‘Harry Potter’ Officially Changes a Classic Book Moment in First Full Scene Release

For millions of Harry Potter fans, that iconic at Hogwarts is one of those moments that's practically impossible to forget. It's a sensory overload with the singing Sorting Hat, the Great Hall, hundreds of floating candles, and nothing short of a mountain of food per person. Chris Columbus brought the scene to life in 2001's Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone, and it's remained one of the most recognizable moments in the franchise ever since. Now, with HBO preparing to take audiences back to Hogwarts this Christmas, we're finally getting a proper look at how the new version compares.

HBO has officially released the first full scene from Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone, and despite the fact it's recognizable, it's also distinctly different from what's come before. The approximately 90-second clip shows Harry arriving in the Great Hall alongside Ron, with Albus Dumbledore preparing to begin the feast. One of the first differences comes when the students begin chanting Dumbledore's name, something that doesn't happen in J.K. Rowling's original novel. Harry then asks Ron whether Dumbledore is a little mad, whereas in the book he directs that question to Ron's older brother Percy.

However, the biggest addition comes when Dumbledore and Professor McGonagall share a private conversation about Harry, with McGonagall commenting on his resemblance to his father, James Potter. The exchange doesn't appear in the novel, which tells the banquet scene from Harry's perspective. It's the first look at how the series will start showing us different perspectives than that of the titular character.

The series is led by Dominic McLaughlin as Harry Potter, Arabella Stanton as Hermione Granger and Alastair Stout as Ron Weasley, alongside John Lithgow (Conclave) as Albus Dumbledore, Janet McTeer (Ozark) as Minerva McGonagall, Paapa Essiedu (I May Destroy You) as Severus Snape, Nick Frost (Shaun of the Dead) as Rubeus Hagrid, Lox Pratt (Lord of the Flies) as Draco Malfoy and Warwick Davis (Willow) as Filius Flitwick. Season 2 is already building its own impressive cast too, with Kit Harington (Game of Thrones) playing Gilderoy Lockhart, Lenny Rush (Doctor Who) voicing Dobby, Billy Barratt (Invasion) as Tom Riddle and Rafe Spall (Jurassic World: Fallen Kingdom) as Arthur Weasley.

The series is written and executive produced by Francesca Gardiner (Succession), with Mark Mylod (The Last of Us) directing multiple episodes. Rowling also serves as an executive producer alongside David Heyman, who produced the original film franchise.

Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone premieres on HBO and HBO Max on Christmas Day, December 25, 2026. Stay tuned to Collider for all the latest news and updates on the biggest and best movies and shows heading to your favorite streaming platforms soon.
