#3416. Why Do AI Posters All Look Like That?

You know “the look” by now. Every poster for a business or event has pictures of uncanny-looking people, buildings that don’t look right, and always that one font. But why? If generative AI is supposedly able to “think” and be “creative,” why do so many of its results come out looking exactly the same? The answer is complicated, and it has to do with what chatbots define as “thinking.”

At this point, gone are the days of chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini simply generating text immediately in response to a prompt. Some very fast models do, but most employ what’s known as “thinking models”, which are a bit of a misnomer. The “thinking” really just consists of generating a set of sub-prompts before executing the main one. And it’s in that hidden, generated text that most of the “choices” (to the extent that we can call the statistical output of an AI model a “choice”) occur that determine how a design looks.

To borrow a classic and implausible example, if you were to give an AI chatbot the instruction “Make a peanut butter and jelly sandwich,” it would start by generating step-by-step instructions on how to make the sandwich before trying to make one (if it could). Most of this happens invisibly in the background, and many proprietary chatbots won’t show you their in-process “thinking” prompts even if you ask.

In the case of an AI poster, it might break down “make a poster” into smaller steps such as “create a design brief for a poster.” To demonstrate this while doing some testing for this piece, I added additional prompts for ChatGPT to explain the “design briefs” it generated, which included details like layout, colors, and typography.

The problem is those instructions are still subject to the same flaws as any other AI-generated text. They can’t properly fact-check; they can’t walk into the real world and see the thing they’re describing; and they can hallucinate or fall back on stale formats that become easy to notice after a while.

For example, while testing, I had ChatGPT generate a poster for a Lifehacker-themed nightclub. In every case, the underlying brief it generated outlined some basic details, but occasionally it added things I hadn’t asked for. This included additional text, iconography, and in one case it even added the “design brief” explanation I had requested as the bottom half of the poster.

Those mistakes filter into the final product, when the brief is then fed into the image generator that ultimately makes the poster. In my case, ChatGPT showed me the underlying explanations for its reasoning (though even that could be different from what was actually sent to the image generator), but most people who use a chatbot for this task won’t see these factors before getting the final result.

While most chatbots won’t show you exactly what underlying “thinking” they use, most can be coaxed into describing the vague outlines of how they reached certain outcomes. And those descriptions provide some insight into why certain chatbots keep outputting similar results over and over. It doesn’t take long for some patterns to emerge. For example, any prompt to generate a poster for a nightclub almost invariably generated a brief that had specifications for a color palette including “electric purple,” “electric yellow,” and “electric pink.”

The reason for this should be pretty obvious: When the statistical model underlying LLMs needs to come up with an example for “colors for a nightclub poster,” the most obvious answers are neon, high-energy colors. Unless you know something about the specific club’s vibe (and write that out and feed it to the chatbot), the AI will have to fill in the gaps with something. And that something will be based on the same statistics it uses to predict any word.

This pattern of repetition was everywhere in all the design rationale ChatGPT gave me. Across multiple attempts to generate a Club Lifehacker poster, the generated design brief added an overarching “concept” that described the fictional club’s atmosphere as “high-energy” and “futuristic.” Every bot mentioned using images with the “silhouette” of either the DJ or a dancing crowd (often both). All the text had to be “bold” and “futuristic."

If there's one dead giveaway that a poster was made with AI, it's that one brush-stroke font that they all seem to use. Now, this is a bit more speculative, but I have a theory on where that specific design comes from. And it’s worth noting upfront that this seems to only apply to posters generated by ChatGPT specifically.

One of the most common factors I found in my design brief testing was the use of phrases like “brush lettering” or “brush script.” Brush lettering is a design term that refers to using any number of methods like markers, paint brushes, or brush pens to write text. In digital design, that can take the form of fonts that are designed to emulate the look of fancy, handwritten text.

In every test poster I created, however, ChatGPT seemed to take the phrase “brush lettering” rather literally. Every instance I encountered of a design brief that mentioned any kind of “brush” text generated an image with letters that looked as though they were created with a broad paint brush. A human designer would understand “brush lettering” to mean “something that looks handwritten," but ChatGPT didn’t seem capable of understanding the phrase as anything other than using an actual paint brush.

The generated posters aren’t even using a “font,” strictly speaking. (Often, letters that should be identical had slight variations.) The image generator part of the chatbot is still a diffusion model, so it can’t employ a vector-based font, per se. But the brush-style font is so common that its look surfaces in any statistical model.

This is an odd quirk of ChatGPT specifically, and it’s possible that it could change in the future. Especially if OpenAI intentionally tries to train this behavior out of its chatbot. However, it’s helpful to illustrate the underlying mechanism. The only way a chatbot can conceptualize design elements in a visual medium is to generate more specific text to feed to the image generator. And that text is just as prone to mistakes and blandness as any other AI model.

I’ve been examining this with a focus on the kinds of posters ChatGPT generates because they’re very common, but posters (or any AI-generated content) from other models might look different. Every model has its own tendencies. For example, a lot of vibecoded websites are made with Anthropic’s Claude, and you can often tell by the tiny text, buttons with rounded corners, and tile-based layouts.

To a certain extent, this is inevitable. While AI models are very different from humans and do not make “choices” in the same way people do, design elements still have to come from somewhere, and whether human or AI, it’s impossible to make these decisions in a vacuum. Humans will have preferences based on the things they like or emotionally resonate with, and AI models will have tendencies based on what their statistical model determines is the most appropriate output.

That means that an AI model’s “style” is naturally going to change over time. Even if a model improves or makes fewer mistakes, it’s impossible to ever change the fact that all ChatGPT images are made by ChatGPT. Whatever you generate with any particular model will have a lot in common with what everyone else who uses the same tool generates.

#3413. 9 Essential Movies to Watch Before 'The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth'

Ben Brewster is a filmmaker, critic, screenwriter, and actor whose work sits at the intersection of film culture, craft analysis, and storytelling.

He is a movie list contributing writer at Collider and a contributing writer for High on Films, where he covers contemporary cinema, independent film, and festival releases with an eye toward narrative structure, performance, and visual language.

Ben is an active film festival participant, having worked with Newport Film, the Nantucket Film Festival and as a screener for the Austin, Boston & Woodstock film festivals.  He brings to that work a programming instinct shaped by years of close engagement with independent and documentary cinema. This comes with a deep investment in the kinds of films that rarely find their way into the mainstream conversation without someone willing to advocate for them.

His background spans documentary and narrative filmmaking, film marketing, and production, including work with award-winning directors. This as well as developing his own indie production company, Lilac Creative Studio, through which he develops and produces original work across fiction and nonfiction forms.  His debut documentary, Diamond in the Rust, is an examination of economic redevelopment and displacement in the Queens area of New York City. The film was recently accepted to the Unisphere Film Festival, the Defense of Democracy Film Festival, and the Urbanite Arts & Film Festival. This would mark his first festival recognition as a director.  In addition to his writing and programming work, Ben hosts Beneath the Bloom, a film podcast exploring the work behind the scenes in cinema, and the struggles one can face to make a movie become a reality. The show reflects the same sensibility that runs through all of his work. A conviction that film is not merely entertainment but one of the most powerful tools human beings have for understanding each other.

Across mediums, his work is driven by a deep belief in film as a communal, transformative art form.

The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth arrives in IMAX theaters on November 25th for a two-week run, then streams on Netflix on December 23rd. Brad Pitt's Oscar-winning stuntman Cliff Booth is back, and he has traded Tarantino's direction for David Fincher's. Based on Tarantino's script, the story picks up in 1977, eight years after Once Upon a Time in Hollywood. It reunites Pitt and Fincher for the first time since The Curious Case of Benjamin Button in 2008, and also marks Netflix's first IMAX release.

Walking in cold is possible, but a little homework helps. The nine movies below follow three thematic lines, which are Tarantino's stunt world, Fincher's version of crime, and the Los Angeles detective tradition. Fincher has mentioned that one of the first questions was whether the script should be a movie or a series, which hints at how big the story is. Netflix describes the movie as Cliff doing odd jobs and dangerous favors with the fairy tale of Hollywood being long over. Elizabeth Debicki, Scott Caan, Carla Gugino, Yahya Abdul-Mateen II, Peter Weller, and Timothy Olyphant lead the stacked supporting cast.

A note on how this list works. I picked movies that shape the tone, the setting, or the style of Fincher's latest, and ranked them based on how useful and rewatchable they are as preparation. Once Upon a Time in Hollywood is the only direct prerequisite. The others are optional, but each enriches the dynamic 1970s Los Angeles period piece setting that The Further Mis-Adeventures of Cliff Booth lives in. Filming took place in the second half of 2025, and Tarantino's novelization of his new story arrives from HarperCollins on December 8th. Spoilers stay light, though a few key moments come up.

Death Proof was half of the 2007 Grindhouse double feature, paired with Robert Rodriguez's Planet Terror. Kurt Russell stars as Stuntman Mike, a scarred former stunt performer who hunts young women with his reinforced "death proof" car. Tarantino splits the story in two, with the first half in Austin and the second half in Tennessee on the backdrop of a 1970s car chase movie aesthetic. The movie fakes the look of a worn-out print and even weaves in a missing reel. Stuntwoman Zoë Bell plays herself in the second half, spending part of a chase strapped to a hood of a Dodge Challenger.

Rosario Dawson, Tracie Thoms, Rose McGowan, Mary Elizabeth Winstead, and Vanessa Ferlito round out the cast. Death Proof was a box office disappointment and critics split on its long, talky stretches. It has since found a bit of a following, mostly for its car chase and Russell's grinning menace. It matters here because Cliff Booth lives in that same stunt world, and both Bell and Russell turn up again in Once Upon a Time in Hollywood. Tarantino pays tribute to stunt performers and the people who risk their bones for a shot. Stuntman Mike shows the dark side of that world, which makes him a useful contrast to Cliff Booth.

Richard Rush's The Stuntman stars Peter O'Toole as Eli Cross, a flamboyant, godlike film director. He hires a fugitive as a stunt double, Cameron (Steve Railsback), a Vietnam veteran. Cameron accidentally causes the death of the original stuntman and Eli offers to hide him in plain sight. The Stuntman has to be the strangest film on this list and it begins with its own chase scene.

Rush mixes the film's mood between comedy, thriller and satire, which netted it three Oscar nominations. Barbara Hershey plays the star of the movie, and O'Toole was nominated for his role. O'Toole plays Eli with huge, theatrical charm, and he treats the set like his own personal kingdom. It was released to little fanfare but has built a cult following over the decades. The movie portrays how dangerous movie stunt work can be, and how directors can manipulate people, risking their lives. A veteran with a shady past who finds work as a stuntman echoes and exudes Cliff Booth energy.

Before there was Madden, Rudy runs through the tunnel, Boobie Miles blows out a knee, and a blimp circles the Super Bowl.

Se7en drops two cops into a rain-soaked city and ties their case to a killer who stages murders around the seven deadly sins. From director David Fincher, the story follows two detectives, the veteran William Somerset (Morgan Freeman) days from retirement and the hot-headed newcomer David Mills (Brad Pitt). Gwyneth Paltrow plays Mill's wife, Tracy, and Kevin Spacey enters late as John Doe. Howard Shore's score adds a mournful eeriness along with Darius Khondji, who shot the project in beautiful dark and grimy tones.

Fincher's second feature and initial collaboration with Pitt grossed more than $327 million worldwide and made him into the big name hit director he is today. Cliff Booth marks their fourth film together, and Se7en is the best place to see their rapport. Pitt plays Mills with an impulsive, volatile energy, which is a sharp contrast to Cliff's laid-back aura. The climax is among the most talked about endings in thriller history, and Fincher builds it up with a methodical discipline.

Tony Scott directed True Romance from a script by Quentin Tarantino, who sold it to help fund Reservoir Dogs. The movie follows the life of a comic book store clerk named Clarence (Christian Slater) and Alabama, a call-girl he falls for played by Patricia Arquette. Clarence steals a suitcase of cocaine from her pimp, and the young couple heads to Los Angeles to sell it. Dennis Hopper plays Clarence's father, and he shares a legendary scene with Christopher Walken. Gary Oldman, Val Kilmer, Samuel L. Jackson, James Gandolfini and Brad Pitt fill small but memorable roles.

Hans Zimmer's score gives the violent love story a dreamy rhythm. Pitt's Floyd is a stoned roommate who barely leaves the couch. Scott softened Tarantino's original ending, and the movie leans more romantic than the script, providing a warmer glow. Seeing someone else direct a Tarantino script is a useful preview of the Fincher collaboration. Tarantino's dialogue sparkles, and Scott's glossy visuals keep it moving.

Doc Sportello, played by Joaquin Phoenix, is a shaggy private eye in 1970 Los Angeles who tends to smoke more than he does investigate. Paul Thomas Anderson adapted Thomas Pynchon's 2009 novel into Inherent Vice, a stoned detective story. Anderson's plot focuses on a missing real estate developer, a vanished ex-girlfriend, and a shadowy group called the Golden Fang. Josh Brolin is Bigfoot Bjornsen, a crew-cut cop who bullies and torments Doc. Owen Wilson, Reese Witherspoon, Benicio del Toro, Martin Short and Jena Malone appear in the sprawling ensemble. Joanna Newsom narrates, giving the movie a dreamy voice.

Johnny Greenwood produced and composed the score, and Robert Elswit shot the movie in warm hues and a hazy glow. Inherent Vice earned Oscar nominations for Adapted Screenplay and Costume Design. The narrative takes place just after the Manson murders, and the paranoia in the air feels close to the mood of 1969 Hollywood. Taking place just one year after Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, the laid-back mood fits for a story about odd jobs and dangerous favors. Critics were divided on the plot, which is deliberately tangled and complex, but many loved the atmosphere. It plays like a hangout movie with a mystery buried inside.

Robert Altman's The Long Goodbye reimagines Raymond Chandler's detective Philip Marlowe as a mumbling, chain-smoking drifter in 1973 Los Angeles. Elliot Gould is the lead detective — playing him with a shrug, a cat, and a shaky grip on the plot as though he woke up in the wrong decade. Leigh Brackett wrote the script, adapting Chandler's 1953 novel. Nina van Pallandt, Sterling Hayden, Mark Rydell, and Henry Gibson give vivid supporting turns, and Arnold Schwarzenegger has a small, uncredited role as a thug.

Marlowe's loyalty to his friend Terry Lennox drives the narrative, and Altman treats the mystery as background noise. Vilmos Zsigmond's roaming camera gives The Long Goodbye this loose kind of floating look. A repeated tune plays throughout the movie in different arrangements, from a doorbell chime to a mariachi band. The movie divided critics upon release and is now considered a landmark of 1970s neo-noir. Its shaggy-esque tone is a clear ancestor to Inherent Vice, and to the hangout feel of Once Upon a Time in Hollywood. Gould's Marlowe never loses his sense of humor, even when the world turns cruel.

Chinatown stars Jack Nicholson as J.J. Gittes, a private detective in 1937 Los Angeles. He's hired for a rather simple case, to follow a man accused of infidelity, but it rapidly unravels into a conspiracy about water and land that reaches the city's richest families. Faye Dunaway plays Evelyn Mulwray, a woman with secrets, and John Huston is Noah Cross, the powerful man behind the whole scheme. Robert Towne's script won the Oscar for Best Original Screenplay. Jerry Goldsmith wrote the trumpet-drenched score in about 10 days. Nicholson brings an air of dry wit and growing sense of fear.

Roman Polanski directed, and he also plays the small man who slits Gittes's nose. Polanski was married to Sharon Tate, who was murdered in 1969, and links Chinatown to Once Upon a Time in Hollywood. His 1977 arrest in Los Angeles also complicates the movie's legacy. Chinatown netted 11 Oscar nominations and its ending is considered among the bleakest in Hollywood history. The orange groves and dusty offices of the Los Angeles of Chinatown still shape how modern filmmakers picture the city.

Once Upon a Time in Hollywood introduces Cliff Booth as the longtime stunt double and driver for television actor Rick Dalton, played by Leonardo DiCaprio. Pitt plays Cliff, a WWII veteran who lives in a trailer with his dog Brandy and handles Rick's chores. Tarantino sets the story in Los Angeles in 1969, as the Manson family circles the edges of Hollywood. Margot Robbie plays Sharon Tate, who lives next door to Rick. Tarantino fills the movie with period detail, from radio jingles to television Westerns.

The movie netted 10 Oscar nominations and grossed more than $370 million worldwide. Pitt won the Oscar for Best Supporting Actor as Cliff, and the movie also won for Production Design. Cliff's calm, deadpan style makes him one of Tarantino's most beloved characters. His visit to Spahn Ranch and the fight scene with Bruce Lee are two of the more memorable sequences in Tarantino's entire filmography. A rumor that Cliff killed his wife hangs over him, and Tarantino never confirms it. The ending rewrites history in a way that gives the movie its fairy-tale feel. Netflix says the sequel opens eight years later, in a Hollywood where the fairy tale is long over.

Zodiac shows exactly how David Fincher depicts California in the 1970s. Jake Gyllenhaal is Robert Graysmith, a newspaper cartoonist consumed by the riddles of the Zodiac Killer case. Fincher traces the story across multiple decades in the San Francisco Bay Area. Mark Ruffalo plays inspector Dave Toschi, Robert Downey Jr. is reporter Paul Avery, and Anthony Edwards, Brian Cox, and Chloë Sevigny fill out the ensemble. James Vanderbilt (The Nuremburg Trials) wrote the script directly off of Graysmith's books and Fincher shot it digitally, recreating the era with his textbook precision and attention to detail.

Fincher stages the cab murder and the Lake Berryessa attack with chilling emotional restraint. He hones in on how obsession can wear people down and have lasting effects on their lives. A basement scene late in the movie is one of the most unnerving he has directed. Zodiac was not a hit in 2007, but it has since been reappraised, and has found its place on the New York Times list of the best movies of the 21st century. The patient camera, muted colors, and exceptional precise period detail point toward what Fincher might do with 1977 Los Angeles.

#3412. The Out-of-Touch Adults' Guide to Kid Culture: Looksmaxxing With Dangerous Drugs

A weekly deep dive into the current trends, slang, and viral videos of youth culture in terms that even the squarest can understand.

This week's column is bleak. First, there's the looksmaxxing trend where teenagers are taking dangerous chemicals to correct perceived physical shortcomings. Then there are the AI job interviewers. Depressing, but at least some young people are having a little fun with their dystopian hellscape.

You can judge a generation by the illegal drugs it pioneers. In the 1960s, hippies smoked weed and dropped acid to expand their consciousness; the yuppies of the go-go '80s fueled their drive to acquire with Colombian cocaine; but kids today don’t want to go deeper or work harder. They have a smaller, sadder goal: They take drugs to look better. The substance of choice for a growing number of teenage boys are steroids, peptides, and other exotic chemicals designed to enhance appearance.

Would-be muscle-men have been injecting themselves with black market ‘rhoids since the Eisenhower administration, but that was a small cult of adult weirdos with a specific goal. In 2026, kids are into it, and they aren’t using steroids to win a $500 prize in the Mr. Topeka contest; they’re using unapproved research chemicals to looksmaxx. Looksmaxxing is an online movement of young men trying to maximize their physical appearance. Teenagers are taking the normal desire to look their best to dangerous, pathological levels. Driven by a combination of undiagnosed body dysmorphia and relentless social media algorithms that turn amoral “red pill” kooks into gurus, teenage boys are ingesting a panoply of exotic and dangerous compounds in a quest to fix the angle of their jawlines, change their skin tone, lose weight, grow taller, and otherwise “correct” perceived physical problems.

In the "good old days" of steroid abuse, people generally stuck to abusing anabolic-androgenic steroids that had at least been tested for decades. Teens today are buying SARMs (Selective Androgen Receptor Modulators) and synthetic peptides marked "not for human consumption" from shady laboratories online. Steroids primarily affect the muscles, but many of these newer substances target different biological systems. A recent Rolling Stone article reports that kids are “heightmaxxing” by swallowing erdafitinib, a drug that treats advanced urothelial cancer, because the drug is known to trigger growth spurts (that can result in a curvature of the spine and other nasty side effects). They’re also trying MK-677 to get taller, an experimental growth hormone secretagogue that carries the risk of insulin resistance, water retention, and high blood pressure. Others are injecting Melanotan II, a synthetic peptide that forces a long-lasting deep tan, with side effects of extreme nausea and the sudden, aggressive darkening of moles. (And they're doing steroids too.)

In the looksmaxxing community, softmaxxing is doing generally-considered-acceptable things to look better, like getting enough sleep, exercising regularly, and eating a balanced diet. Hardmaxxing is taking more extreme measures like plastic surgery, smashing your face with a hammer, or taking experimental drugs.

In the bodybuilding and looksmaxxing community, “natty” refers to a natural, non-steroid-enhanced physique.

Here's something more lighthearted than the growing popularity of illicit self-esteem chemicals: the bicep heart and waist heart trends. The Bicep heart came first. Thirst trap videos started appearing on Instagram and TikTok in October in which dudes make a heart with their hand and bicep. Then people started posting variations where they frame the shot with someone they love inside the heart. The bicep heart quickly led to women posting the waist heart.

Okay. So maybe it's not that lighthearted of a trend. While there are some videos of dudes with skinny arms doing the bicep heart, it's mostly jacked dudes. And the waist heart doesn't seem like it would work at all unless you are a specific shape, as this video illustrates. So maybe this isn't a silly meme but an illustration of how young people are inundated with content that can trigger feelings of physical unworthiness, even if they're just looking for silly memes.

As if searching for a job wasn't alienating and horrible enough, some companies have begun using AI agents to conduct interviews. Begging a robot to let you work in a cubicle farm is as dystopian as anything Phillip K. Dick ever imagined, but don't count humanity out yet. Young people are sticking a finger in the eye of the machine by creating comedy videos that focus on trolling these AI job interviewers. They're hilarious because AI is the ultimate straight person in a comedy team, and the raw compute costs to run these interviews means corporate money is burning with each second of wasted time. Here are some of the top creators in the genre.

Bo Bongo: This YouTuber shows up to AI interviews shirtless but insists he's wearing a "corporate tube top," then focuses on daring the interviewer to notice he's doing things like smoking a cigarette or eating a rotisserie chicken.

Cam Whitt likes to wind up AI by arguing, interrupting, telling outrageous lies, and asking the dumbest questions imaginable, like, "When does the interview actually start?" and "How do I figure out what my name is?"

Grahamn Raabe: Among this YouTuber's schticks is speaking only in nonsense, like describing his professional background as "freight cadence, walnut, a little bit of Richard, spruce wood—six years of spruce wood."

Nick Reid: Is so obnoxious, he seems to make the AI furious at him, even though it's a computer without emotions. Two thumbs up!

#3411. ChatGPT app gains enhanced Live Dictation streaming without 10-minute limit

ChatGPT dictation is getting a boost today. OpenAI has updated the speech-to-text feature with Live Dictation that improves both speed and reliability. The enhanced dictation update also removes the 10-minute limit.

“Dictation in ChatGPT is getting faster and more reliable,” OpenAI announced on X.

“With Live Dictation, your speech turns into text as you talk, so you spend less time waiting for your message to finish transcribing,” the company continued.

Atty Eleti, who works on voice features at OpenAI, added that the 10-minute dictation limit has also been removed as part of the dictation streaming upgrade.

More details from today’s app update release notes below:

Dictation in ChatGPT is getting faster and more reliable.

With Live Dictation, your speech turns into text as you talk, so you spend less time waiting for your message to finish transcribing. Tap or click on the waveform to show or hide text as you go. We’ve also removed the 10-minute recording limit.

Live Dictation is rolling out globally to all ChatGPT plans on iOS, Android, web, and the desktop app.
